title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Why this book
Macroeconomics begins with facts. Before we write down a model of economic growth, we want to know how fast living standards have risen, and why some countries are so much richer than others. Before we write down a model of recessions, we want to know how output, unemployment and inflation move together when the economy turns down. Models are our best attempt to explain these facts, and the facts tell us which models deserve our attention.
This book is built on that idea, in two steps. First, you use data science to find the facts: you download, plot and explore real macroeconomic data, and you decide for yourself what pattern the data show. Second, you use macroeconomic models to explain them: you move sliders, change parameters and edit the Python code of each model, and you check how well it accounts for the facts you found. Each chapter is an interactive notebook that you can read on this website or run in Google Colab, with nothing to install.
crumbs: Preface

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Stylized facts: where models begin
A stylized fact is a broad regularity that holds across many countries or over long periods of time. It is “stylized” because it leaves out details and exceptions to keep the essential pattern. Not every year or every country fits it exactly, but the pattern is strong enough that a good theory should be able to explain it.
The term comes from the Cambridge economist Nicholas Kaldor. In a 1961 essay on capital accumulation and economic growth, Kaldor argued that theory should start from a summary of the facts rather than from convenient assumptions, and he listed six stylized facts of growth:

Output per worker grows at a roughly constant rate over long periods.
Capital per worker also grows over time.
The rate of return on capital is roughly constant.
The ratio of capital to output is roughly constant.
The shares of labor and capital in national income are roughly constant.
The growth rate of output per worker differs substantially across countries.

These facts set the agenda for growth theory. The Solow model of Chapters 5 and 6, once it includes technological progress, reproduces the first five on its balanced growth path, while the sixth pushed economists to ask why countries differ so much (Chapters 3 to 6).
Stylized facts are not carved in stone, however. They are summaries of data, and new data can revise them. Jones (Chapter 2) notes that labor’s share of income, long described as “about two-thirds,” has drifted down since around 1970. In the Chapter 2 notebook you check this yourself with the latest U.S. national accounts: labor earned 0.65 of income on average from 1950 to 2025, close to two-thirds, but its share has been below 0.60 since 2022. Is the old fact still a fact? The data alone do not settle it, but they tell you exactly which question to ask.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
section: From data to facts: the data-science step
text:
From data to facts: the data-science step
Charles I. Jones’s Macroeconomics stands out among intermediate textbooks for the weight it gives to data: its models are judged by how well they account for the figures of real economies that fill its chapters. This book takes that approach one step further: instead of reading the facts from a printed figure, you derive them yourself.
Every data figure in this book is interactive, and every one is built from public data, usually updated to the latest available year. You can:

Explore the figures. Hover over any point to read its value, zoom into a period, and press play to watch countries move over time.
Change the question. Switch countries, years and variables with simple widgets, or with a one-line change in the code. Does the fact you see for the United States also hold for Japan, Brazil or Nigeria? Does it survive if the sample starts in 1990 instead of 1960?
Get fresh data. Appendix B shows how to download data directly from FRED, the World Bank, the IMF, the ECB, Eurostat, the OECD, the Penn World Table, the Maddison Project and Our World in Data, so your facts are as current as the data.
Go further with AI. Colab includes Gemini, an AI assistant that can explain a line of code, fix an error or write a new plot from a request in plain language. Other assistants, such as Claude or ChatGPT, work just as well. Use them freely, but always check what they produce: read the code and make sure the numbers make sense. An AI assistant can write code that runs and still answers the wrong question.

The aim is not to replace the textbook’s facts, but to make you comfortable asking the data a question and judging the answer, which is what macroeconomists do every day.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
section: From facts to models: the modeling step
text:
From facts to models: the modeling step
Once you have a fact, you want to know why it holds. That is the job of a model. The models in this book are motivated by the ones in Jones: the production model, the Solow model and the Romer model of ideas for the long run; the IS curve, monetary policy, the Phillips curve and the AS/AD framework for the short run; and models of consumption, investment, government budgets, trade and exchange rates in the later chapters. Here, however, every model is something you can operate:

On this website, each model figure has a slider. Move it to see how the outcome changes when a parameter changes.
In Colab, each model figure gets live sliders and buttons that solve the model again as you move them.
In the code, each model is written out in a few lines of plain Python, right next to its figure. Change a parameter value, add a shock or replace an equation, and see what happens. This is where you can go beyond the textbook.

Then you close the loop and put the model next to the data. Which facts does the model explain? Which does it miss? A model that misses an important fact is not a failure: it is the reason for the next chapter. The Solow model, for example, explains much of why some countries are rich and others poor, but on its own it cannot explain why growth continues decade after decade. That gap is what the economics of ideas in Chapter 6 fills.

section: A companion to Jones, not a substitute
text:
A companion to Jones, not a substitute
This book is an interactive data-science companion to Charles I. Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th edition (W. W. Norton). Its 21 chapters have the same titles and follow the same sequence as the textbook’s, so you can work through the two side by side. I recommend reading a chapter of Jones first, for the economic reasoning and the full discussion, and then opening the matching notebook to work with the data and the models. The notebooks do not repeat the textbook’s explanations, and they are not a substitute for it.
This book is independent: it is not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or the publisher of the textbook. Every figure is an original adaptation, drawn with the book’s own code. Data figures are inspired by the textbook’s figures and rebuilt from public data, usually updated to the latest year and extended to other countries. Model figures are adapted from the textbook’s diagrams, with their own parameter values, layout and interactive controls. None is a copy of an original figure. A Sources note directly below every figure names the textbook figure that inspired it and links to the data sources, so you can open them and explore the data yourself.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Who this book is for

Undergraduate students in intermediate macroeconomics, who want to see the ideas of the course at work in real data and learn practical Python along the way.
Self-learners, who want a hands-on path through macroeconomics at their own pace, with no software to install.
Data-science learners, who know some Python and want meaningful economic questions to apply it to.
Macroeconomists, who know the theory and want to learn Python for data science with models they already know.

No programming experience is assumed. Appendix A is a guided tour of Colab, Python and the data science libraries used in the book, and Appendix C reviews the math, with Python code for each calculation.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
How the book is organized
Like Jones, the book follows the three features of one famous graph, U.S. GDP per person since 1870: a long-run upward trend, short-run fluctuations around it, and the question of what the future holds.

Preliminaries (Chapters 1–2): what macroeconomics studies and how we measure the macroeconomy.
The long run (Chapters 3–8): economic growth, production, the Solow model, ideas, the labor market and inflation.
The short run (Chapters 9–15): economic fluctuations, the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic, the IS curve, monetary policy and the Phillips curve, the AS/AD framework, financial crises and DSGE models.
Applications and microfoundations (Chapters 16–20): consumption, investment, the government, international trade and exchange rates.
Conclusion (Chapter 21): parting thoughts on what macroeconomics has learned and what remains open.
Appendices A–C: Colab and Python, live access to macroeconomic data, and a math review.

Every chapter has the same shape. A Model overview builds the chapter’s main model step by step, from its assumptions to its solution and predictions, and ends with the model in code. Thematic sections then work through the chapter’s figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, …), each with a goal, the code that draws it, and a “What to notice” summary. Your turn tasks, with hints, ask you to change the data or the model and interpret the result. The Concluding remarks sum up what the data showed and what the models explained.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, …); the next cell builds those menus.


Show the helper code
# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table (country, x, y), leaving out the countries in skip."""
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name, mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' traces hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them (G7, a region, ...).

    The traces already in fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and slider steps only switch those."""
    n = len(fig.data)
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update", args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig




Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website's one-country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value (e.g. per country)."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Model overview
Macroeconomics asks big questions: why some countries are so much richer than others, why whole economies sometimes shrink, and why prices sometimes rise quickly. To answer them, economists first collect the facts and then build a model: a simplified economy written as a few equations. We feed the model some numbers that we choose, and it tells us the outcomes we want to explain.
This first chapter uses the smallest possible model, supply and demand in the labor market, to show how that works. Below we write its two equations, solve them for the wage and the number of hours worked, and turn them into Python functions. The sections that follow first look at the big facts with real data, then come back to these functions to explain what a model is and to run experiments with it.
Here is the model. Workers supply hours of work \(L^s\), and they offer more hours when the wage \(w\) is higher. Firms demand hours of work \(L^d\), and they hire fewer hours when the wage is higher. In the textbook’s worked exercise both relations are straight lines:
\[L^s = \bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} \qquad\qquad L^d = \bar{f} - w\]
A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number the model builder chooses:

\(\bar{a}\) is the slope of labor supply: the extra hours offered when the wage rises by one dollar;
\(\bar{\ell}\) is the number of hours people would work even at a zero wage;
\(\bar{f}\) is the number of hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, a measure of its capacity.

In the code we simply write a, l and f. The wage \(w\) and employment \(L\) are the endogenous variables: the model determines them. The labor market is in equilibrium when supply equals demand, \(\bar{a}w + \bar{\ell} = \bar{f} - w\). Solving this one equation gives
\[w^* = \frac{\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}} \qquad\qquad L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\]
With the textbook’s numbers (\(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\), \(\bar{f} = 60\)), \(2w + 30 = 60 - w\), so \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\).

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma.


def labor_supply(w, a=2.0, l=30.0):
    """Hours of work offered at the wage w: L^s = a w + l   (Exercise 5)."""
    return a * w + l


def labor_demand(w, f=60.0):
    """Hours of work the firm wants to hire at the wage w: L^d = f - w   (Exercise 5)."""
    return f - w


def equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """The wage and employment at which supply equals demand: w* = (f - l) / (1 + a), L* = f - w*."""
    w_star = (f - l) / (1 + a)
    L_star = labor_demand(w_star, f)
    return w_star, L_star

Let us check the functions against the textbook’s answer.

Python note. w_star, L_star = equilibrium() stores the two results of the function in two variables. An f-string such as f"w* = {w_star:.1f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1f means “show one decimal”.


w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
print(f"Equilibrium wage       w* = {w_star:.1f}")
print(f"Equilibrium employment L* = {L_star:.1f}")
print(f"At w*, supply = {labor_supply(w_star):.1f} and demand = {labor_demand(w_star):.1f}: the market clears")

Equilibrium wage       w* = 10.0
Equilibrium employment L* = 50.0
At w*, supply = 50.0 and demand = 50.0: the market clears

text:
Income over time and across countries
The first big fact of macroeconomics is how unequal incomes are, both across countries and across time. We compare GDP per person for six economies and for many more.

Fig. 1: GDP per person in six countries
Goal. Document the first big fact of macroeconomics: income differs enormously across countries and over time.
The data come from the Maddison Project, which estimates GDP per person for every country over long periods. GDP (gross domestic product) is the overall income of a country; Chapter 2 explains how it is measured. All values are in 2022 dollars, so they can be compared across years.

Before we use a new file, we check that it agrees with the one we trust. For the six countries at the benchmark years, the two files should hold exactly the same numbers.

Python note. .isin(list) is True for the rows whose value is in the list. .merge(other, on=[...]) joins two tables, matching rows with the same year and country; columns with the same name get the endings _x and _y.

Every country keeps the same color in every figure. The textbook’s countries get fixed colors of our palette, and each of the other countries one of 24 distinct colors.

Python note. for i, name in enumerate(...) hands over each name together with its position i (0, 1, 2, …). i % 24 is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24 colors repeat in turn. if name not in COLORS: skips the names that already have a color.


COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "United Kingdom": TEAL, "Japan": GREEN, "Argentina": "#5aa0d8",
          "South Africa": "#0b4f47", "China": "#e0a33b", "Euro area": "#7b5ea7", "Europe": "#7b5ea7"}
OTHER = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24                 # 24 distinct colors for the other countries
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    if name not in COLORS:
        COLORS[name] = OTHER[i % len(OTHER)]

The textbook draws this figure on a ratio scale: each step up the vertical axis doubles the value (1,000, 2,000, 4,000, …). Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a country growing at a steady rate draws a straight line. Chapter 3 explains ratio scales in detail.

Python note. px.line draws one line per value of color=, and color_discrete_map=COLORS fixes each country’s color. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, and tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis (Plotly’s own labels are hard to read on a ratio scale). On a ratio scale, the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(800). The if ... else blocks run one branch or the other: here they widen the axis, in one step, when a chosen country is very poor or very rich, and x if condition else y picks x when the condition is true. set(chosen) - set(data.country) keeps the chosen names that have no data, and ", ".join(missing) writes them in one line, separated by commas.


BOOK = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Japan", "Argentina", "South Africa", "China")
TICKS = [500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000]


def gdp_per_person(scale="ratio", chosen=BOOK):
    """Fig. 1.1: GDP per person at the textbook's benchmark years, 1870-2022 (2022 dollars)."""
    data = on_benchmarks[on_benchmarks.country.isin(chosen)]
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    title = "2022: U.S. income per person 5× South Africa's; China's up 24-fold since 1950"
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", hover_name="country", markers=True,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"), color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  title=title, labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    low = 800 if data.gdppc.min() >= 800 else 400              # a very poor country: one step lower
    high = 90000 if data.gdppc.max() <= 90000 else 250000      # a very rich country: one step higher
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=TICKS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high - 10000])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2027])
    return fig

What to notice.

In every year, the richest of the six countries has several times the income of the poorest. In 2022 the United States leads and South Africa is last.
The U.K. was richer than the United States in 1870 and 1890; by 1900 the United States was ahead.
Japan’s income fell between 1929 and 1950 (World War II) and then rose very fast: it passed South Africa in the 1950s and Argentina in the 1960s. China was almost flat until 1950 and has grown fast since, passing Argentina by 2020.
Switch to the linear scale: the lines for poorer countries are squeezed near zero, and the early growth of every country becomes invisible. That is why the textbook uses a ratio scale.
Add South Korea: with 1,288 dollars per person in 1950 it was poorer than Japan was in 1870. It grew so fast that by 2020 it had passed Japan. Many countries have no estimate before 1950, so their lines start there.

Ratios differ a lot across countries, from below 30 percent (e.g. Yemen) to above 80 percent (e.g. Tanzania, Qatar). Low ratios often mean that few women work for pay; very high ones often mean that people cannot afford not to work. The chart below draws the chosen economies. The vertical axis runs from −5 to 25 percent, and it is widened in steps (to 50, 100, … percent) when a chosen country had higher inflation. add_hline draws a horizontal line, here a dashed zero line: below it, prices fall (deflation).

Python note. for top in [...]: tries the steps in order, and break leaves the loop at the first step that is high enough. data.inflation.idxmax() is the row label of the highest inflation, and data.loc[row] reads that row.


BOOK_INFLATION = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Euro area", "Japan")


def inflation_chart(chosen=BOOK_INFLATION):
    """Fig. 1.3: CPI inflation, 1960-2025, for the chosen economies."""
    data = world_inflation[world_inflation.country.isin(chosen)]
    for top in [25, 50, 100, 250, 1000, 5000, 25000, 100000]:  # widen the axis in steps
        if data.inflation.max() <= top:
            break
    title = "Inflation peaked in the 1970s (24% in the U.K.) and surged again in 2021–22"
    if set(chosen) != set(BOOK_INFLATION) and len(data) > 0:
        row = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
        title = f"Highest inflation shown: {row.country}, {row.inflation:,.1f}% in {row.year}"
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country", title=title,
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-5, data.inflation.min() - 2), top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

The textbook says that over the past two decades unemployment has been “nearly twice as high in Europe as in the United States” (Jones 2024). The function below draws the chosen economies, shades a period, and computes the average ratio of the European rate to the U.S. rate in that period. Python note. start, end = period unpacks a pair of numbers into two variables. unemp[(unemp.year >= start) & (unemp.year <= end)] keeps the rows where both conditions are true; & means “and”, and each condition needs its own brackets.


BOOK_UNEMP = ("United States", "Europe", "Japan")


def unemployment_chart(period=(2006, 2025), chosen=BOOK_UNEMP):
    """Fig. 1.4: unemployment rates, with the average Europe/U.S. ratio over a shaded period."""
    start, end = period
    chosen_years = unemp[(unemp.year >= start) & (unemp.year <= end)]
    ratio = (chosen_years["Europe"] / chosen_years["United States"]).mean()
    data = world_unemp[world_unemp.country.isin(chosen)]
    title = f"{start}–{end}: Europe's rate was {ratio:.2f} times the U.S. rate on average"
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="unrate", color="country", hover_name="country", title=title,
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "unrate": "Unemployment rate (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    top = 14 if data.unrate.max() <= 14 else (30 if data.unrate.max() <= 30 else 40)   # widen in steps
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1954, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

text:
What a model does
With the facts in hand, we turn to the tool that explains them. A small live model shows how inputs go in and outcomes come out.

Fig. 6: The structure of economic models
Goal. See what a model does: it takes inputs and determines outcomes.
Every economic model has the same structure. The model builder picks the inputs:

parameters, fixed numbers such as \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{\ell}\), \(\bar{f}\), or a minimum wage set by law;
exogenous variables, inputs that may change over time in a way the model builder decides in advance, such as the number of people in the economy.

The model, a set of equations, then determines the endogenous variables, here the wage and employment. The textbook draws this as three boxes: inputs → MODEL → outcomes. Below, the boxes are live: every slider is an input, and the right box shows the outcomes the model computes.
We add one input the textbook mentions as an example of a parameter: a minimum wage. If it is below \(w^*\), it has no effect. If it is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the minimum wage, firms hire only the hours they demand at that wage, and the hours that workers offer but cannot sell are unemployment, \(L^s - L^d\). (Think of \(\bar{\ell}\) as growing with the number of people in the economy: more people offer more hours at any wage.)

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="rect", ...) draws a rectangle and fig.add_annotation(...) writes text; <br> starts a new line and <b>...</b> makes text bold. An annotation with showarrow=True draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y). max(w_star, w_min) is the larger of the two numbers. The loops run once per box and once per arrow.


def structure_of_models(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0, w_min=0.0):
    """Fig. 1.6 as a live model: inputs (parameters) -> MODEL -> outcomes (endogenous variables)."""
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                         # a minimum wage above w* sets the wage
    L = labor_demand(w, f)                         # firms hire the hours they demand at that wage
    unemployed = max(labor_supply(w, a, l) - L, 0.0)   # hours offered but not hired (zero, not -0.00, if w = w*)
    inputs = (f"<b>INPUTS</b><br><i>parameters and exogenous<br>variables</i><br><br>supply slope a = {a:.1f}"
              f"<br>hours at zero wage l = {l:.0f}<br>demand at zero wage f = {f:.0f}<br>minimum wage = {w_min:.0f}")
    model = "<b>MODEL</b><br><br>Lˢ = a·w + l<br>Lᵈ = f − w<br>Lˢ = Lᵈ, unless<br>a minimum wage<br>is above w*"
    outcomes = (f"<b>OUTCOMES</b><br><i>endogenous variables</i><br><br>wage w = {w:.2f}"
                f"<br>employment L = {L:.2f}<br>unemployment = {unemployed:.2f}")
    fig = go.Figure()
    for x0, x1, text in [[0.0, 0.33, inputs], [0.39, 0.61, model], [0.67, 1.0, outcomes]]:
        fig.add_shape(type="rect", x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.12, y1=0.88, fillcolor="#ecf3fa", line=dict(color=BLUE))
        fig.add_annotation(x=(x0 + x1) / 2, y=0.5, text=text, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    for x_from, x_to in [[0.33, 0.39], [0.61, 0.67]]:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x_to, y=0.5, ax=x_from, ay=0.5, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                           text="", showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=4, arrowcolor=GREEN)
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Inputs → model → outcomes: wage w = {w:.2f}, employment L = {L:.2f}")
    return fig

         f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5, description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE),
         w_min=FloatSlider(value=0, min=0, max=20, step=1, description="minimum wage", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

With the textbook’s inputs, the outcomes are \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), and nobody who wants to work at that wage is left out.
A minimum wage of 5 or 10 changes nothing, because it is not above the market wage. A minimum wage of 12 raises the wage to 12, cuts employment to 48, and leaves 6 hours of unemployment.
You never set the wage or employment directly: they are endogenous. You only change inputs, and the model works out the outcomes. That is what the textbook means by running an experiment with a model.

One chart organizes the whole textbook: the steady rise of U.S. income per person over 150 years, and the swings around that trend.

Fig. 7: Per capita GDP in the United States
Goal. See the three features of the graph that organizes the whole textbook: long-run growth, short-run fluctuations, and the question of what comes next.
The file has two columns. gdppc_actual is real GDP per person. gdppc_potential is potential output: what GDP per person would be if prices were fully flexible and all resources were fully employed. From 1949 on, potential output comes from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO); before 1949 it is a smooth statistical trend of the actual series, so the early years should be read with care.

The average annual growth rate \(g\) between 1870 and 2025 is the constant rate that turns the 1870 value into the 2025 value in 155 years: \(y_{2025} = y_{1870}(1+g)^{155}\), so \(g = (y_{2025}/y_{1870})^{1/155} - 1\).

Average annual growth, 1870-2025: 1.88%


The same chart can be drawn for any country in the Maddison file of Fig. 1. Only the United States has an official estimate of potential output (from the CBO), so other countries show actual GDP per person only.

Python note. data.iloc[0] is the first row and data.iloc[-1] the last, so the growth formula uses each country’s own first and last year. On a ratio-scale axis, an annotation’s height is also given in powers of ten: y=np.log10(30000).


def per_capita_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 1.7: per capita GDP on a ratio scale with its average growth rate (U.S.: also potential)."""
    if country == "United States":
        data = usgdp.rename(columns={"gdppc_actual": "Actual", "gdppc_potential": "Potential"})
        series = ["Actual", "Potential"]
    else:
        data = world[world.country == country].rename(columns={"gdppc": "Actual"})
        series = ["Actual"]
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    growth = (last.Actual / first.Actual) ** (1 / (last.year - first.year)) - 1
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=series, log_y=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Per capita GDP (2022 dollars, ratio scale)", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}: GDP per person grew {round(100 * growth, 1) + 0.0:.1f}% a year, "
                        f"{first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}")       # + 0.0: no -0.0
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential"), line_dash="dash")
    low = 3500 if data.Actual.min() >= 3500 else (1000 if data.Actual.min() >= 1000 else 400)
    high = 100000 if data.Actual.max() <= 100000 else 250000
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000],
                     range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2030])
    fig.add_annotation(x=1870, y=np.log10(0.8 * high), showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(size=14),
                       text=f"Income in {last.year:.0f}: {last.Actual / first.Actual:.1f} times<br>its {first.year:.0f} level")
    return fig

What to notice.

The long run. Income per person rose enormously, and on a ratio scale the line is close to straight: growth of almost 2 percent a year, sustained for over 150 years.
The short run. Actual GDP (solid) moves around potential output (dashed). The Great Depression of the 1930s and the World War II boom of the 1940s are the only deviations you can see easily.
The future. The line raises an obvious question: will growth continue at the same rate?

The textbook reports $4,200 in 1870 and $76,000 in 2022, “more than a factor of 15”. Our 2022 value is close ($77,942). Our 1870 value is about 10 percent higher, because we use newer historical estimates (the Maddison Project) for the years before 1929. The rise is a factor of almost 17, and average growth is 1.9 percent a year, which the textbook rounds to 2 percent.
This series also lets us revisit the claim of Fig. 1. Here, U.S. income in 2022 is about 8.1 times its 1922 level: more than the 5.8 of the Maddison data, but still short of “more than 10 times”. The two sources disagree because estimating income a century ago is hard, and they measure prices differently. When sources disagree, report the range.


The short run: the output gap
This part stays U.S.-only: potential output comes from the CBO, which estimates it only for the United States. (The IMF and the OECD publish output-gap estimates for rich countries, but only since about 1980 and from models that differ from the CBO’s.)
The gap between actual and potential output, in percent, is \(100 \times (\text{actual} / \text{potential} - 1)\). It is negative in recessions. The chart below plots it for every year, and the title converts the gap of the chosen year into dollars per person and for a family of four.

Python note. usgdp["gap"] = ... adds a new column, computed row by row from two other columns. usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0] picks the one row of the chosen year. px.bar draws a bar chart, and :+,.0f in an f-string shows a sign, thousands separators and no decimals.


usgdp["gap"] = 100 * (usgdp.gdppc_actual / usgdp.gdppc_potential - 1)


def output_gap_chart(year=2009):
    """Fig. 1.7, second feature: actual GDP per person relative to potential, in percent."""
    row = usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0]
    dollars = row.gdppc_actual - row.gdppc_potential
    fig = px.bar(usgdp, x="year", y="gap", color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL],
                 labels={"year": "Year", "gap": "Actual relative to potential (percent)"})
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[year], y=[row.gap], mode="markers", name=str(year),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-20, 25])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{year}: gap {row.gap:+.1f}%, or {dollars:+,.0f} dollars per person "
                            f"({4 * dollars:+,.0f} for a family of four)")
    return fig

What to notice.

The Great Depression is by far the deepest gap: 17 percent below potential in 1933. The World War II boom put output 23 percent above potential in 1944.

section: Solving a model: the labor market
text:
Solving a model: the labor market
Finally, we draw the labor-market model from the Model overview and use it for experiments, changing one input at a time.

Fig. 8: The labor market
Goal. Draw the supply-and-demand diagram of the labor market and see how the equilibrium moves when a parameter changes.
The diagram puts employment \(L\) on the horizontal axis and the wage \(w\) on the vertical axis. Labor supply \(L^s = \bar{a}w + \bar{\ell}\) slopes up, and labor demand \(L^d = \bar{f} - w\) slopes down. They cross at the equilibrium \((L^*, w^*)\). When you move a slider away from the textbook’s values, the textbook’s curves stay on the chart as dashed gray lines, so you can see the shift.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 30, 100) creates 100 evenly spaced wages from 0 to 30. Because the wage is on the vertical axis, we compute the hours supplied and demanded at each wage and use them as x. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and each add_trace adds one curve or set of points. As in the textbook, the curves are named on the chart: add_annotation writes the labels Lˢ and Lᵈ at the ends of the curves, and xanchor/yanchor say which corner of the label touches that point.


def labor_market(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """Fig. 1.8: labor supply and demand, and the equilibrium (L*, w*)."""
    w = np.linspace(0, 30, 100)
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if (a, l, f) != (2.0, 30.0, 60.0):             # keep the textbook's curves for comparison
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_supply(w), y=w, name="Textbook curves (a=2, l=30, f=60)",
                                 line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_demand(w), y=w, showlegend=False, line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_supply(w, a, l), y=w, name="Lˢ", showlegend=False, line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_demand(w, f), y=w, name="Lᵈ", showlegend=False, line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    w_end = min(30, (100 - l) / a)                 # supply leaves the chart at the top or at the right edge
    fig.add_annotation(x=labor_supply(w_end, a, l), y=w_end, text="Lˢ", showarrow=False,
                       xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(size=18, color=TEAL))
    fig.add_annotation(x=labor_demand(30, f), y=30, text="Lᵈ", showarrow=False, xshift=-4,
                       xanchor="right", yanchor="top", font=dict(size=18, color=BLUE))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, L_star, L_star], y=[w_star, w_star, 0], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_star], y=[w_star], mode="markers", name="Equilibrium (L*, w*)",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Equilibrium: wage w* = {w_star:.2f}, employment L* = {L_star:.2f}", showlegend=True,
                      xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 30]))
    return fig


interact(labor_market,
         a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="supply slope a", style=WIDE),
         l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=20, max=40, step=5, description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
         f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5, description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 1.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the textbook’s parameters the curves cross at \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), the answer to the textbook’s worked exercise.
A higher \(\bar{f}\) shifts labor demand to the right: the wage and employment both rise.
A higher \(\bar{\ell}\) shifts labor supply to the right: employment rises but the wage falls.
A larger \(\bar{a}\) makes supply respond more to the wage. The supply curve gets flatter in this diagram, and it pivots around the point where the wage is zero.


Key numbers: three experiments
The formulas \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\) show how much each parameter moves the outcomes. With \(\bar{a} = 2\), raising \(\bar{f}\) by 3 raises \(w^*\) by \(3/3 = 1\); raising \(\bar{\ell}\) by 3 lowers \(w^*\) by 1.

Python note. This loop goes through a list of lists: each inner list holds a name and three parameter values, which the line for name, a, l, f in ... unpacks.


for name, a, l, f in [["textbook", 2, 30, 60], ["l up by 3", 2, 33, 60], ["f up by 3", 2, 30, 63]]:
    w_new, L_new = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    print(f"{name:10}  w* = {w_new:5.2f}   L* = {L_new:5.2f}")

textbook    w* = 10.00   L* = 50.00
l up by 3   w* =  9.00   L* = 51.00
f up by 3   w* = 11.00   L* = 52.00


Your turn. Find values of \(\bar{\ell}\) and \(\bar{f}\) that keep the wage at \(w^* = 10\) but raise employment to \(L^* = 60\) (keep \(\bar{a} = 2\)). Check your answer with equilibrium.


Hint

\(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\), so \(L^* = 60\) with \(w^* = 10\) needs \(\bar{f} = 70\). Then choose \(\bar{\ell}\) so that \((\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/3 = 10\). Try it with the sliders too.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Concluding remarks

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole. Its big questions start from facts like these: huge income gaps across countries, deep recessions such as 2008–09 and 2020, the inflation of the 1970s and of 2021–22, high unemployment in Europe, and large U.S. budget and trade deficits.
It answers them in four steps: document the facts, build a model, compare the model with the facts, and use the model for experiments.
A model takes parameters and exogenous variables as inputs and determines the endogenous variables. In the labor-market model, \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1 + \bar{a})\) and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\).
U.S. GDP per person has grown at almost 2 percent a year since 1870 (the long run), with deviations from potential output that are small except in the Great Depression and World War II (the short run).
Checking claims against the data matters: some textbook numbers hold exactly, others change with newer data.
The next chapter shows how GDP, the measure behind most of these figures, is defined and measured.

Python note. import loads a library, a toolbox written by other people. We give each library a short nickname, for example pd for pandas, so that the code stays short. Text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it, and it is there for human readers. The try ... except block runs one Colab-only line and simply skips it anywhere else.


# Libraries used in this chapter
import numpy as np                    # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go     # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio
from ipywidgets import interact, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple

DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch02/"

The next cell defines a helper that only the book website needs. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, …); the next cell builds those menus.


Show the helper code
# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table (country, x, y), leaving out the countries in skip."""
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name, mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' traces hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them (G7, a region, ...).

    The traces already in fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and slider steps only switch those."""
    n = len(fig.data)
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update", args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig




Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website's one-country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value (e.g. per country)."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        if "yaxis2" in f.layout.to_plotly_json():       # a second vertical axis (Fig. 2)
            layout["yaxis2"] = f.layout.yaxis2.to_plotly_json()
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

title: Chapter 2: Measuring the Macroeconomy
text:
Model overview
Before we can explain why an economy grows or shrinks, we need to measure it. The main measure is gross domestic product (GDP): the value of everything an economy produces in a year. A nice property of GDP is that we can count it three ways, by what is produced, by what is spent, and by what is earned, and all three give the same total, because every dollar spent on a good is a dollar of income for someone.
This chapter has no economic model, so this section collects the measurement tools instead: shares of a total, the value of production at fixed prices, chain-weighted growth, and the conversion of GDP across currencies. The sections below use them to split U.S. GDP by who buys it and who earns it, and then to separate price changes from real growth.
These accounting rules come back in every later chapter.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of the final goods and services produced in an economy in a given period. It can be measured in three ways that give the same number: as total production, as total spending, and as total income. On the spending side, the national income identity splits GDP by who buys the goods:
\[Y = C + I + G + NX \qquad (2.1)\]
where \(Y\) is GDP, \(C\) consumption, \(I\) investment, \(G\) government purchases, and \(NX\) net exports (exports minus imports). To compare the parts, we divide each one by GDP and get its share.
GDP measured at today’s prices is nominal GDP. It can rise because prices rise or because the economy produces more. Real GDP values production at a fixed set of prices, so it only changes when quantities change:
\[\text{nominal GDP} = \text{price level} \times \text{real GDP} \qquad (2.2)\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. .sum() adds up all the values of a column or a row.


def share(part, total):
    """Share of a part in a total, in percent (Tables 2.1 and 2.2)."""
    return 100 * part / total


def gdp_value(prices, quantities):
    """Value of production: price times quantity, added over all goods (nominal or real GDP)."""
    return (prices * quantities).sum()


def chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche):
    """Chain-weighted growth: the average of the Laspeyres and Paasche growth rates (Section 2.3)."""
    return (g_laspeyres + g_paasche) / 2


Table 2.4: real GDP in an economy with apples and computers
The textbook’s example economy produces only apples and computers. We store its prices and quantities in two small tables, one row per year.

Python note. pd.DataFrame({...}, index=[...]) builds a table from a dictionary: each key becomes a column and the index gives the row labels. prices.loc[2026] picks the row for 2026. Multiplying two rows, prices.loc[2026] * quantities.loc[2027], multiplies the matching columns.


prices = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [1, 2, 3], "computers": [900, 1000, 1000]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
quantities = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [500, 500, 550], "computers": [5, 5, 6]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
prices

Nominal GDP uses each year’s own prices. Real GDP holds the prices fixed. The Laspeyres index measures the change from 2026 to 2027 with the initial (2026) prices, and the Paasche index with the final (2027) prices. Chain weighting averages the two growth rates.

Python note. An f-string such as f"{x:,.0f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text: , adds thousands separators, .0f shows no decimals and .1% shows a share as a percentage with one decimal.


for year in [2025, 2026, 2027]:
    print(f"Nominal GDP in {year}: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[year], quantities.loc[year]):,.0f}")

g_nominal = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_laspeyres = gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_paasche = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)
print(f"Real GDP in 2027 at 2026 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]):,.0f}")
print(f"Real GDP in 2026 at 2027 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]):,.0f}")
print(f"Growth 2026-2027: nominal {g_nominal:.1%}, Laspeyres {g_laspeyres:.1%}, "
      f"Paasche {g_paasche:.1%}, chain-weighted {g_chain:.1%}")
print(f"Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: ${7650 / (1 + g_chain):,.0f}")
print(f"Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  {g_nominal - g_chain:.1%}")

Nominal GDP in 2025: $5,000
Nominal GDP in 2026: $6,000
Nominal GDP in 2027: $7,650
Real GDP in 2027 at 2026 prices: $7,100
Real GDP in 2026 at 2027 prices: $6,500
Growth 2026-2027: nominal 27.5%, Laspeyres 18.3%, Paasche 17.7%, chain-weighted 18.0%
Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: $6,482
Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  9.5%


These are the numbers of Table 2.4: real growth is 18.3 percent at 2026 prices, 17.7 percent at 2027 prices, and 18.0 percent chain-weighted. Nominal GDP grew 27.5 percent, so prices rose by about \(27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5\) percent. (The textbook gets $6,483 for chained real GDP in 2026, because it rounds the growth rate to 18.0 percent first; with the unrounded rate we get $6,482.)


Comparing countries: exchange rates and purchasing power parity
To compare GDP across countries we first convert it to a common currency with the exchange rate. But prices also differ across countries, so we then value production at common prices, which is called purchasing power parity (PPP):
\[\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}\times\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} \qquad (2.6)\]

def to_dollars(gdp_local, exchange_rate):
    """Convert GDP in local currency into dollars at the market exchange rate (Section 2.4)."""
    return gdp_local / exchange_rate


def at_common_prices(gdp_dollars, relative_price_level):
    """Real GDP at U.S. prices: dollar GDP divided by the price level relative to the U.S. (equation 2.6)."""
    return gdp_dollars / relative_price_level


china_dollars = to_dollars(95.1, 6.91)                  # 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar (2019)
china_ppp = at_common_prices(china_dollars, 0.684)      # goods in China cost 68.4% of U.S. prices
print(f"China at the exchange rate: ${china_dollars:.1f} trillion, {china_dollars / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
print(f"China at common prices:     ${china_ppp:.1f} trillion, {china_ppp / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")

China at the exchange rate: $13.8 trillion, 67% of U.S. GDP
China at common prices:     $20.1 trillion, 98% of U.S. GDP


With the textbook’s 2019 numbers, China’s economy looks like two-thirds of the U.S. economy at the exchange rate, but almost exactly as large at common prices.

The World Bank’s investment share is about 4 points higher and its government share about 4 points lower: the same spending sits in a different box. Consumption and net exports agree. Before you compare countries, check that the numbers use the same definitions.
The textbook stacks the shares on top of each other: net exports at the bottom, then consumption, investment, and government purchases up to 100 percent. px.area stacks areas in the order of category_orders, and color_discrete_map gives each component a fixed color. Because net exports are negative in recent decades, consumption starts below zero in those years. The function draws the BEA’s U.S. data, or the World Bank’s data for any other country.

Python note. np.floor and np.ceil round down and up, so 10 * np.ceil(x / 10) is the next multiple of 10 above x: the axes grow in steps of 10 points for countries with unusual shares. data.groupby("year").share.sum() adds up the four shares within each year (the top of the stack), and max(a, b) is the larger of two numbers.


ORDER = ["Net exports", "Consumption", "Investment", "Government purchases"]
COLORS_GDP = {"Net exports": "#e0a33b", "Consumption": "#5aa0d8", "Investment": GREEN, "Government purchases": TEAL}
LABELS = {"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "component": "Component"}
WB_NAMES = {"consumption": "Consumption", "investment": "Investment", "government": "Government purchases",
            "net_exports": "Net exports"}
BEA = "United States (BEA)"


def composition_chart(style="stacked areas", country=BEA):
    """Fig. 2.1: the expenditure shares of GDP, stacked or as separate lines (BEA, or World Bank data)."""
    data = long
    title = "Since 1950: consumption ≈ 64%, government ≈ 20%, investment ≈ 17% of U.S. GDP"
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[world.country == country].melt(id_vars="year", value_vars=list(WB_NAMES), value_name="share")
        data["component"] = data.variable.map(WB_NAMES)
        title = f"Composition of GDP in {country} (World Bank definitions)"
    if style == "stacked areas":
        fig = px.area(data, x="year", y="share", color="component", color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,
                      category_orders={"component": ORDER}, labels=LABELS, title=title)
    else:
        fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="share", color="component", color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,
                      category_orders={"component": ORDER}, labels=LABELS, title=title)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    top = max(data.groupby("year").share.sum().max(), data.share.max())     # stacked total or largest share
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min(), 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-10, 10 * np.floor(data.share.min() / 10)), max(100, 10 * np.ceil(top / 10))])
    return fig

The function below builds the table for any year. Population is in thousands, so GDP per person in dollars is billions × 1,000,000 / population.

EXPENDITURE = {"gdp": "Gross domestic product", "consumption": "Personal consumption expenditures",
               "motor_vehicles": "   Motor vehicles and parts", "food": "   Food", "housing": "   Housing",
               "medical": "   Medical care", "investment": "Gross private domestic investment",
               "structures": "   Structures (nonresidential)", "equipment": "   Equipment",
               "ipp": "   Intellectual property products", "residential": "   Residential",
               "government": "Government purchases", "defense": "   National defense",
               "net_exports": "Net exports of goods and services", "exports": "   Exports", "imports": "   Imports"}


def expenditure_table(year):
    """Table 2.1: the expenditure approach to U.S. GDP in one year."""
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(EXPENDITURE)]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
                          "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
                          "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"]})
    table.index = list(EXPENDITURE.values())
    return table.round(1)

Python note. px.line with a list of columns as y draws one line per column. We then add the consumption line with fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...)), and yaxis="y2" attaches it to a second vertical axis. In update_layout, overlaying="y" puts that axis on top of the first one, and side="right" puts its labels on the right. .rename(columns=WB_NAMES) gives the World Bank’s columns the same names as ours, data.iloc[0] is the first row and data.iloc[-1] the last, and "rose" if a > b else "fell" picks one of two words.


def shares_chart(country=BEA):
    """Fig. 2.2: expenditure shares since 1970, consumption on the right axis (BEA, or World Bank data)."""
    data = recent
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[(world.country == country) & (world.year >= 1970)].rename(columns=WB_NAMES)
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    verb = "rose" if last.Consumption > first.Consumption else "fell"
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"],
                  color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, GREEN, "#e0a33b"],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Share of GDP (percent)", "variable": "Component"},
                  title=f"{country}: consumption {verb} from {first.Consumption:.0f}% to {last.Consumption:.0f}% "
                        f"of GDP, {first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=data.year, y=data.Consumption, name="Consumption (right axis)",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), yaxis="y2"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    others = data[["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"]]
    low, high = min(-6, 10 * np.floor(others.min().min() / 10)), max(46, 10 * np.ceil(others.max().max() / 10) + 20)
    c_low, c_high = min(36, 10 * np.floor(data.Consumption.min() / 10) - 30), max(70, 10 * np.ceil(data.Consumption.max() / 10))
    fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25] if high == 46 else None),
                      yaxis2=dict(title="Consumption (percent of GDP)", overlaying="y", side="right",
                                  range=[c_low, c_high], tickvals=[60, 64, 68] if c_low == 36 else None, showgrid=False),
                      legend=dict(x=1.1), xaxis=dict(range=[1969, 2026]))      # legend clear of the right axis
    return fig

Python note. wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year] subtracts one row from every row of the table, column by column. The result is the change of each share since the base year, in percentage points. .reset_index() turns the year labels back into an ordinary column, which melt and Plotly need.


CHANGE_COLORS = {"Consumption": BLUE, "Investment": GREEN, "Government purchases": TEAL, "Net exports": "#e0a33b"}


def changes_chart(base_year=1970):
    """Fig. 2.2, second view: change in each expenditure share since base_year (percentage points)."""
    changes = (wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]).reset_index()
    long_changes = changes.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="component", value_name="change")
    fig = px.line(long_changes, x="year", y="change", color="component", color_discrete_map=CHANGE_COLORS,
                  range_x=[1970, 2025], range_y=[-8, 10],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "change": f"Change since {base_year} (percentage points)",
                          "component": "Component"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    c = wide.loc[2025] - wide.loc[base_year]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{base_year}–2025: C {c['Consumption']:+.1f}, I {c['Investment']:+.1f}, "
                            f"G {c['Government purchases']:+.1f}, NX {c['Net exports']:+.1f} points")
    return fig

Who earns GDP: labor’s share
The same GDP is also income. Here we ask how much of it goes to workers, and whether that share has really stayed constant.

Fig. 3: Labor’s share of GDP
Goal. Check one of the classic “stylized facts” of macroeconomics: that labor earns about two-thirds of GDP, year after year.
The income approach splits GDP into the income earned by workers (compensation: wages, salaries and benefits) and the income earned by the owners of capital. Two parts need care. Taxes on production (such as sales taxes) are income of neither, so they are left out. And the income of the self-employed (proprietors’ income) mixes both, so it is split between labor and capital in the same proportion as in the rest of the economy. The result is
\[\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}}\]
where GDI is gross domestic income, the income-side measure of GDP.

Python note. for i, name in enumerate(...) hands over each name together with its position i (0, 1, 2, …). i % 24 is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24 colors repeat in turn. if name not in COLORS: skips the names that already have a color.


COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "Germany": TEAL, "Japan": GREEN, "China": "#e0a33b", "United Kingdom": "#5aa0d8"}
OTHER = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24                 # 24 distinct colors for the other countries
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    if name not in COLORS:
        COLORS[name] = OTHER[i % len(OTHER)]

The textbook points to a downward trend since about 1970. Our chart adds a straight trend line fitted to the data: pick the year where the line starts, and see how steep the decline is. You can also add other countries from the Penn World Table (including the United States, to compare the two measures).

Python note. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits the best straight line \(y = a + bx\) through the points (by least squares) and returns the slope \(b\) first and the intercept \(a\) second. SelectMultiple is a list from which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click to add or remove one. .isin(chosen) keeps the rows of the chosen countries, and for name, part in extra.groupby("country"): hands over each country’s name and rows in turn, so each gets its own line. pd.concat([a, b]) stacks two columns into one, and x if condition else y picks x when the condition is true.


def labor_share_chart(start=1970, chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.3: labor's share of GDP, 1950-2025, with a trend line from `start`; other countries from PWT."""
    after = labor[labor.year >= start]
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(after.year, after.labor_share, 1)
    fig = px.line(labor, x="year", y="labor_share", labels={"year": "Year", "labor_share": "Labor share of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(22, 82, 140, 0.12)",
                      name="Labor share (textbook)", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=after.year, y=intercept + slope * after.year, name=f"Trend since {start}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    extra = pwt[pwt.country.isin(chosen)]
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.year, y=part.labor_share, name=f"{name} (PWT)", line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    shown = pd.concat([labor.labor_share, extra.labor_share])      # every value on the chart
    low = 0.55 if shown.min() >= 0.55 else 0.05 * np.floor(shown.min() / 0.05)      # widen in steps of 0.05
    high = 0.75 if shown.max() <= 0.75 else 0.05 * np.ceil(shown.max() / 0.05)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1950, 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high], tickvals=[0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75] if low == 0.55 else None)  # no corner label
    # slope is per year, as a fraction: x 100 for percentage points, x 10 for a decade
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Labor share: trend since {start} is {1000 * slope:+.1f} percentage points per decade")
    return fig

What to notice.

On average, labor earned 0.65 of income from 1950 to 2025, close to the two-thirds of the stylized fact. Until 2021 the share stayed between 0.60 and 0.70.
But the share is not constant. It peaked at 0.69 in 1970 and has drifted down since: from 1970 the trend falls by about 1.3 percentage points per decade. Move the starting year to 1990 or 2000 and the decline looks even steeper.
Since 2022 the share has been below 0.60 for the first time in these data (0.586 in 2025). Our values for the last years in the textbook are slightly lower than the book’s, because of the 2023 data revision. Part of the decline reflects how the national accounts treat software and R&D, which is still debated by researchers.
Add other countries. The labor share fell in Germany too (0.69 in 1970, 0.64 in 2023), but it rose in Japan (0.51 to 0.59) and South Korea (0.42 to 0.55). Two-thirds is a rough rule for rich countries, not a law of nature. Oil exporters such as Qatar (0.18) and Kuwait (0.25) have very low shares, because most of their income is oil revenue. Some values are doubtful: the Penn World Table puts Venezuela at exactly 0.0844 in every year from 2019 to 2023, a value carried forward, not measured. Look at the extremes before you trust a cross-country file.


Key numbers: Table 2.2, the income approach

INCOME = {"gdp": "Gross domestic product", "compensation": "Compensation of employees",
          "wages": "   Wages and salaries", "benefits": "   Benefits",
          "taxes_less_subsidies": "Taxes less subsidies on businesses",
          "net_operating_surplus": "Net operating surplus of businesses",
          "depreciation": "Depreciation of fixed capital"}


def income_table(year):
    """Table 2.2: the income approach to U.S. GDP in one year."""
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(INCOME)]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
                          "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
                          "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"]})
    table.index = list(INCOME.values())
    return table.round(1)

Nominal GDP rises when prices rise and when production rises. These figures pull out the price part: the price level and its growth rate, inflation.

Goal. Follow the U.S. price level since 1947, as measured by the GDP deflator.
The GDP deflator is the price level in equation (2.2): nominal GDP divided by real GDP. It is an index: its value in a chosen base year is set to 100. The data are quarterly, with one row per quarter labeled by the first day of the quarter.

Python note. parse_dates=["date"] tells pandas that the date column holds dates, not plain text. Plotly then draws a proper time axis, and we can pick rows by year.

FRED shades the recessions in gray. The file recessions.csv lists the first and last month of each recession since 1947, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER).

Python note. range(len(recessions)) gives the row numbers 0, 1, 2, …, so the for loop visits every recession once. fig.add_vrect draws a vertical band between two dates.


def shade_recessions(fig):
    """Add a gray band for every NBER recession, as FRED does (Figs. 2.4 and 2.5)."""
    for i in range(len(recessions)):
        fig.add_vrect(x0=recessions.start[i], x1=recessions.end[i], fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.25, line_width=0)
    return fig

The World Bank publishes the GDP deflator of about 200 countries, once a year. Each country publishes its index with its own base year, so deflator_world.csv has been rebased: every country’s deflator is divided by its 2012 value and multiplied by 100, like the U.S. series. The file also holds the yearly inflation rate of each deflator, which Fig. 5 uses. We place each yearly value in the middle of its year.

Python note. .astype(str) turns numbers into text, so deflators.year.astype(str) + "-07-01" builds dates such as "2012-07-01", and pd.to_datetime turns that text into real dates.

The chart draws the U.S. quarterly series and, if you choose them, other countries’ yearly series. When a chosen country’s prices were far lower or higher, the axis widens tenfold until every value fits.

Python note. A while loop repeats its indented lines as long as its condition is true: here it multiplies the top of the axis by 10 until the largest value fits below it (and divides the bottom of the ratio scale by 10 until the smallest value fits above it).


def deflator_chart(scale="linear", chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.4: the GDP deflator (2012 = 100), U.S. quarterly since 1947, other countries yearly."""
    fig = px.line(deflator, x="date", y="gdp_deflator_2012_100", log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  labels={"date": "Quarter", "gdp_deflator_2012_100": "GDP deflator (index, 2012 = 100)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), name="United States (quarterly)", showlegend=True)
    extra = deflators[deflators.country.isin(chosen)].dropna(subset=["deflator_2012_100"])
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.deflator_2012_100, name=name, line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    shade_recessions(fig)
    shown = pd.concat([deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100, extra.deflator_2012_100])
    low, high = 9, (170 if scale == "ratio" else 150)
    while low > shown.min():
        low = low / 10                   # widen the axis tenfold at a time until every value fits
    while high < shown.max():
        high = high * 10
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[10, 20, 40, 80, 160] if (low, high) == (9, 170) else None,
                         range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    factor = deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[-1] / deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[0]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"The U.S. price level rose about {factor:.0f}-fold from 1947 to 2026")
    return fig

What to notice.

Prices rose slowly until the mid-1960s, much faster in the 1970s and early 1980s, and then at a steadier pace, until the jump of 2021–2022.
On the linear scale the line rises about as steeply in the 2000s as in the 1970s, because the same percentage increase adds more index points when prices are already high. Switch to the ratio scale: there the slope is the percentage rate of change, and the 1970s clearly stand out.
Add Japan: its deflator fell from 119 in 1994 to 100 in 2013, two decades of deflation. Add Turkey on the ratio scale: its price level in 2025 was more than 30,000 times its 1990 level.


Python note. With dates as row labels, level["1965"] picks the four quarters of 1965, and .mean() averages them. The formula \((\text{end}/\text{start})^{1/\text{years}} - 1\) is the average annual growth rate.


level = deflator.set_index("date").gdp_deflator_2012_100
for start, end in [(1947, 1965), (1965, 1983), (1983, 2019), (2019, 2025)]:
    yearly = (level[str(end)].mean() / level[str(start)].mean()) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1
    print(f"{start}-{end}: prices rose {yearly:.1%} a year on average")

1947-1965: prices rose 2.1% a year on average
1965-1983: prices rose 6.0% a year on average
1983-2019: prices rose 2.2% a year on average
2019-2025: prices rose 3.6% a year on average



Key numbers: nominal GDP = price level × real GDP
The textbook asks how much more real GDP the United States produced in 2022 than in 1995. Real GDP in our national accounts file is measured in chained 2017 dollars.

real_ratio = nipa.loc[2022, "real_gdp"] / nipa.loc[1995, "real_gdp"]

print(f"Nominal GDP grew by a factor of {nominal_ratio:.2f}")
print(f"Real GDP grew by a factor of    {real_ratio:.2f}")
print(f"So the price level grew by      {nominal_ratio / real_ratio:.2f}")

Nominal GDP: $7.6 trillion (1995), $26.1 trillion (2022)
Nominal GDP grew by a factor of 3.41
Real GDP grew by a factor of    1.93
So the price level grew by      1.76


Nominal GDP more than tripled, but real GDP did not quite double: the rest of the rise came from a price level that went up by about three-quarters. (The textbook’s $7.4 trillion for 1995 is now $7.6 trillion after revisions.)
Taking growth rates of equation (2.2) gives a handy approximation: the growth of nominal GDP is about the growth of the price level plus the growth of real GDP.

Python note. .pct_change() computes the change from the previous row as a fraction, for every row at once. The first row has no previous row, so it gets NaN (“not a number”).

Fig. 5: The annual inflation rate using the GDP deflator
Goal. Turn the price level into an inflation rate, the percentage change of the price level.
FRED’s “Percent Change from Year Ago” compares each quarter with the same quarter one year earlier:
\[\pi_t = 100 \times \left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-4}} - 1\right)\]
where \(P_t\) is the GDP deflator in quarter \(t\). A second common measure compares each quarter with the quarter before and turns the change into an annual rate: \(100 \times \left[(P_t/P_{t-1})^4 - 1\right]\).

Python note. .shift(4) moves a column down by four rows, so that each quarter sits next to the value from one year earlier. The first four rows get NaN, because there is nothing to compare them with.

quarterly = 100 * ((level / level.shift(1)) ** 4 - 1)

def inflation_chart(measure="change from a year ago", chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.5: inflation of the GDP deflator since 1947, with recession bands; other countries yearly."""
    series = rates[measure].dropna().reset_index()
    fig = px.line(series, x="date", y=measure, labels={"date": "Quarter", measure: "Inflation (percent)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2), name="United States (quarterly)", showlegend=True)
    extra = deflators[deflators.country.isin(chosen)].dropna(subset=["inflation"])
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.inflation, name=name, line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    shade_recessions(fig)
    shown = pd.concat([series[measure], extra.inflation])
    low, high = -5, 16
    while low > shown.min():
        low = low * 2                    # widen the axis in steps until every value fits
    while high < shown.max():
        high = high * 2
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    last = series.iloc[-1]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Inflation, {measure}: {last[measure]:.1f}% in {last.date.year} Q{last.date.quarter}")
    return fig
