rate_source says where the rate comes from. For the United States it is the Treasury-bill rate of the textbook. For the other countries it is the OECD’s 3-month money-market (interbank) rate, a rate at which banks lend to each other. That is a slightly different rate: in the United States the OECD’s 3-month rate has been 0.6 points above the Treasury-bill rate on average.
Before plotting, we give the columns readable names for the legend. Inflation is hidden at first; click it in the legend to show it. Hover over the chart to read all three numbers of a year and check that \(i = R + \pi\). Rates in some countries were much higher than in the United States, so the vertical axis widens in steps.

RATE_RANGES = [[-10, 16], [-20, 32], [-40, 64], [-80, 128], [-200, 250]]


def rate_range(low, high):
    """The first range in RATE_RANGES that contains both low and high (the widest one if none does)."""
    for bottom, top in RATE_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return RATE_RANGES[-1]


def interest_rates(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.5: the nominal rate i, the real rate R = i - pi and inflation pi of one country."""
    data = rates_panel[rates_panel.country == country]
    named = data.rename(columns={"short_rate": "Nominal rate, i", "real_rate": "Real rate, R = i − π",
                                 "inflation": "Inflation, π"})
    negative = (data.real_rate < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Nominal rate, i", "Real rate, R = i − π", "Inflation, π"], hover_name="year",
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE], labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent"},
                  title=f"{country}: the real rate R = i − π was negative in {negative} of {data.real_rate.count()} years")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Inflation, π"), visible="legendonly", line=dict(dash="dot"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    yr = rate_range(data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].min().min(),
                    data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].max().max())
    fig.update_yaxes(range=yr, tickvals=[-5, 0, 5, 10, 15] if yr == [-10, 16] else None)   # no label in the corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig

What to notice.

The nominal rate is high when inflation is high. It peaked at just over 14 percent in 1981, a year after inflation peaked.
The real rate was negative in the 1970s, in most years since 2008, and sharply negative in 2021–2022, when inflation jumped while the nominal rate was still near zero.
In 2009 the real rate was above the nominal rate. Show inflation in the legend: it was negative that year.
Choose Germany. In 1974 the U.S. real rate was −3.2 percent, but Germany’s was +2.9 percent: its central bank fought the inflation of the 1970s earlier and harder, and German inflation never went above 7 percent (Fig. 1).
Choose Turkey: in 2022 its short rate was 14 percent and inflation 72 percent, a real rate of −58 percent by \(R = i - \pi\). With rates this high the shortcut is poor; the exact real rate, \((1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1\), is −34 percent.

RATIO_TICKS = [0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000]   # no label in the bottom-left corner
LINEAR_TICKS = [500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000]                            # (the textbook's linear scale)
LINEAR_TOPS = [3500, 7000, 15000, 75000]


def disinflation(data):
    """Figs. 8.6-8.7: the highest peak among the chosen countries, and when that country fell below 25%."""
    top = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    own = data[data.country == top.country]
    later = own[(own.year > top.year) & (own.inflation < 25)]
    if len(later) > 0:
        return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, below 25% by {later.year.min():.0f}"
    return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, still above 25% in {own.year.max():.0f}"


def inflation_paths(countries=("Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"), scale="linear"):
    """Figs. 8.6 and 8.7: inflation in the chosen countries, on a linear or a ratio scale."""
    data = paths[paths.country.isin(countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("Argentina",))]
    title = disinflation(data)
    if scale == "ratio":
        data = data[data.inflation > 0]                  # a ratio scale cannot show zero or falling prices
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", log_y=(scale == "ratio"), hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=PATH_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.add_hline(y=500, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, annotation_text="500%: hyperinflation",
                  annotation_position="bottom left")
    peak = data.inflation.max()
    if scale == "ratio":
        top = 5000 if peak < 5000 else 200000
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=RATIO_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.1), np.log10(top)])
    else:
        top = axis_top(1.1 * peak, LINEAR_TOPS)
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=LINEAR_TICKS if top == 3500 else None, range=[-top / 35, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1960, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend_title_text="")
    return fig

The inflation tax
Why would a government let money grow so fast? Because printing money is one way to pay its bills. The government budget constraint says that spending \(G\) is paid with taxes \(T\), new borrowing \(\Delta B\), or new money \(\Delta M\):
\[G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M \qquad (8.7)\]
The revenue from new money is called seignorage, or the inflation tax. It is paid by everyone who holds money: when the price level doubles, a 200-dollar bill buys only what 100 dollars bought before.

title: Chapter 8: Inflation
text:
Concluding remarks

Inflation is the growth rate of the price level. U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980, stayed near 2 percent for two decades, and jumped to 8 percent in 2022. A price index turns past prices into today’s dollars.
The quantity theory of money gives \(P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\) and \(\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y\): in the long run, faster money growth means higher inflation, one for one. U.S. decades and 165 economies line up as predicted, although velocity is not really constant.
The Fisher equation \(i = R + \pi\) turns nominal interest rates into real ones. U.S. real rates were negative in the 1970s and in most years since 2008.
Hyperinflations happen when governments cannot pay their bills with taxes or borrowing and print money instead: persistent high inflation is a fiscal problem. They can end as quickly as they start.
The next chapter starts the short-run part of the book, with an introduction to economic fluctuations.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig




Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website's country legends (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def add_legend_traces(fig, traces, keep=()):
    """Website: add traces that start hidden but stay in the legend (click to show), except those named in keep.

    If the figure has a slider, its steps only switch the figure's own traces, so the countries you
    clicked on stay on the chart when you move the slider.
    """
    n = len(fig.data)
    for t in traces:
        if t.name not in keep:
            t.visible = "legendonly"
        fig.add_trace(t)
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        steps = []
        for step in slider.steps:
            steps.append(dict(method=step.method, label=step.label, args=[step.args[0], step.args[1], list(range(n))]))
        slider.steps = steps
    return fig

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Model overview
So far the book has studied the long run: what sets income per person, growth and inflation over decades. But from year to year the economy does not follow its trend smoothly. It booms, it falls into recessions, jobs are lost and found, and inflation speeds up and slows down. This chapter is a first look at these short-run fluctuations, and at the tools economists use to measure them.
The short-run model takes the long run as given: potential output and long-run inflation come from the earlier chapters. What it explains is how far actual output strays from potential, measured as short-run output, and what that gap does to inflation (the Phillips curve) and to unemployment (Okun’s law). Below we write these three relationships as small functions and add the data helpers, such as recession shading and data for other countries, that the sections reuse: first to separate trend from cycle, then to document U.S. fluctuations, and finally to fit the Phillips curve and Okun’s law and run a simple experiment.
The short-run model takes the long run as given. Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) and the long-run inflation rate \(\bar{\pi}\) come from the long-run model, so they carry bars: they are exogenous here. The model explains how actual output \(Y_t\) and inflation \(\pi_t\) move around them.
Actual output is the long-run trend plus short-run fluctuations (equation 9.1). We measure the fluctuations in percent of potential output and call them short-run output:
\[\tilde{Y}_t \equiv \frac{Y_t - \bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t} \qquad (9.2)\]
When the economy booms, \(Y_t > \bar{Y}_t\) and \(\tilde{Y}_t > 0\). In a recession, \(\tilde{Y}_t < 0\). Two more relationships complete this first look at the short run:

the Phillips curve: inflation rises when output is above potential and falls when it is below, \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\). Chapter 12 calls the slope \(\bar{\nu}\) (the Greek letter nu);
Okun’s law: unemployment is above its natural rate \(\bar{u}\) when output is below potential, \(u_t - \bar{u} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{Y}_t\) (equation 9.3).

In the code, \(\tilde{Y}\), \(\Delta\pi\) and \(u-\bar{u}\) are all measured in percent (or percentage points), as in the textbook’s figures.
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook’s diagrams 9.1 and 9.6 print no numbers, so all the model figures of this notebook share one illustrative baseline:

potential output starts at \(\bar{Y}_0 = 100\) and grows by \(\bar{g} = 2\) percent a year;
short-run output swings between \(+2\) and \(-2\) percent (the \(\pm 2\%\) marked in Fig. 9.1), in a cycle that repeats every 8 years;
the slope of the Phillips curve is \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), the textbook’s “about 1/3” for the United States;
long-run inflation is \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, and Okun’s slope is \(-1/2\).

Fig. 9 is the worked answer to a textbook exercise, which gives its own numbers (\(\bar{\nu} = 1\), \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\)), and we use those there.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing g=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and np.sin is the sine function, which draws a smooth wave (np.pi is the number π).


def potential_output(t, g=2.0, Y0=100.0):
    """Potential output Ybar_t: a smooth trend that grows g percent a year, from Y0 in year 0."""
    return Y0 * (1 + g / 100) ** t


def actual_output(t, A=2.0, g=2.0, cycle=8):
    """Actual output Y_t: potential output times (1 + a wave of +-A percent that repeats every `cycle` years)."""
    return potential_output(t, g) * (1 + A / 100 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / cycle))


def short_run_output(Y, Ybar):
    """Short-run output in percent: 100 (Y - Ybar) / Ybar   (equation 9.2)."""
    return 100 * (Y - Ybar) / Ybar


def phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu=0.33):
    """Change in inflation, percentage points: delta pi = nu * Y_tilde   (the Phillips curve, Fig. 9.6)."""
    return nu * Y_tilde


def okun_law(Y_tilde, slope=-0.5):
    """Cyclical unemployment u - u_bar, percentage points: slope * Y_tilde   (Okun's law, equation 9.3)."""
    return slope * Y_tilde

The textbook writes the name of each curve next to it, so our model figures do the same instead of using a legend. side says whether the name sits above ("bottom"), beside ("middle") or below ("top") the end point.

Python note. a if condition else b is a one-line choice: it gives a when the condition is true and b otherwise. Here it moves the name 4 pixels away from the point, to the right or to the left.


def add_end_label(fig, x, y, text, color, side="middle", row=None, col=None, xanchor="left"):
    """Write a curve's name next to its end point (x, y), in the curve's color."""
    fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor=xanchor, yanchor=side,
                       xshift=4 if xanchor == "left" else -4, font=dict(color=color, size=15), row=row, col=col)

Let us try the functions on the textbook’s own examples.

Python note. An f-string such as f"Y~ = {value:+.2f}%" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals” and the + adds a sign.


print(f"Actual 980, potential 1,000:  Y~ = {short_run_output(980, 1000):+.2f}%")
print(f"Output 3% above potential:    delta pi = {phillips_curve(3.0):+.2f} points (slope 0.33)")
print(f"Output 6% below potential:    u - u_bar = {okun_law(-6.0):+.2f} points (Okun's law)")
print(f"Baseline in year 2: potential {potential_output(2):.2f}, actual {actual_output(2):.2f}, "
      f"Y~ = {short_run_output(actual_output(2), potential_output(2)):+.2f}%")

Actual 980, potential 1,000:  Y~ = -2.00%
Output 3% above potential:    delta pi = +0.99 points (slope 0.33)
Output 6% below potential:    u - u_bar = +3.00 points (Okun's law)
Baseline in year 2: potential 104.04, actual 106.12, Y~ = +2.00%


The first line is the textbook’s example: output of 980 against a potential of 1,000 is \(-20/1{,}000 = -2\) percent. With a slope of \(0.33\), output 3 percent above potential raises inflation by about 1 percentage point, and Okun’s law turns a 6 percent shortfall of output into unemployment 3 points above its natural rate.

Shading recessions
Several data figures shade the U.S. recessions, so we write the shading once, here. A small file lists the start (peak) and end (trough) month of every U.S. recession since 1960, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER).

Python note. pd.read_csv reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns, and parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2020-02-01" into real dates. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each recession: zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time. The if skips recessions that ended before the chart starts, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between two dates.


recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start="1960-01-01"):
    """Figs. 9.3 and 9.5: shade every NBER recession (peak to trough) that ends after the date start."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)

        PALETTE.append(c)
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)                                                     # ... and 20 more: 44 in all
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                    # a medium blue, too close to the U.S. navy: used last


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used in `used` (the group-mates' colors), preferring one no country has `taken` yet."""
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):                  # from the end, far from the colors always on show
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                             # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best


Python note. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (an empty dictionary when there are none), continue skips a country that already has a color, and used collects the colors of the countries that are shown together with this one.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    names: every country; groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color}
    for the textbook's countries, so the default view keeps the book's colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors

The United States keeps the chapter’s blue, and every other country gets a color that no country of its groups uses.

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Trend and cycle
We start with a made-up economy to see the key idea of the chapter: actual output equals potential output plus short-run fluctuations around it.

Fig. 1: Economic fluctuations and short-run output
Goal. See how removing the trend from actual output leaves the ups and downs of the business cycle.
Panel (a) draws actual output \(Y_t\) around a smooth potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\). Panel (b) draws short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) from equation (9.2): the same wiggle, with the trend taken out. The gray bars in panel (a) are the gaps \(Y - \bar{Y}\) at the top of the boom and at the bottom of the slump.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 8, 200) creates 200 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 8: the years at which we draw the curves. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) makes a figure with two panels, and row=..., col=... tells add_trace where to draw. fig.add_hline draws a horizontal line. We fix the axis ranges so that you can see the curves move when a parameter changes.


def fluctuations(A=2.0, g=2.0):
    """Fig. 9.1: actual and potential output (a) and short-run output (b), over one 8-year cycle."""
    t = np.linspace(0, 8, 201)                          # time, in years: t[50] = 2 and t[150] = 6
    Y, Ybar = actual_output(t, A, g), potential_output(t, g)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) Actual and potential output",
                                                        "(b) Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Y, name="Actual output, Y", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Ybar, name="Potential output, Ȳ", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")),
                  row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[2, 2, None, 6, 6], y=[Ybar[50], Y[50], None, Ybar[150], Y[150]],   # boom and slump
                             name="Gap, Y − Ȳ", mode="lines", line=dict(color=GRAY, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=short_run_output(Y, Ybar), name="Short-run output, Ỹ",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dash"), row=1, col=2)      # Ỹ = 0: output at potential
    add_end_label(fig, 8, Y[-1], "Y", BLUE, "bottom", 1, 1)          # Y and Ȳ meet at t = 8: one above,
    add_end_label(fig, 8, Ybar[-1], "Ȳ", GREEN, "top", 1, 1)         # one below
    add_end_label(fig, 8, 0, "Ỹ", TEAL, "bottom", 1, 2)
    fig.add_annotation(x=2, y=A, xref="x2", yref="y2", text="Boom: Ỹ > 0", showarrow=False, yshift=14)
    fig.add_annotation(x=6, y=-A, xref="x2", yref="y2", text="Slump: Ỹ < 0", showarrow=False, yshift=-14)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Time (years)", range=[0, 8])
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Output", range=[94, 145], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5.2, 5.2], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Boom: Ỹ = +{A:.1f}%   Slump: Ỹ = −{A:.1f}%   |   potential grows {g:.1f}% a year",
                      showlegend=False)
    return fig

Now the interactive version. Move the sliders and compare the two panels.

Source. Adapted from Fig. 9.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

Panel (b) looks just like actual output in panel (a), without the upward trend. That is why economists also call \(\tilde{Y}\) detrended output.
Raise the growth of potential output to 4 percent. In panel (a) the slump almost disappears: even at the bottom of the cycle, actual output still grows by more than 2 percent a year. In panel (b) nothing changes. Strong growth hides the cycle, which is exactly what happens with real GDP in Fig. 2.
Set \(\bar{g} = 0\) and the two panels look the same: potential output is then a constant 100, so \(Y - \bar{Y}\) and \(\tilde{Y}\) are the same numbers.

The Great Depression shows up clearly: output was 23 percent below potential in 1933. During World War II it was 35 percent above potential in 1944. But look at the first row: output 25 percent above potential in 1929. That is not a real boom. Nobody published potential output for those years, so the early values are only an estimate. Now the chart. On a ratio scale (a logarithmic axis), equal distances mean equal percentage changes. You can also pick another country. Its GDP comes from the OECD, in trillions of 2021 dollars at PPP, and starts later.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names for the legend. px.line with a list y=[...] draws one line per column. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis, and on a ratio scale the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(0.9).

def gdp_levels(country):
    """Fig. 9.2: actual and potential GDP of one country (U.S.: CBO, 2022 dollars; others: OECD, 2021 PPP dollars)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return us_levels
    data = others[others.country == country].dropna(subset=["gdp_real"])
    return data.rename(columns={"gdp_real": "Actual GDP", "gdp_potential": "Potential GDP"})


def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Tick values 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, ... (more of them for a narrow range) from low to high."""
    steps = [1, 2, 5] if high / low > 8 else [1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 7]
    if high / low < 3:
        steps = [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]       # a narrow range needs more ticks
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 3):
        for step in steps:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 3))
    return ticks


Python note. .idxmin() gives the row label of the smallest value, and .notna().any() is True when a column has at least one number.


def gdp_title(country, data):
    """Fig. 9.2: a title with the finding: the deepest slump below potential output."""
    gaps = short_run_output(data["Actual GDP"], data["Potential GDP"])
    if country == "United States":
        return "Actual and potential GDP move together, except in the 1930s and 1940s"
    if gaps.notna().any():
        return f"{country}: the deepest slump was {-gaps.min():.1f}% below potential, in {data.year[gaps.idxmin()]}"
    return f"{country}: actual GDP only (the OECD estimates no potential output)"


def gdp_chart(scale="ratio", country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.2: real GDP, actual and potential, of one country (ratio or linear scale)."""
    data = gdp_levels(country)
    unit = "Trillions of 2022 dollars" if country == "United States" else "Trillions of 2021 dollars (PPP)"
    title = gdp_title(country, data)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=["Actual GDP", "Potential GDP"], log_y=(scale == "ratio"), title=title,
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN], labels={"year": "Year", "value": unit, "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential GDP"), line_dash="dash")
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Actual GDP"), line_width=3)
    if country == "United States":
        ticks, ratio_range, linear_top = TICKS, [np.log10(0.9), np.log10(32)], 30
    else:
        low, high = 0.9 * data["Actual GDP"].min(), 1.1 * data["Actual GDP"].max()
        ticks, ratio_range, linear_top = ratio_ticks(low, high), [np.log10(low), np.log10(high)], 1.05 * high
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ticks, range=ratio_range)
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, linear_top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min() - 1, 2026])
    return fig

What to notice.

Since about 1950 the two lines are hard to tell apart. Growth is so large that the fluctuations become hard to see, an illusion of scale that Fig. 3 removes.
On the linear scale, everything before 1960 is squeezed near the bottom.
Potential output grows more slowly after the Great Recession of 2007–09 (see the key numbers below). The CBO builds potential output with a Solow-type model, so weak investment after 2008 meant less capital and slower potential growth.
Choose Greece. After 2008 its GDP fell far below potential, to 10.6 percent below in 2012, and the OECD now estimates that Greece’s potential output itself shrank, by 0.5 percent a year from 2007 to 2025. Choose Japan: potential output has grown by less than 1 percent a year since 1995.


Key numbers: the Depression, the war and slower potential growth

def potential_growth(start, end):
    """Average annual growth of potential output from year start to year end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((potential[end] / potential[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)

    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    shade_recessions(fig, "1970-01-01")

Key numbers: what does a recession cost?
The textbook adds up the output lost in a slump: about 6 percent of a year’s GDP in a typical recession. We can measure it. We walk through the quarters, and each time \(\tilde{Y}\) turns negative we start adding up the shortfall until output is back at potential. A quarter is a quarter of a year, so each quarter adds \(-\tilde{Y}/4\) percent of a year’s GDP.

Python note. series.short_run_output.items() hands over one (date, value) pair at a time. None means “no value yet”: start is None is true while we are not inside a slump. total += x is short for total = total + x.


slumps = []
start, total = None, 0.0
for date, value in series.short_run_output.items():
    if value < 0:
        if start is None:                      # a new slump begins
            start, total = date, 0.0
        total += -value / 4                    # lost output, percent of a year's GDP
    elif start is not None:                    # output is back at potential: the slump is over
        years = (date - start).days / 365.25
        slumps.append([start.strftime("%Y-%m"), date.strftime("%Y-%m"), years, total])
        start = None

Python note. px.bar draws one bar per row. fig.add_annotation writes a label with an arrow that points at a data point; ax and ay set where the label sits, in pixels from that point. f"{date:%B %Y}" prints a date as “April 2020”, and date.quarter is its quarter of the year (1 to 4).


def employment_data(country):
    """Fig. 9.4: the employment changes of one country (U.S.: monthly payroll jobs; others: quarterly, OECD)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return jobs, "Monthly"
    return emp_q[emp_q.country == country], "Quarterly"


def employment_chart(view="full range", country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.4: the percent change in employment from the month (or quarter) before."""
    data, freq = employment_data(country)
    low = data.loc[data.emp_change_pct.idxmin()]
    when = f"{low.date:%B %Y}" if country == "United States" else f"{low.date.year} Q{low.date.quarter}"
    title = "Employment grows in most months; 2008–09 and April 2020 stand out"
    if country != "United States":
        title = f"{country}: employment fell most in {when}, by {-low.emp_change_pct:.1f}% in one quarter"
    fig = px.bar(data, x="date", y="emp_change_pct", title=title,
                 labels={"date": "Year", "emp_change_pct": f"{freq} change in employment (percent)"})
    fig.update_traces(marker_color=BLUE, marker_line_width=0)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    if view == "full range":
        fig.add_annotation(x=low.date, y=low.emp_change_pct, text=f"{when}: {low.emp_change_pct:.1f}%",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=-110, ay=0)
        if country == "United States":
            fig.update_yaxes(range=[-15, 4.5], tickvals=[-14, -12, -10, -8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-1, 2], tickvals=[-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.date.min() - pd.DateOffset(months=6), data.date.max() + pd.DateOffset(months=6)])
    return fig

INFLATION_RANGES = [[-2.5, 15.5], [-5, 31], [-10, 62], [-20, 124], [-50, 310]]


def inflation_range(low, high):
    """The first range in INFLATION_RANGES that contains low and high (the widest one if none does)."""
    for bottom, top in INFLATION_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return INFLATION_RANGES[-1]

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
The Phillips curve
When output is above potential, inflation tends to rise. We draw this relationship in the model and then measure it in U.S. data.

Fig. 6: The Phillips curve
Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how short-run output moves inflation.
Think of a hot holiday toy. When demand is high, the firm that makes it runs overtime and pays its workers more, and the toy is scarce. So its price rises faster than usual. In a booming economy, it is as if every firm made the hot toy: all of them raise prices faster than the current inflation rate, so inflation goes up. In a slump the opposite happens. The Phillips curve puts this in one line:
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
When output is at potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\)), inflation is steady. Our function phillips_curve from “The model in code” draws the line. The black dot is the economy, at the short-run output you choose.

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a straight segment, here the dashed guides from the dot to the axes. An if ... elif ... else block picks one of three cases.


def phillips_diagram(nu=0.33, Y_tilde=0.0):
    """Fig. 9.6: the Phillips curve delta pi = nu * Y_tilde, with the economy at Y_tilde."""
    Y_end = min(6.0, 2.6 / nu)                          # stop the line where its name still fits below the top
    Y = np.linspace(-Y_end, Y_end, 100)
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    if dpi > 0:
        verdict = "inflation rises"
    elif dpi < 0:
        verdict = "inflation falls"
    else:
        verdict = "inflation is steady"
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name="Phillips curve", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    add_end_label(fig, Y_end, phillips_curve(Y_end, nu), "Phillips curve", TEAL, "bottom", xanchor="right")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[Y_tilde], y=[dpi], name="The economy", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=13)))
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=Y_tilde, y0=-3.2, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"))
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=-6.5, y0=dpi, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=-3.2, y=2.8, text="← Ỹ < 0: output below potential", showarrow=False)
    fig.add_annotation(x=3.2, y=-2.8, text="Ỹ > 0: output above potential →", showarrow=False)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Ỹ = {Y_tilde:+.2f}%  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = {dpi:+.2f} points: {verdict}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-6.5, 6.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Change in inflation, Δπ (points)", range=[-3.2, 3.2], tickvals=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]),
                      showlegend=False)                  # tick values: no labels in the bottom-left corner
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 9.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

To the right of zero (a boom), \(\Delta\pi > 0\): inflation rises. To the left (a slump), \(\Delta\pi < 0\): inflation falls.
The line always goes through the origin: only output at potential keeps inflation steady.
A steeper curve (a larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means a boom raises inflation faster, but also that a slump brings it down faster.


How the short-run model works: the Volcker disinflation
In 1979 U.S. inflation was above 11 percent (Fig. 5), and the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker set out to bring it down. The Phillips curve says that the only way to lower inflation is to push output below potential. Tight monetary policy did exactly that: short-run output averaged about \(-6\) percent in 1982 (Fig. 3 shows the quarters). The model then predicts falling inflation, and inflation did fall to about 3 percent by 1983.
Let us check the model’s prediction for 1981–1983 with the annual short-run output of Fig. 7 below.

Python note. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits the best straight line \(y = a + bx\) through the points (by least squares, also called OLS) and returns the slope \(b\) first and the intercept \(a\) second.

The fitted slope is about 0.35, close to the textbook’s “about 1/3”. Now we draw the data with our model line \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\), and you choose \(\bar{\nu}\). The title adds up the squared misses, the squared vertical distances between the points and the line. The smaller that number, the better the line fits.

Python note. .where(condition, "") keeps a value where the condition is true and puts "" elsewhere, so only a few years get a text label (hover over any point to see its year). np.where(condition, a, b) picks a or b row by row.


LABELS = [1966, 1974, 1975, 1979, 1982, 1983, 2009, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
phillips["label"] = phillips.year.astype(str).where(phillips.year.isin(LABELS), "")
phillips["period"] = np.where(phillips.year <= 2022, "1961–2022 (in the textbook)", "2023–2025 (new data)")
X_RANGES, Y_RANGES = [[-8.5, 6.5], [-13, 19]], [[-5.5, 5.5], [-12, 12]]   # the textbook's ranges, and wider ones


def wider(values, ranges):
    """The first range that holds all values (the last one if none does)."""
    for low, high in ranges:
        if low <= values.min() and values.max() <= high:
            return [low, high]
    return ranges[-1]

For another country, the points are the OECD’s output gap and the change in World Bank CPI inflation.

Python note. .diff() gives the change from the row before: here, \(\Delta\pi_t = \pi_t - \pi_{t-1}\).


def phillips_data(country):
    """Fig. 9.7: one point per year, short-run output and the change in inflation (U.S.: the textbook's data)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return phillips
    data = others[others.country == country].copy()
    data["d_inflation"] = data.inflation.diff()
    data = data.rename(columns={"output_gap": "short_run_output"}).dropna(subset=["short_run_output", "d_inflation"])
    data["label"] = ""
    data["period"] = f"{data.year.min()}–{data.year.max()} (OECD data)"
    return data


def phillips_fit(nu=0.33, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.7: the data with the model line delta pi = nu * Y_tilde; the title measures the fit."""
    data = phillips_data(country)
    misses = data.d_inflation - phillips_curve(data.short_run_output, nu)
    ols = np.polyfit(data.short_run_output, data.d_inflation, 1)[0]
    fig = px.scatter(data, x="short_run_output", y="d_inflation", color="period", text="label", hover_name="year",
                     color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN, "#0b4f47"],
                     labels={"short_run_output": "Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
                             "d_inflation": "Change in inflation, Δπ (points)", "period": "Years"})
    fig.update_traces(textposition="middle right", textfont_size=11, marker_size=9)
    xr, yr = wider(data.short_run_output, X_RANGES), wider(data.d_inflation, Y_RANGES)
    Y = np.linspace(xr[0], xr[1], 50)                # the model line spans the whole x-axis
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name=f"Model: Δπ = {nu:.2f} × Ỹ", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    off = (~data.d_inflation.between(yr[0], yr[1]) | ~data.short_run_output.between(xr[0], xr[1])).sum()
    note = f"  |  {off} off the chart" if off > 0 else ""
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{country}, ν = {nu:.2f}: squared misses {(misses ** 2).sum():,.1f}  |  OLS slope {ols:.2f}{note}",
                      xaxis_range=xr, yaxis_range=yr)
    return fig

The axes widen once when a country’s points need more room; points beyond even the wider axes are counted in the title.

Output below potential also means more people out of work. Okun’s law puts a number on that link.

Fig. 8: Okun’s law for the U.S. economy

For other countries we need a natural rate of unemployment too. The OECD no longer publishes its estimates in the Economic Outlook, so our file has a stand-in: unemployment_trend, a smooth trend through each country’s unemployment rate (a Hodrick–Prescott trend). Cyclical unemployment is then \(u - \text{trend}\). How much does this choice matter? We can try it on the United States, where we have both:

us_oecd = panel[panel.country == "United States"].set_index("year")
trial = pd.DataFrame({"Y_tilde": okun.set_index("year").short_run_output,
                      "cyclical": us_oecd.unemployment - us_oecd.unemployment_trend}).dropna()

      f"{np.polyfit(trial.Y_tilde, trial.cyclical, 1)[0]:.2f}")

Okun slope with the CBO natural rate: -0.62;  with a smooth trend instead: -0.38


The slope is smaller with the trend, because a trend follows unemployment up in long slumps and counts part of the slump as “natural”. Keep this in mind when you compare countries: their slopes use the trend, the U.S. one the CBO.

okun["label"] = okun.year.astype(str).where(okun.year.isin([1966, 1969, 1982, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021]), "")
OKUN_Y_RANGES = [[-3.5, 4.5], [-7, 9]]          # the textbook's range, and a wider one


def okun_data(country):
    """Fig. 9.8: one point per year, short-run output and cyclical unemployment (U.S.: the textbook's data)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return okun
    data = others[others.country == country].copy()
    data["cyclical_unemployment"] = data.unemployment - data.unemployment_trend
    data = data.rename(columns={"output_gap": "short_run_output"}).dropna(subset=["short_run_output", "cyclical_unemployment"])
    data["label"] = ""
    return data


def okun_fit(slope=-0.5, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.8: the data with the model line u - u_bar = slope * Y_tilde; the title measures the fit."""
    data = okun_data(country)
    misses = data.cyclical_unemployment - okun_law(data.short_run_output, slope)
    ols = np.polyfit(data.short_run_output, data.cyclical_unemployment, 1)[0]
    fig = px.scatter(data, x="short_run_output", y="cyclical_unemployment", text="label", hover_name="year",
                     color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN],
                     labels={"short_run_output": "Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
                             "cyclical_unemployment": "Cyclical unemployment, u − ū (points)"})
    fig.update_traces(textposition="middle right", textfont_size=11, marker_size=9, showlegend=True,
                      name=f"{country}, {data.year.min()}–{data.year.max()}")
    xr, yr = wider(data.short_run_output, X_RANGES), wider(data.cyclical_unemployment, OKUN_Y_RANGES)
    Y = np.linspace(xr[0], xr[1], 50)                # the model line spans the whole x-axis
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=okun_law(Y, slope), name=f"Model: u − ū = {slope:.2f} × Ỹ", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{country}, slope {slope:.2f}: squared misses {(misses ** 2).sum():.2f}  |  OLS slope {ols:.2f}",
                      xaxis_range=xr, yaxis_range=yr)
    return fig

What to notice.

This cloud is much tighter than the Phillips curve’s: output and unemployment move together closely.
The textbook’s rule of thumb is a slope of \(-1/2\). The best line through the origin is a bit steeper: try \(-0.6\) and compare the squared misses. The OLS slope is about \(-0.62\).
2020 lies far above the line: unemployment jumped much more than the fall in output alone predicts, as businesses closed and laid off workers during the pandemic.

Key numbers: Okun’s law in 2009 and 2020

for year in [2009, 2020]:
    row = okun[okun.year == year].iloc[0]
    print(f"{year}: Y~ = {row.short_run_output:+.2f}%, Okun predicts u - u_bar = "
          f"{okun_law(row.short_run_output):+.2f}, actual {row.cyclical_unemployment:+.2f}")

Python note. okun[okun.year == year].iloc[0] picks the one row of that year, and row.short_run_output reads one value from it.

In both years the rule of thumb falls short. In 2009 it predicts unemployment 2.3 points above the natural rate, against 3.9 in the data, and in 2020 it predicts 1.6 points against 3.6. Part of the reason is the data revisions of Fig. 7, which moved both years to the right. The textbook’s example, output about 6 percent below potential with unemployment just over 3 points above normal, fits the rule exactly: \(-\tfrac{1}{2} \times (-6) = 3\).
Your turn. Okun’s law also works backward. In which year since 1960 was cyclical unemployment lowest, and what short-run output does Okun’s law imply for it? Compare with the data.


Hint

Find the row with okun.cyclical_unemployment.idxmin(). Solving \(u - \bar{u} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\tilde{Y}\) gives \(\tilde{Y} = -2\,(u - \bar{u})\).

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Overstimulating the economy
We end with an experiment: what happens to inflation if policymakers keep output above potential year after year?

Fig. 9: The Phillips curve and the booming economy
Goal. Answer the textbook’s exercise “Overstimulating the economy”: what happens if policymakers keep output 3 percent above potential every year?
The economy starts at potential with inflation at its long-run rate, \(\bar{\pi} = 2\%\). Then output is held at \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\). The Phillips curve says inflation rises by \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) every year:
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
With the textbook’s slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), inflation goes from 2 to 5, 8 and 11 percent in three years. A computer can apply this equation year after year: a simulation.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each year. pi_path[-1] is the last number in the list, last year’s inflation, and pi_path.append(...) adds this year’s at the end. range(1, years + 1) counts 1, 2, …, years.


def simulate_inflation(pi_bar=2.0, nu=1.0, Y_tilde=3.0, years=5):
    """Inflation year by year when output is held at Y_tilde: pi_t = pi_(t-1) + nu * Y_tilde."""
    pi_path = [pi_bar]                                    # year 0: inflation at its long-run rate
    for year in range(1, years + 1):
        pi_path.append(pi_path[-1] + phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu))
    return np.arange(years + 1), np.array(pi_path)


years, pi_path = simulate_inflation()
print("Inflation, years 0 to 5:", pi_path)

Inflation, years 0 to 5: [ 2.  5.  8. 11. 14. 17.]


The figure has two panels: (a) the Phillips curve with the economy at potential and in the boom (the two black dots), and (b) the inflation path \(\pi\) that the boom produces, against long-run inflation \(\bar{\pi}\) (dashed).

def booming_economy(pi_bar=2.0, nu=1.0, Y_tilde=3.0):
    """Fig. 9.9: the economy held at Y_tilde on the Phillips curve (a) and the inflation path (b)."""
    years, pi_path = simulate_inflation(pi_bar, nu, Y_tilde)
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    Y = np.linspace(-6.5, 6.5, 100)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) The Phillips curve", "(b) Inflation, year by year"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name="Phillips curve", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)),
                  row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, Y_tilde], y=[0, dpi], name="At potential and in the boom", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=pi_path, name="Inflation, π", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), marker=dict(size=9)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 5], y=[pi_bar, pi_bar], name="Long-run inflation, π̄", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
    up = pi_path[-1] >= pi_bar                            # does inflation end above its long-run rate?
    add_end_label(fig, 5, pi_path[-1], "π", BLUE, "bottom" if up else "top", 1, 2)
    add_end_label(fig, 5, pi_bar, "π̄", GRAY, "top" if up else "bottom", 1, 2)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-6.5, 6.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Change in inflation, Δπ", range=[-6.5, 6.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Years of the boom", range=[-0.3, 5.3], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Inflation (percent)", range=[-36, 42], tickvals=[-30, -20, -10, 0, 10, 20, 30], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = {dpi:+.2f} a year: "
                            f"π = {pi_path[0]:.2f} → {pi_path[1]:.2f} → {pi_path[2]:.2f} → {pi_path[3]:.2f}%",
                      showlegend=False)
    return fig

This time we use interact_manual. It adds a button, so nothing happens until you press it. Set the three sliders, then press Run the economy.

run_economy(booming_economy,

            nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.1, max=1.5, step=0.01, description="slope ν", style=WIDE),
            Y_tilde=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=-4.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="short-run output Ỹ (%)", style=WIDE));

slider_figure(booming_economy, "nu", [0.25, 0.33, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5], start=1.0, label="slope of the Phillips curve ν")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 9.9 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., the textbook’s worked answer to Exercise 3 of Chapter 9 (“Overstimulating the economy”), which also inspired panel (b): the simulated inflation path is our own addition.
What to notice.

Holding output above potential does not raise inflation once: it raises it every year. The cost of a permanent boom is ever-rising inflation.
The steeper the Phillips curve, the faster inflation climbs. With the U.S. slope of about 0.33, inflation rises by about 1 point a year instead of 3, slower but without end.
Set \(\tilde{Y}\) below zero and the same mechanism brings inflation down: that is how a recession fights inflation.

Your turn. The textbook’s oil-shock exercise starts with inflation at 6 percent. With a slope of \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), what constant short-run output brings inflation down to 3 percent in exactly 3 years? Find it with the sliders, then check it with simulate_inflation.


Hint

Inflation must fall by 3 points in 3 years, so by 1 point a year. Solve \(-1 = 0.5 \times \tilde{Y}\), then call simulate_inflation(pi_bar=6.0, nu=0.5, Y_tilde=...).

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Concluding remarks

Actual output is potential output plus short-run fluctuations. Short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t = (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\) is positive in a boom and negative in a recession.
U.S. recessions push output a few percent below potential, cost millions of jobs and, in total, several percent of a year’s GDP. Potential output is only estimated, so the measured gaps change when the data are revised.
Inflation usually falls during a recession. The Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) captures this, with a U.S. slope of about 1/3; oil and other shocks move inflation too.
Okun’s law links output and unemployment: each point of output below potential adds about half a point of unemployment.
The next chapter uses this short-run lens on the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic.

Setup
We first load the Python libraries we need. You only have to run this cell once.

Python note. import loads a library, a toolbox written by other people. We give each library a short nickname, for example np for NumPy, so that the code stays short. Text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it, and it is there for human readers. The try ... except block runs one Colab-only line and simply skips it anywhere else.


# Libraries used in this chapter
import numpy as np                    # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go     # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio
from ipywidgets import interact, Dropdown, ToggleButtons, SelectMultiple

# One light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
ORANGE = "#e0a33b"                              # an extra color for the six-country comparison
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)   # same size in Colab and on the website
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full widget labels

# Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# The data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch10/"

The next cell defines a helper that only the book website needs. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 10: The Great Recession and the Covid-19 Pandemic: A First Look
text:
Model overview
This chapter tells the story of two recent shocks with data rather than with a new model. The global financial crisis of 2007–09 began in the housing market and spread through banks and financial markets to the whole economy. The Covid-19 pandemic of 2020 was a very different shock: a sudden stop in activity that was deeper but much shorter. To compare the two episodes with each other and with earlier recessions, we keep asking the same few questions: how far did a series fall from its peak, when did it hit bottom, and how long did it take to recover?
Below we write the small tools that answer those questions once, so that every figure can reuse them: a percent change, a peak-to-trough measure, shaded bands for the recessions dated by the NBER, helpers for comparing many countries, and the balance sheet of a bank, which shows how borrowed money (leverage) turns a modest fall in asset prices into a crisis.
This chapter has no new economic model. It describes two recessions with data, and it adds a few tools from financial economics that later chapters use. We put the tools here once and reuse them.
Measuring a crash. Most figures ask the same question: how far did a series fall from its peak to its trough? The answer is a percent change,
\[\%\Delta = 100 \times \left(\frac{X_{\text{trough}}}{X_{\text{peak}}} - 1\right).\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description. For a pandas Series with dates as row labels, series[start:end] keeps the rows between two dates, .idxmax() gives the date of the largest value and .idxmin() the date of the smallest. A function can return several results at once, separated by commas.


def percent_change(new, old):
    """Percent change from old to new: 100 (new / old - 1)."""
    return 100 * (new / old - 1)


def peak_to_trough(series, start, end):
    """The highest point between start and end, the lowest point after it, and the fall in percent."""
    window = series[start:end]
    peak = window.idxmax()                      # date of the highest value
    trough = window[peak:].idxmin()             # date of the lowest value after the peak
    return peak, trough, percent_change(window[trough], window[peak])


def low_to_high(series, start, end):
    """The opposite measure: the highest point between start and end, the lowest point before it, and the rise."""
    window = series[start:end]
    high = window.idxmax()                      # date of the highest value
    low = window[:high].idxmin()                # date of the lowest value before it
    return low, high, window[high] - window[low]

For a series that rises in a recession, such as the unemployment rate, low_to_high measures the rise from the lowest point to the highest one, in the units of the series (percentage points for a rate).
Recessions. Five figures shade the U.S. recessions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file recessions.csv lists, for each recession since 1953, the peak (the last month before the recession) and the trough (its last month), and the same dates in quarters. One small function adds the shaded bands to any figure.

Python note. parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2007-12-01" into real dates. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each recession: zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time. The if skips recessions that ended before the chart starts, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between two dates.


recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv",
                         parse_dates=["peak", "trough", "peak_quarter", "trough_quarter"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start="2000-01-01"):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after `start` (Figs. 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9)."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    return fig

The Great Recession runs from the peak in December 2007 to the trough in June 2009, and the Covid-19 recession from February to April 2020, only two months.

Tools for comparing countries
The textbook’s figures show the United States, and two of them the U.K. and the euro area. But the financial crisis and the pandemic hit the whole world, and the same data exist for many other economies: the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) collects house prices and central bank interest rates, the OECD unemployment, employment, stock prices and output gaps, and the IMF and Eurostat consumer prices. Most figures below therefore get a “Beyond the U.S.” part, where you pick the countries. Each of those data files is long: one row per country and date. The small file countries.csv lists every economy with its region.

countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")

A country should keep its color in every chart, so we give each one a fixed color once. The textbook’s economies keep the chapter’s colors.

Python note. enumerate(...) hands over each country name together with its position i (0, 1, 2, …). i % len(PALETTE) is the remainder of the division, so the positions cycle through the list of colors. .update({...}) overwrites some entries of a dictionary.


PALETTE = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet + px.colors.qualitative.Light24
COUNTRY_COLORS = {}
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    COUNTRY_COLORS[name] = PALETTE[i % len(PALETTE)]
COUNTRY_COLORS.update({"United States": BLUE, "United Kingdom": GREEN, "Euro area": TEAL,
                       "S. Korea": "#5aa0d8", "Sweden": ORANGE, "Germany": "#0b4f47"})

Three small functions do the work in every “Beyond the U.S.” chart. pick keeps the rows of the chosen countries and lists the chosen countries that have no data. largest_fall and largest_rise apply peak_to_trough and low_to_high to each chosen country and report the most extreme one.

Python note. panel.country.isin(names) is true for the rows of the chosen countries, and panel[column].notna() for the rows with a value; & requires both. for name, rows in chosen.groupby("country") visits one country at a time, with rows holding its rows. None means “nothing found yet”. ", ".join(missing) glues a list of names into one text, separated by commas. In a Plotly title, <br> starts a new line and <sup>...</sup> writes smaller text.


def pick(panel, names, column):
    """Rows of the chosen countries that have a value in `column`, and the chosen countries without data."""
    chosen = panel[panel.country.isin(names) & panel[column].notna()]
    missing = []
    for name in names:
        if name not in set(chosen.country):
            missing.append(name)
    return chosen, missing


def no_data_note(missing):
    """A second, smaller title line that names the chosen countries without data."""
    if missing:
        return "<br><sup>No data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"
    return ""


def largest_fall(chosen, column, start, end):
    """Among the chosen countries, the largest peak-to-trough fall between start and end."""
    worst = None
    for name, rows in chosen.groupby("country"):
        series = rows.set_index("date")[column]
        if len(series[start:end]) > 1:
            peak, trough, change = peak_to_trough(series, start, end)
            if worst is None or change < worst[3]:
                worst = (name, peak, trough, change)
    return worst                                # (country, peak date, trough date, percent change)


def largest_rise(chosen, column, start, end):
    """Among the chosen countries, the largest rise from a low to a later high between start and end."""
    most = None
    for name, rows in chosen.groupby("country"):
        series = rows.set_index("date")[column]
        if len(series[start:end]) > 1:
            low, high, rise = low_to_high(series, start, end)
            if most is None or rise > most[3]:
                most = (name, low, high, rise)
    return most                                 # (country, low date, high date, rise in points)

The website cannot run Python, so its versions of these charts draw every country at once and show only the textbook’s countries; a click on a name in the legend adds a country, and a menu shows one region at a time. The next helper sets that up. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions with all countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def all_countries(make_figure, names, shown):
    """Draw make_figure(names) for every country; show only `shown` and add a menu by region."""
    fig = make_figure(tuple(names))
    fig.update_layout(title=make_figure(tuple(shown)).layout.title)      # the title of the textbook's view
    region = dict(zip(countries.country, countries.region))
    choices = [("Textbook's view", list(shown)), ("All countries", list(names))]
    for r in ["Americas", "Europe", "Asia and Pacific", "Africa and Middle East"]:
        choices.append((r, [n for n in names if region.get(n) == r]))
    buttons = []
    for label, members in choices:
        visible = [True if t.name in members else "legendonly" for t in fig.data]
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace in fig.data:
        trace.visible = True if trace.name in shown else "legendonly"
        # a lighter page: the country name once in the hover text instead of once per point, months without the
        # day and time, and values rounded to 2 decimals
        trace.hovertemplate = trace.hovertemplate.replace("%{hovertext}", trace.name)
        trace.hovertext = None
        if trace.x is not None and len(trace.x) > 0 and hasattr(trace.x[0], "strftime"):
            trace.x = [d.strftime("%Y-%m") for d in pd.to_datetime(trace.x)]
        trace.y = np.round(np.asarray(trace.y, dtype=float), 2)
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True, tickmode="auto")                  # the y-axis follows the visible countries
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), legend=dict(title_text="Click to add"),
                      updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", direction="down", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left",
                                        yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons, showactive=True)])
    return fig




Balance sheets and leverage (Table 10.3)
A balance sheet lists what an institution owns, its assets, and what it owes, its liabilities. The difference is its equity, or net worth: the value that belongs to its owners. Leverage is the ratio of liabilities to net worth:
\[\text{net worth} = \text{assets} - \text{liabilities}, \qquad \text{leverage} = \frac{\text{liabilities}}{\text{net worth}}.\]
The textbook’s hypothetical bank (Table 10.3, billions of dollars) is a small table.

Python note. pd.Series({...}) builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary, a set of key: value pairs in curly braces. .sum() adds up all the values. In an f-string, f"...", Python fills in the value of each expression in curly braces: {x:,} adds thousands separators and {x:.0f} rounds to 0 decimals.


def net_worth(assets, liabilities):
    """Equity (net worth) = total assets - total liabilities (Table 10.3)."""
    return assets - liabilities


def leverage(liabilities, equity):
    """Leverage ratio = total liabilities / net worth."""
    return liabilities / equity


assets = pd.Series({"Loans": 1000, "Investments": 900, "Cash and reserves": 100})
liabilities = pd.Series({"Deposits": 1000, "Short-term debt": 400, "Long-term debt": 400})
equity = net_worth(assets.sum(), liabilities.sum())
print(f"Total assets {assets.sum():,}, total liabilities {liabilities.sum():,}, net worth {equity:,}")
print(f"Leverage = {liabilities.sum():,} / {equity} = {leverage(liabilities.sum(), equity):.0f}")
print(f"Capital ratio = {100 * equity / assets.sum():.0f}% of assets; reserves = "
      f"{100 * assets['Cash and reserves'] / liabilities['Deposits']:.0f}% of deposits")

Total assets 2,000, total liabilities 1,800, net worth 200
Leverage = 1,800 / 200 = 9
Capital ratio = 10% of assets; reserves = 10% of deposits


With a leverage of 9, each 10 dollars of assets is financed by 9 dollars of debt and only 1 dollar of the owners’ money. Now let the investments gain or lose value. The liabilities do not change, so all of the gain or loss lands on net worth:

for new_investments in [1000, 600]:
    new_equity = net_worth(assets.sum() - assets["Investments"] + new_investments, liabilities.sum())
    print(f"Investments {assets['Investments']} -> {new_investments}: return "
          f"{percent_change(new_investments, assets['Investments']):+.1f}%, net worth {equity} -> {new_equity}, "
          f"return to the owners {percent_change(new_equity, equity):+.1f}%")

Investments 900 -> 1000: return +11.1%, net worth 200 -> 300, return to the owners +50.0%
Investments 900 -> 600: return -33.3%, net worth 200 -> -100, return to the owners -150.0%


A gain of 11 percent on the investments is a gain of 50 percent for the owners. A loss of a third of the investments, only 15 percent of all assets, turns net worth negative: the bank is insolvent. The same arithmetic works for a house bought for 500,000 dollars with 20 percent down:

house, mortgage = 500_000, 400_000
for price_change in [10, -10, -20]:
    new_equity = net_worth(house * (1 + price_change / 100), mortgage)
    print(f"House price {price_change:+d}%: equity {house - mortgage:,} -> {new_equity:,.0f} "
          f"({percent_change(new_equity, house - mortgage):+.0f}%)")

House price +10%: equity 100,000 -> 150,000 (+50%)
House price -10%: equity 100,000 -> 50,000 (-50%)
House price -20%: equity 100,000 -> 0 (-100%)


How small a fall wipes out the owners? Net worth is the share \(1/(1+\text{leverage})\) of assets, so a fall in asset values of that size leaves nothing. Bear Stearns had a leverage of about 35 when it collapsed in 2008:

for L in [9, 35]:
    print(f"Leverage {L}: assets need to fall by only {100 / (1 + L):.1f}% to wipe out net worth")

Leverage 9: assets need to fall by only 10.0% to wipe out net worth
Leverage 35: assets need to fall by only 2.8% to wipe out net worth


With a leverage of 35, a fall of less than 3 percent in the value of its assets was enough. The rest of the chapter shows how far house and stock prices actually fell.

title: Chapter 10: The Great Recession and the Covid-19 Pandemic: A First Look
text:
The Great Recession of 2007–2009
The financial crisis in four pictures: a boom and bust in house prices, the Fed’s interest rate, the stress between banks, and the stock market crash.

Fig. 1: A bursting bubble in U.S. housing prices?
Goal. Measure the boom and bust in U.S. house prices that started the financial crisis.
Robert Shiller’s index measures the price of a typical U.S. house, divided by the consumer price index so that it is in real terms, with 1953 = 100. We read it with dates as row labels, as a Series called house.

Python note. set_index("date") makes the dates the row labels, and .real_home_price_index then picks one column as a Series. .tail() shows the last five rows.

The index has one value per month from January 1953 to July 2026. Each boom and bust gets a search window, and peak_to_trough finds the peak and trough inside it.

Python note. BUSTS is a dictionary: each name (the key) gives a pair of dates (the value), and BUSTS[bust] looks one up. start, end = ... unpacks the pair into two variables. px.line draws the index as a line, and log_y=True gives the ratio scale. fig.add_vrect shades the bust, and fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...)) adds the two black dots for the peak and the trough. In an f-string, {peak:%b %Y} prints a date as “Dec 2005”, and {change:+.1f} a number with its sign. On a ratio (log) axis, Plotly wants the axis range as powers of ten, so we pass np.log10(...). With xref="paper" and yref="paper", a label’s position is a share of the plot area (0 = left or bottom, 1 = right or top), not a date or a value.


BUSTS = {"1970s boom and bust": ("1977-01-01", "1985-12-01"),
         "1980s boom and bust": ("1986-01-01", "1997-12-01"),
         "2000s boom and bust": ("2000-01-01", "2015-12-01"),
         "2020s so far": ("2021-01-01", "2026-07-01")}


def housing_chart(bust="2000s boom and bust"):
    """Fig. 10.1: the real home price index (ratio scale), with one boom and bust shaded."""
    start, end = BUSTS[bust]
    peak, trough, change = peak_to_trough(house, start, end)
    fig = px.line(housing, x="date", y="real_home_price_index", log_y=True,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "real_home_price_index": "Real home prices (1953 = 100)"},
                  title=f"{bust}: real home prices fell {-change:.1f}% from {peak:%b %Y} to {trough:%b %Y}")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=TEAL, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak, trough], y=[house[peak], house[trough]], mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11), showlegend=False, name="Peak and trough"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=0.02, y=0.97, xref="paper", yref="paper", xanchor="left", yanchor="top", showarrow=False,
                       text=f"Shaded: {peak:%b %Y} to {trough:%b %Y}<br>real prices {change:+.1f}%", font=dict(size=13))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=["1952-01-01", "2027-06-01"])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200], range=[np.log10(84), np.log10(250)])
    return fig


Python note. interact calls housing_chart and shows the figure it returns. bust=Dropdown(...) turns the argument bust into a menu (list(BUSTS) gives the names in the dictionary), and the figure is drawn again each time you pick an episode. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

Prepared file: data/ch10/fig10-1.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

Real house prices hardly changed for 45 years: the index was still near 100 in the late 1990s. Then it rose steeply to a peak of 171 in December 2005 and fell by 35.7 percent to February 2012.
Choose the 1970s and 1980s episodes: those busts were 12.2 and 14.4 percent, less than half of the 2006–2012 bust. That is why the textbook calls the decline after 2006 “by far the largest” since 1953.
On a ratio scale, equal distances are equal percentage changes, so the busts of different decades can be compared by eye. Since 2022 the index has stayed close to its new record (choose “2020s so far”).


Key numbers: the bubble in numbers
The textbook gives three numbers: a decline of 36 percent from the middle of 2006 to the first quarter of 2012, a next-largest decline of 14 percent, and a rise “by a factor of nearly 3 between 1996 and 2006”. house.cummax() is the highest value reached so far, so house / house.cummax() - 1 is the fall from the latest record, called the drawdown.

drawdown = 100 * (house / house.cummax() - 1)
print(f"Largest drawdown since 1953: {drawdown.min():.1f}% in {drawdown.idxmin():%b %Y}")
mid_2006, early_2012 = house["2006-04-01":"2006-06-01"].mean(), house["2012-01-01":"2012-03-01"].mean()
print(f"2006Q2 to 2012Q1 (quarterly averages): {percent_change(early_2012, mid_2006):.1f}%")
factor = house["2006"].mean() / house["1996"].mean()
print(f"1996 to 2006 (annual averages): prices x {factor:.2f}, or {100 * (factor ** (1 / 10) - 1):.1f}% a year")

Largest drawdown since 1953: -35.7% in Feb 2012
2006Q2 to 2012Q1 (quarterly averages): -35.1%
1996 to 2006 (annual averages): prices x 1.72, or 5.6% a year


The first two numbers match the textbook. The third does not: in this real index, prices rose by a factor of 1.72 between 1996 and 2006, or 5.6 percent a year, not “nearly 3” and “about 10 percent per year”. The textbook’s prose probably uses another index (for example nominal prices, or a 20-city index with the booming coastal markets). Always check which series a number comes from.


Beyond the U.S.: house prices in other countries
Was the U.S. bubble unusual? The BIS publishes real residential property prices (house prices divided by the consumer price index) for about 60 economies, quarterly, as an index with 2010 = 100. For the U.S. the BIS uses a different house-price index than Shiller, but it tells the same story: a fall of 38.9 percent from the 2006 peak, against Shiller’s 35.3 percent in quarterly averages.

Four periods tell the story. The menu zooms in on one of them, and the title reports the lowest and highest rate in that window.

Python note. px.area draws a line with the area below it filled in. fig.update_xaxes(range=[a, b]) sets the dates shown. shade_recessions(fig) is our function from “Model overview”.


PERIODS = {"2000–2026": ("2000-01-01", "2026-09-01"),
           "2004–06 hikes": ("2003-06-01", "2007-06-01"),
           "2007–08 cuts": ("2007-06-01", "2009-06-01"),
           "2022–23 hikes": ("2021-06-01", "2024-06-01")}


def fed_chart(period="2000–2026"):
    """Fig. 10.2: the effective Fed funds rate, with recessions shaded, over one period."""
    start, end = PERIODS[period]
    window = fed_rate[start:end]
    low, high = window.idxmin(), window.idxmax()
    fig = px.area(fed, x="date", y="fed_funds", labels={"date": "Year", "fed_funds": "Percent"},
                  title=f"{period}: lowest {window[low]:.2f}% ({low:%b %Y}), highest {window[high]:.2f}% ({high:%b %Y})")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fillcolor="rgba(138, 150, 163, 0.3)")
    shade_recessions(fig)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[pd.Timestamp(start) - pd.DateOffset(months=6), pd.Timestamp(end) + pd.DateOffset(months=3)])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 8], tickvals=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])   # no 0 label: it would crowd the first year
    return fig

What to notice.

After the 2001 recession, the Fed kept the rate at about 1 percent until mid-2004, then raised it step by step to above 5 percent by mid-2006. Higher rates made mortgages more expensive just as house prices peaked.
From August 2007 the Fed cut, and by December 2008 the rate was close to zero. It stayed there for seven years: zero is a floor for interest rates, the zero lower bound of Chapters 11 and 14.
In 2020 the rate went back to zero. In 2022 the Fed raised it again, quickly, to fight inflation (Fig. 10), to 5.33 percent by August 2023.


Key numbers: target rates and effective rates
The textbook says that between May 2004 and May 2006 the Fed raised its rate “from 1.25 percent to 5.25 percent”.

def policy_world(names=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 10.2 beyond the U.S.: BIS central bank policy rates (end of month) in the chosen countries."""
    chosen, missing = pick(rates_panel, names, "policy_rate")
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="date", y="policy_rate", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COUNTRY_COLORS, line_shape="hv",          # rates change in steps
                  labels={"date": "Year", "policy_rate": "Policy rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    most = largest_rise(chosen, "policy_rate", "2021-01-01", "2024-12-31")
    title = "No data for 2021–24"
    if most is not None:
        name, low, high, rise = most
        title = f"Largest 2021–24 hike: {name}, +{rise:.2f} points ({low:%b %Y} to {high:%b %Y})"
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=title + no_data_note(missing))
    return fig

Fig. 3: Liquidity and risk shocks from interest rate spreads
Goal. See the financial crisis in the price banks paid to borrow from one another.
The TED spread is the 3-month LIBOR rate (what banks charged one another) minus the 3-month Treasury bill rate (what the U.S. government pays). Lending to the government is safe, so the spread is a risk premium: it rises when banks fear that other banks might not repay. LIBOR was discontinued in 2022, so the data file adds a second, similar spread that continues: AA-rated financial commercial paper minus the Treasury bill.

The textbook’s “modest premium of 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points” is the calm phase, on average 0.33 points. From August 2007 the spread averaged 1.31 points, close to the textbook’s “between 1.0 and 1.5”. The textbook’s “more than 4.5 percentage points” refers to single days in October 2008: monthly averages, as in our file, smooth the spike to 3.35 points.


Beyond the U.S.: stress in other money markets
The TED spread exists only in U.S. dollars, and LIBOR is gone. But the OECD publishes two money-market rates for 35 economies: a 3-month interbank rate (a 3-month loan between banks, like LIBOR) and an overnight interbank rate (a one-day loan, which follows the policy rate). Their difference is a risk premium too: a bank that lends for three months instead of one day fears more that the borrower fails. It is not the TED spread, and it also moves when banks expect the policy rate to change. For the U.S. it peaks in the same month as the TED spread, October 2008, but at 2.22 instead of 3.35 points.

Python note. If \(L = 100 \ln(P_t/P_{t-12})\), then \(P_t/P_{t-12} = e^{L/100}\), and the percent change is \(100\,(e^{L/100} - 1)\). np.exp is the exponential function \(e^x\), and it works on a whole column at once. def percent_from_log(log_change):
    """Turn a log change 100 ln(P_t / P_t-12) into a percent change 100 (P_t / P_t-12 - 1)."""
    return 100 * (np.exp(log_change / 100) - 1)

The y-axis keeps the textbook’s range up to 12 percent and widens in a few fixed steps only when a chosen country needs it, so the chart does not jump around with every country you add.

Python note. axis_top walks through a short list of possible tops and returns the first one that is not below the highest value. Fixed steps keep the axis still while you add countries with similar inflation.


def axis_top(value, tops=(12, 25, 50, 100, 150)):
    """The smallest of a few fixed axis tops that is at least `value`."""
    for top in tops:
        if value <= top:
            return top
    return tops[-1]

def core_chart(view="core, all three"):
    """Fig. 10.11: core inflation in three economies, or headline and core inflation in one."""
    if view == "core, all three":
        data = both.rename(columns={CORE["U.S."]: "U.S.", CORE["U.K."]: "U.K.", CORE["Euro area"]: "Euro area"})
        series, colors = ["U.S.", "U.K.", "Euro area"], AREA_COLORS
