What to notice.

The bust alone (panel a) takes output to \(-2\) percent. Cutting \(R\) from 5 to 4 percent (panel b) brings it back to potential: in the model, monetary policy can fully offset a demand shock.
The larger the shock, the larger the cut. The flatter the IS curve (larger \(\bar{b}\)), the smaller the cut needed.
In practice this is hard. It takes time to see how large the shock is, and Milton Friedman’s “long and variable lags” mean that interest rates need 6–18 months to have their main effect. In 2008 the housing bust turned out to be much more than an ordinary demand shock (Chapter 14).

Python note. .dropna(subset=["spread"]) drops the months in which one of the two rates is missing. The loop over [(-10, 15), (-20, 35)] widens both ends of the axis in two steps, only when a chosen country needs it.


def spread_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.6, extended: the term spread (10-year minus 3-month rate) of the chosen countries."""
    part = yields[yields.country.isin(countries)].dropna(subset=["spread"])
    low, high = -3, 5
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(-10, 15), (-20, 35)]:
        if part.spread.min() < low or part.spread.max() > high:
            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y="spread", color="country", color_discrete_map=SPREAD_COLORS,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "spread": "10-year minus 3-month rate (points)", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Below zero, the yield curve is inverted" + missing_or_off(part, "spread", countries, low, high))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2000-01-01", "2026-12-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

text:
The Phillips curve
The Phillips curve links output to changes in inflation. We add a price shock, such as an oil price increase, and look at U.S. inflation over the long run.

Fig. 7: The Phillips curve
Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how the state of the economy changes inflation.
Imagine you run a firm and inflation has been 5 percent a year. You expect it to stay there, so normally you raise your prices by 5 percent. If demand for your products is weak, you raise them by less, to win back customers; if demand is strong, by more. When all firms do this, inflation equals last year’s inflation plus an adjustment for demand:
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}.\]
A booming economy (\(\tilde{Y} > 0\)) raises inflation; a slumping one lowers it. The slope \(\bar{\nu}\) measures how strongly prices react to demand. As with the IS diagram, one function draws three textbook figures: the Phillips curve itself (12.7), an oil shock (12.8) and a recession (12.11). Its arguments are short-run output Y_new, the price shock o_new and the slope nu.

Python note. for x, y, anchor, text in REGIONS: takes the list of (x, y, anchor, text) groups one at a time and unpacks each into four names. dict(X_OUTPUT, title=...) copies the settings of X_OUTPUT and replaces the title. Y_DPI if fits else Y_DPI_WIDE is a one-line if: it gives the first axis when fits is true (both conditions joined by and hold) and the wider one otherwise. yaxis["range"][1] looks up the axis range and takes its second number, the top of the axis.


REGIONS = [(-7.6, 3.4, "left", "Δπ > 0:<br>inflation rises"), (7.6, -3.4, "right", "Δπ < 0:<br>inflation falls")]
X_SLUMP_BOOM = dict(X_OUTPUT, title="←  Below potential (slump)          Short-run output, Ỹ (%)          Above potential (boom)  →")


def pc_experiment(Y_new=0.0, o_new=O_BAR, nu=NU):
    """Figs. 12.7, 12.8, 12.11: the Phillips curve, a price shock o' that shifts it, and the economy at Y~."""
    dpi = phillips(Y_new, nu, o_new)
    fits = abs(dpi) <= 3.4 and abs(phillips(2.0, nu, o_new)) <= 3.4
    yaxis = Y_DPI if fits else Y_DPI_WIDE                  # a wider axis only when B or the shift would not fit
    top = yaxis["range"][1]
    fig = go.Figure()
    if o_new != O_BAR:
        add_pc(fig, "PC", GRAY, nu, O_BAR, "dash", top=top)
        add_pc(fig, "PC′", GREEN, nu, o_new, top=top)
        add_arrow(fig, 2.0, phillips(2.0, nu), 2.0, phillips(2.0, nu, o_new))      # the shift of the curve
    else:
        add_pc(fig, "Phillips curve", GREEN, nu, top=top)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, phillips(0.0, nu, o_new), "A", -8, -top, where="top left")  # top left: off the rising curve
    if Y_new != 0.0:
        add_point(fig, Y_new, dpi, "B", -8, -top, where="top left")
        add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.3 - top, Y_new, 0.3 - top)                            # the change in output
    for x, y, anchor, text in REGIONS:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor=anchor, font=dict(size=13, color=GRAY))
    set_axes(fig, X_SLUMP_BOOM, yaxis)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Ỹ = {Y_new:+.1f}%, ō = {o_new:+.1f}  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_new:+.1f}) + ({o_new:+.1f}) = {dpi:+.2f}")
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

At potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\), point \(A\)) inflation is steady: this year’s inflation equals last year’s.
An economy 2 percent above potential raises inflation by \(0.5 \times 2 = 1\) point a year, and it keeps rising as long as the boom lasts.
A steeper curve (larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means prices react more to demand. With a flat curve it takes a deep recession to lower inflation by one point.

A brief history. A. W. Phillips first related the level of (wage) inflation to economic activity. In the 1960s many economists concluded that a country could keep output high for ever by accepting, say, 5 instead of 2 percent inflation. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that firms would soon build the higher inflation into their prices: holding output above potential would make inflation rise year after year, which is the version of the curve used here. The rising inflation of the 1970s proved them right.

Fig. 8: An oil price increase
Goal. See how a price shock moves inflation even when output is at potential.
When oil prices jump, gasoline, airline tickets and heating cost more at once, and firms that use oil as an input pass the higher cost on to their prices. In the model this is a positive price shock \(\bar{o}\): the Phillips curve shifts up by \(\bar{o}\) for one period. Even at potential, inflation now rises by \(\bar{o}\). Economists call such increases cost-push inflation, and the \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) term demand-pull inflation. Price shocks can also come from other inputs (steel), from large union wage settlements (\(\bar{o} > 0\)), or from a large inflow of workers that holds wages down (\(\bar{o} < 0\)). The textbook’s figure has no number; we use \(\bar{o} = 1\) point.

To keep inflation steady after the shock, output would have to fall to \(\tilde{Y} = -\bar{o}/\bar{\nu} = -2\) percent: a price shock confronts the central bank with a hard choice.
Quantity theory or Phillips curve? Chapter 8 found that faster growth of real GDP lowers inflation; here a boom raises it. The two are about different things: the quantity theory is a long-run model in which more output means more supply of goods; here higher short-run output means more demand than the economy’s potential.


Key numbers: demand-pull and cost-push
The change in inflation has two parts, \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) and \(\bar{o}\). A loop computes them for a few cases.

def inflation_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 12.9: inflation, the policy rate i and the real interest rate R = i − π of one country."""
    part = world[world.country == country]
    worst = part.loc[part.inflation.idxmax()]
    low, high = -8, 18
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(-20, 40), (-50, 100)]:   # a wider axis only when the country needs it
        if part.inflation.max() > high or part.policy_rate.max() > high or part.real_rate.min() < low:
            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    title = f"{country}: inflation peaked at {worst.inflation:.1f}% in {worst.year}"
    if country == "United States":
        title = f"Inflation peaked at {worst.inflation:.1f}% in {worst.year} and tends to fall after shaded recessions"
    if part.inflation.max() > high or part.policy_rate.max() > high or part.real_rate.min() < low:
        title += " (off the chart)"
    fig = px.area(part, x="date", y="inflation", labels={"date": "Year", "inflation": "Percent"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(name="Inflation (CPI)", showlegend=True, line_color=TEAL)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.policy_rate, visible="legendonly", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2),
                             name="Fed funds rate, i" if country == "United States" else "Policy rate, i"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.real_rate, name="Real interest rate, R = i − π",
                             visible="legendonly", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    if country == "United States":
        shade_recessions(fig, "1960-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1959-01-01", "2026-12-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high],
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

Using the short-run model: disinflation and the Great Inflation
Now we put the three pieces together and run the model through time, first for the Volcker disinflation of the early 1980s and then for a policy mistake of the 1970s.

Fig. 10: Tightening monetary policy
Goal. Follow the first step of the Volcker disinflation in the IS/MP diagram.
By 1979 inflation exceeded 10 percent. Paul Volcker’s Fed slowed money growth, which means raising the nominal interest rate. Because inflation is sticky, the real rate rises too: \(R' = i' - \pi\). With inflation at 10 percent, a nominal rate of 15 percent keeps \(R = 5\% = \bar{r}\); raising it to 16 percent lifts the real rate to 6 percent, and output falls to the textbook’s \(-2\) percent. The function reuses ismp_experiment and only adds the Fisher step.

def tightening(i_new=16.0, pi=10.0):
    """Fig. 12.10: with sticky inflation pi, a higher nominal rate i' raises R' = i' - pi and lowers output."""
    R_new = real_rate(i_new, pi)
    fig = ismp_experiment(R_new=R_new)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"i′ = {i_new:.1f}% and sticky π = {pi:.1f}%  →  R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ = {is_curve(R_new):+.1f}%")
    return fig

         i_new=FloatSlider(value=16.0, min=13.0, max=17.5, step=0.5, description="new nominal interest rate i′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         pi=FloatSlider(value=10.0, min=9.0, max=11.0, step=0.5, description="sticky inflation π (%)", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

Only the real rate matters for output: \(i' = 16\) with \(\pi = 10\) has the same effect as \(i' = 7\) with \(\pi = 1\).
If inflation were not sticky (if the classical dichotomy held even in the short run), a higher nominal rate could simply come with lower inflation and leave output alone. Stickiness is what gives monetary policy real effects.
In 1981 the effective fed funds rate averaged 16.4 percent, and the real rate was about 6 percent (Fig. 9): the deepest recession in decades followed.

Fig. 12: The disinflation over time
Goal. Run the Volcker policy year by year and watch inflation come down.
The Fed raises the real interest rate in year 0 and keeps it high until year \(t^*\), when inflation has fallen enough; then it returns \(R\) to \(\bar{r}\). Each year the model takes three steps: the MP curve sets \(R_t\), the IS curve gives \(\tilde{Y}_t\), and the Phillips curve gives \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\). That is exactly our simulate function. Inflation starts at the textbook’s 10 percent. Inflation in year 0 already falls, because \(\pi_0 = (P_1 - P_0)/P_0\): firms set next year’s prices when they see this year’s recession.

Python note. np.arange(-2, 10) is the years \(-2, -1, \ldots, 9\). np.where(condition, a, b) gives a where the condition is true and b elsewhere: here a high rate from year 0 to \(t^* - 1\) and \(\bar{r}\) otherwise. & means “and”. line_shape="hv" draws steps: a flat line, then a jump. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers. pi_path.min() is the smallest number in the array: if a long, deep recession pushes inflation below zero (deflation), the inflation axis extends below zero to show it.


def disinflation(Y_rec=-2.0, t_star=5, nu=NU):
    """Fig. 12.12: the Fed holds R high from year 0 to t*; output is Y_rec and inflation falls from 10%."""
    years = np.arange(-2, 10)
    R_path = np.where((years >= 0) & (years < t_star), rate_for_output(Y_rec), R_BAR)
    Y_path, pi_path = simulate(R_path, pi_start=10.0, nu=nu)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, horizontal_spacing=0.09,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) R held high until t*", "(b) Output below potential", "(c) Inflation steps down"))
    paths = [R_path, Y_path, pi_path]
    colors, shapes = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN], ["hv", "hv", "linear"]
    axes = [dict(title="Real interest rate, R (%)", range=[2.5, 7.5]), dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (%)", range=[-4.5, 1.5]),
            dict(title="Inflation, π (%)", range=[min(0.0, pi_path.min() - 1.0), 11.5])]   # widens only below zero
    for k in range(3):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=paths[k], mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, line_shape=shapes[k],
                                 line=dict(color=colors[k], width=4), marker=dict(color="black", size=9)), row=1, col=k + 1)
        set_axes(fig, dict(title="Year", tickvals=[0, t_star], ticktext=["0", "t*"], range=[-2.5, 9.5]), axes[k], 1, k + 1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"π: 10.0% → {pi_path[-1]:.1f}% with Ỹ = {Y_rec:+.1f}% until t* = {t_star};"
                            f"  output lost: {-Y_path.sum():.1f} %-years")
    return fig

What to notice.

Five years at \(\tilde{Y} = -2\) percent bring inflation from 10 to 5 percent, one point a year. When the Fed returns \(R\) to \(\bar{r}\), output goes back to potential and inflation stays at its new, lower level.
The price is 10 “percent-years” of lost output: 2 percent of GDP for five years, or 2 percent-years for each point of inflation removed.
A deeper recession gets there faster, at about the same total cost: with \(\tilde{Y} = -4\) it takes 2.5 years. Only a steeper Phillips curve makes the disinflation cheaper.
In reality, inflation fell from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983 (Fig. 9), faster than in this example, and the recession of 1981–1982 was the deepest in decades.

Fig. 13: Mistaking a slowdown in potential for a recession
Goal. See how a slowdown in potential output, mistaken for a recession, can feed inflation.
From the early 1970s, U.S. productivity growth slowed down, so potential output grew more slowly. At the time, policymakers thought potential output was still growing at its old rate. They saw actual output fall behind that believed path, read it as a recession (\(\tilde{Y}_{\text{perceived}} < 0\)), and lowered interest rates. In truth output was then above its true potential (\(\tilde{Y}_{\text{true}} > 0\)), and through the Phillips curve inflation rose.
The textbook’s figure is stylized, so we describe it with three numbers: potential growth before 1973 (g_old), after 1973 (g_new), and how far the stimulus eventually pushes output above true potential (gap_max, reached gradually). Output is an index with 1973 = 100. This small model is used only here, so we define it in this section.

Python note. np.exp is the exponential function: an index growing at g percent a year is \(100\,e^{g\,(t - 1973)/100}\). np.minimum(x, 0) keeps the negative values of x and sets the others to 0, and np.maximum(x, 0) does the opposite. continue skips the rest of the loop for the current item.


def output_paths(g_old=3.5, g_new=2.5, gap_max=4.0):
    """Fig. 12.13: believed potential, true potential and actual output (1973 = 100)."""
    years = np.arange(1965, 1986)
    before, after = np.minimum(years - 1973, 0), np.maximum(years - 1973, 0)
    believed = 100 * np.exp(g_old * (years - 1973) / 100)
    true = 100 * np.exp((g_old * before + g_new * after) / 100)
    gap_true = gap_max * (1 - np.exp(-after / 4))      # the stimulus pushes output above true potential
    actual = true * (1 + gap_true / 100)
    return years, believed, true, actual


def slowdown(g_old=3.5, g_new=2.5, gap_max=4.0):
    """Fig. 12.13 with readouts: the perceived and the true output gap, and the rise in inflation."""
    years, believed, true, actual = output_paths(g_old, g_new, gap_max)
    perceived_gap, true_gap = 100 * (actual / believed - 1), 100 * (actual / true - 1)
    dpi = phillips(true_gap[(years > 1973) & (years <= 1980)]).sum()   # Phillips curve, 1974-1980
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=believed, name=f"Believed potential ({g_old:g}% a year)", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=actual, name="Actual output (with the stimulus)", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=true, name=f"True potential ({g_new:g}% a year after 1973)", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4, dash="dash")))
    gaps = [(actual[-1], believed[-1], "seen as Ỹ < 0"), (true[-1], actual[-1], "true Ỹ > 0")]
    for low, high, text in gaps:
        if high - low < 4:                             # no bracket (and no false label) for a gap that is not there
            continue
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1985.4, 1985.4], y=[low, high], mode="lines", showlegend=False, line=dict(color="black", width=2)))
        fig.add_annotation(x=1985.6, y=(low + high) / 2, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(size=13))
    k = 1980 - 1965                                    # the position of 1980 in the arrays
    fig.add_vline(x=1973, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"1980: perceived Ỹ = {perceived_gap[k]:+.1f}%, true Ỹ = {true_gap[k]:+.1f}%;"
                            f" inflation +{dpi:.1f} points since 1973",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[1964, 1990], tickvals=[1965, 1970, 1973, 1980, 1985]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output (index, 1973 = 100)", range=[60, 190]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

By 1980 actual output is 3.7 percent below the believed path, so policymakers see a recession and keep stimulating. Yet it is 3.3 percent above true potential.
The true gap is positive every year after 1973, so the Phillips curve raises inflation every year: about 8 points by 1980 with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\). Actual U.S. inflation rose from 6.3 percent in 1973 to 13.5 percent in 1980, also helped by the oil shocks of 1974 and 1979.
Set the growth rate after 1973 equal to the one before: there is no slowdown, the two dashed paths coincide, and the stimulus is plainly a boom.
Policymakers learn of their mistake through rising inflation, but oil shocks also raise inflation, which made the lesson slow to learn.

def gdp_index_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.14, extended: real GDP of the chosen countries, 2019Q4 = 100."""
    part = gdp_world[gdp_world.country.isin(countries)]
    low, high = 80, 120
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(70, 130), (60, 160)]:   # a wider axis only when a chosen country needs it
        if part.index_2019q4.min() < low or part.index_2019q4.max() > high:
            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    title = "Real GDP since the end of 2019 (2019Q4 = 100)"
    if len(countries) == 1 and len(part) > 0:
        fall = 100 - part.index_2019q4[part.date.dt.year == 2020].min()
        title = f"{countries[0]}: real GDP fell {fall:.1f}% in 2020 (2019Q4 = 100)"
    title += missing_or_off(part, "index_2019q4", countries, low, high)
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y="index_2019q4", color="country", color_discrete_map=GDP_COLORS, markers=True,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "index_2019q4": "Real GDP, 2019Q4 = 100", "country": "Country"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(marker_size=4)
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2014-10-01", "2026-10-01"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

def cpi_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 12.15: 12-month CPI inflation, all items and core, of one country since January 2020."""
    part = cpi_world[cpi_world.country == country].rename(
        columns={"inflation_all": "All items", "inflation_core": "Core (less food and energy)"})
    values = part[["All items", "Core (less food and energy)"]]
    for low, high in [(0, 10), (-4, 12), (-5, 30), (-10, 100), (-20, 300)]:
        if values.min().min() >= low and values.max().max() <= high:
            break                                       # the first range that holds every value
    title = "No all-items CPI data for this country"
    every = part.set_index("date")["All items"].dropna()
    if not every.empty:
        dip = every[every.index.year == 2020]
        later = every[every.index > dip.idxmin()]
        title = f"CPI inflation fell to {round(dip.min(), 1) + 0.0:.1f}% in {dip.idxmin():%B %Y}"
        if not later.empty:
            title += f", then rose to {later.max():.1f}% in {later.idxmax():%B %Y}"
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y=["All items", "Core (less food and energy)"], title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent change over 12 months", "variable": "CPI"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=2, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, annotation_text="2 percent", annotation_position="bottom right")
    if country == "United States":
        shade_recessions(fig, "2020-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2019-12-01", "2026-10-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text=country,
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

At the start of the pandemic, inflation fell, as the Phillips curve predicts for a weak economy: from 2.6 percent in January 2020 to 0.2 percent in May 2020.
Within a year it rose to levels not seen in four decades: 9.0 percent in June 2022 (the last higher reading was 9.6 percent in November 1981). Core inflation peaked later, at 6.6 percent in September 2022.

    title = "General government spending, percent of GDP"
    by_year = part.set_index("year").spending_gdp
    if len(countries) == 1 and by_year.get(2019) is not None and by_year.get(2020) is not None:
        title = f"{countries[0]}: spending went from {by_year[2019]:.1f}% of GDP in 2019 to {by_year[2020]:.1f}% in 2020"
    title += missing_or_off(part, "spending_gdp", countries, 0, high)
    fig = px.line(part, x="year", y="spending_gdp", color="country", color_discrete_map=SPENDING_COLORS, markers=True,

    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[2006.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=[0, high], legend_title_text="")

title: Chapter 12: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
section: How central banks control the nominal interest rate
text:
How central banks control the nominal interest rate
So far the central bank simply chose the interest rate. The money market shows how it does so: by supplying whatever money is demanded at its target rate.

Fig. 18: How the central bank sets the nominal interest rate
Goal. See where “money” comes in: the central bank sets the interest rate through the money market.
The nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding money: cash and checking accounts pay nothing, while a savings or money-market account pays \(i\). At 1 percent you might as well hold cash; at 20 percent you would keep as little as possible. So money demand \(M^d\) falls as \(i\) rises. The central bank decides how much money to supply, \(M^s\): a vertical line. The interest rate \(i^*\) is where people want to hold exactly the money supplied. If \(i\) were higher, people would want less money than there is, and the rate would fall; if lower, the opposite.
As before, one function draws two textbook figures: this one (12.18) and a change in the money supply (12.19). Its arguments are the new money supply M_new and the new level of money demand m0_new (demand is \(M^d = m_0 - i\)).

Python note. "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ" is a one-line if: it gives the first text when the condition is true and the second otherwise.


def money_experiment(M_new=M_BAR, m0_new=M0):
    """Figs. 12.18 and 12.19: money supply and demand set the nominal rate; a change moves i* to i**."""
    i_star, i_new = market_rate(M_BAR), market_rate(M_new, m0_new)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if m0_new != M0:
        add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ", GRAY, M0, "dash")
    add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ", BLUE, m0_new)
    if M_new != M_BAR:
        add_line(fig, [M_BAR, M_BAR], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ", GRAY, "dash")
        add_arrow(fig, M_BAR, 1.0, M_new, 1.0)                     # the change in the money supply
    add_line(fig, [M_new, M_new], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ′" if M_new != M_BAR else "Mˢ", TEAL)
    where = "bottom left" if m0_new > M0 else "top right"      # keep i* clear of a higher demand curve
    add_point(fig, M_BAR, i_star, "i*", 0, 0, where=where)
    if i_new != i_star:
        where = "bottom left" if m0_new < M0 else "top right"  # ... and i** clear of the old, higher one
        add_point(fig, M_new, i_new, "i**", 0, 0, where=where)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.5, i_star, 0.5, i_new)                    # the change in the interest rate
    set_axes(fig, X_MONEY, Y_NOMINAL)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Money supply {M_new:.1f}, demand Mᵈ = {m0_new:.1f} − i  →  i = {i_star:.1f}% → {i_new:.1f}%",
                      margin=dict(r=90))
    return fig

With a supply of 5 and demand \(M^d = 10 - i\), the market clears at \(i^* = 5\) percent.
Move money demand: with the money supply fixed, every shift of demand moves the interest rate one for one. People need more money when prices or output are higher, or less when they pay by card, so demand shifts all the time.
In the short run inflation is sticky, so the money market clears through the interest rate (and the velocity of money), not through the price level as in the quantity theory of Chapter 8.

Fig. 19: Raising the nominal interest rate
Goal. See what “tight money” means: to raise the interest rate, the central bank reduces the money supply.
The money supply shifts left, from \(M^s\) to \(M^{s\prime}\). At the old rate \(i^*\), people now want more money than there is: households ask their banks for cash, and banks must offer a higher interest rate on savings accounts to bring money demand back in line with supply. The rate rises to \(i^{**}\). We use our illustrative cut from 5 to 4 units of money.

# Your turn: try it here



Fig. 20: Targeting the nominal interest rate
Goal. See why central banks set an interest rate rather than a quantity of money.
Money demand shifts all the time (Fig. 18). If the central bank kept the money supply fixed, every shift would move the interest rate, and with it the real rate and output. Instead, modern central banks peg the interest rate: they supply whatever money is demanded at the target rate \(i^*\). The money supply curve becomes horizontal at \(i^*\), and shifts in money demand change the quantity of money, not the rate. Compare the two policies with the toggle.

Python note. ToggleButtons shows one button per option, and the function receives the text of the chosen button.


def rate_target(m0_new=M0, i_target=5.0, policy="peg the interest rate"):
    """Fig. 12.20: pegging i makes money supply horizontal; fixing M lets money-demand shocks move i."""
    fig = go.Figure()
    if m0_new != M0:
        add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ", GRAY, M0, "dash")
    add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ", BLUE, m0_new)
    if policy == "peg the interest rate":
        i_eq, M_eq = i_target, money_demand(i_target, m0_new)
        add_line(fig, [0.5, 10.5], [i_target, i_target], "Mˢ", TEAL)
    else:
        M_eq = money_demand(i_target)                  # the supply that gave i_target before the shock
        i_eq = market_rate(M_eq, m0_new)
        add_line(fig, [M_eq, M_eq], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, M_eq, i_eq, "", 0, 0)
    set_axes(fig, X_MONEY, Y_NOMINAL)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Policy: {policy};  demand shift {m0_new - M0:+.1f}  →  i = {i_eq:.1f}%, M = {M_eq:.1f}",
                      margin=dict(r=90))
    return fig

         policy=ToggleButtons(options=["peg the interest rate", "fix the money supply"], value="peg the interest rate",
                              description="policy", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.20 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the rate pegged at 5 percent, a rise in money demand from \(m_0 = 10\) to 11 is met by more money (6 instead of 5), and the interest rate does not move.
Switch to “fix the money supply”: the same shift raises the interest rate to 6 percent, which would push the real rate up and output down although nothing real happened. Pegging the rate shields the economy from money-demand shocks.
The IS/LM model. An older version of the short-run model keeps the money supply fixed. Then higher output raises money demand and the interest rate, which gives an upward-sloping “LM” curve instead of our flat MP curve. Since central banks in fact adjust the money supply to keep the interest rate at its target, the two approaches lead to the same analysis.


Key numbers: bond prices and interest rates
In an open-market operation the Fed buys or sells bonds, and the interest rate is hidden in the bond’s price. A bond that pays 100 dollars in one year and sells for 97 dollars today yields \(3/97 = 3.1\) percent.

def bond_yield(price, face=100.0):
    """The one-year interest rate implied by a bond's price: (face - price) / price, in percent."""
    return 100 * (face - price) / price


for price in [95.0, 96.0, 97.0, 98.0, 99.0]:
    print(f"Price {price:.0f}  ->  yield {bond_yield(price):.2f}%")

Price 95  ->  yield 5.26%
Price 96  ->  yield 4.17%
Price 97  ->  yield 3.09%
Price 98  ->  yield 2.04%
Price 99  ->  yield 1.01%


When the Fed sells bonds, their price falls and the interest rate rises (tight money); when it buys bonds, their price rises and the rate falls.

text:
Worked exercise: the Great Inflation
The last figure is the textbook’s answer to Exercise 12: what happens when policymakers mistake a slowdown in potential output for a demand shock and keep stimulating.

Fig. 21: The Great Inflation
Goal. Answer Exercise 12 of the textbook: how mistaking the productivity slowdown for a demand shock could have caused the Great Inflation.
The four panels tell the story of Fig. 13 with the model’s diagrams:


Policymakers believe a negative demand shock \(\bar{a}' < 0\) caused the slowdown: they think the IS curve shifted to IS′, and the economy is at \(B\), below potential.


So they lower the real interest rate to \(R' = \bar{r} + \bar{a}'/\bar{b}\), which, they believe, takes the economy back to potential at \(C\).


Demand never actually fell, so the IS curve is where it was. The lower rate moves the economy down the true IS curve, to \(C\), above potential.


With output above potential, the Phillips curve raises inflation: \(\downarrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow \tilde{Y} \Rightarrow \uparrow \pi\).


The figure has four panels, so we split the work: perceived_panels draws the two panels of what policymakers believe, and great_inflation adds the truth and the readout.

def perceived_panels(fig, a_perc, R_new):
    """Fig. 12.21 (a) and (b): the IS/MP diagram as policymakers see it."""
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, dash="dash", row=1, col=col)
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_perc, row=1, col=col)
        add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 1, col)
        add_point(fig, a_perc, R_BAR, "B", -8, 0, 1, col)
        set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 1, col)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE, row=1, col=1)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, a_perc, 0.6, 1, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 1, 2)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, row=1, col=2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 1, 2, where="bottom left")    # below left, clear of A
    add_arrow(fig, a_perc, 0.6, 0.0, 0.6, 1, 2)


def great_inflation(a_perc=-2.0, nu=NU):
    """Fig. 12.21: the Fed sees a demand shock a' that never happened, cuts R, and inflation rises."""
    R_new = rate_for_output(0.0, a_perc)           # the cut that would close the perceived gap
    Y_true = is_curve(R_new)                       # but the true IS curve never moved
    dpi = phillips(Y_true, nu)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.12, vertical_spacing=0.14,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) Belief: demand fell, IS → IS′", "(b) Belief: a cut to R′ restores Ỹ = 0",
                                        "(c) Reality: IS unchanged, Ỹ overshoots", "(d) Reality: Ỹ > 0 pushes Δπ up"))
    perceived_panels(fig, a_perc, R_new)
    add_is(fig, "IS", TEAL, row=2, col=1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 2, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, row=2, col=1)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 2, 1)
    add_point(fig, Y_true, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 2, 1, where="bottom left")  # clear of the old MP line
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_true, 0.6, 2, 1)
    add_pc(fig, "Phillips curve", GREEN, nu, row=2, col=2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, 0.0, "A", -8, -4, 2, 2, where="top left")
    add_point(fig, Y_true, dpi, "B", -8, -4, 2, 2, where="top left")
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 2, 1)
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_DPI, 2, 2)
    fig.update_layout(height=820, title=f"Believed ā′ = {a_perc:.1f}  →  R′ = {R_new:.2f}%  →  true Ỹ = {Y_true:+.1f}%"
                                        f"  →  Δπ = {dpi:+.2f} a year")
    return fig

What to notice.

Believing in a shock of \(-2\), the Fed cuts \(R\) from 5 to 4 percent. On the true IS curve this takes output to \(+2\) percent, not 0, and inflation rises by 1 point a year for as long as the mistake lasts.
The bigger the shock policymakers believe in, the bigger the cut, the bigger the boom, and the faster inflation rises.
How can policymakers find out? Rising inflation with no other shock is the sign that output is above potential. In the 1970s the oil shocks also raised inflation, so the mistake took years to see.

Your turn. Suppose the Fed recognizes its mistake and wants to stop inflation from rising. To what real interest rate should it return? What if, in addition, it wants to bring inflation back down by 1 point a year?


Hint

Steady inflation needs \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) on the true IS curve: rate_for_output(0.0). Lowering inflation by 1 point a year needs \(\tilde{Y} = -1/\bar{\nu}\): try rate_for_output(-2.0).

title: Chapter 12: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Concluding remarks

The short-run model has three building blocks. Through the MP curve, the central bank’s nominal interest rate sets the real interest rate, because inflation is sticky. Through the IS curve, the real rate sets short-run output. Through the Phillips curve, \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\), output changes inflation over time.
In the IS/MP diagram, monetary policy can in principle offset demand shocks such as a housing bust, but long and variable lags make this hard in practice.
Lowering inflation requires a temporary recession: the Volcker disinflation brought inflation from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983, at the cost of the deepest recession in decades. Oil shocks, the belief in a permanent trade-off, and a productivity slowdown mistaken for a recession all contributed to the Great Inflation of the 1970s.
Central banks set the interest rate by supplying whatever money is demanded at their target. Through the term structure, the short rate also moves longer-term rates.
The next chapter adds the central bank’s policy rule and expectations, leading to the AS/AD framework.

Setup

Python note. import loads a library, a toolbox written by other people. We give each library a short nickname, for example np for NumPy, so that the code stays short. Text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it, and it is there for human readers. The try ... except block runs one Colab-only line and simply skips it anywhere else.


# Libraries used in this chapter
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 13: Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
text:
Model overview
This chapter puts the whole short-run model into one picture. The central bank now follows a simple rule: when inflation is above its target, it raises the real interest rate, which cools spending and pulls output below potential. That rule gives a downward-sloping aggregate demand (AD) curve linking inflation to output. The Phillips curve, written in levels, becomes an upward-sloping aggregate supply (AS) curve: inflation this year equals the inflation people expected plus a boost when the economy runs hot. Where the two curves cross we read this period’s output and inflation.
The model takes the inflation target, the strength of the policy response, the slope of the AS curve and any shocks as given. It tells us how output and inflation move from one period to the next as expectations catch up, until the economy is back at its steady state, with inflation on target and output at potential. Below we write the equations, pick one shared set of illustrative numbers, and build the tools every section reuses: a solver for one period, a loop that runs an event over many periods, and the drawing functions. The sections then use them for the AD and AS curves, three events, the U.S. data, and modern monetary policy.
The short-run model of Chapter 12 has three equations: the IS curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r})\), the MP curve (the central bank chooses \(R_t\)) and the Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\). This chapter replaces the MP curve with a monetary policy rule: the central bank raises the real interest rate above the marginal product of capital whenever inflation is above its inflation target \(\bar{\pi}\),
\[R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \qquad (13.1)\]
The parameter \(\bar{m}\) says how hard the central bank leans against inflation. Substitute the rule into the IS curve and you get the AD curve. Write the Phillips curve in levels and you get the AS curve:
\[\text{AD:}\quad \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}), \qquad (13.3)\]
\[\text{AS:}\quad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \qquad (13.4)\]
Last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) in the AS curve is expected inflation: firms expect inflation to stay where it was (adaptive expectations, \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\)). We write it as pi_e in the code, because Fig. 20 will let expectations be formed differently.
The model has two unknowns, \(\tilde{Y}_t\) and \(\pi_t\). Substitute the AS curve into the AD curve and solve for output; then the AS curve gives inflation:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi^e_t + \bar{o} - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers. All the diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of parameters:

inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, the target of the U.S., the U.K., the euro area and Japan;
policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), John Taylor’s value, used again in Fig. 16;
interest sensitivity \(\bar{b} = 2\), as in Chapter 11’s example;
Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\) (illustrative);
the shocks: an inflation shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) points for one period, an aggregate demand shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) points for nine periods, and a disinflation from a target of 4 to 2 percent (the numbers of textbook Fig. 13.20).

With these values \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\), so the denominator above is 2: after any shock, the economy closes half of the remaining inflation gap every period. That matches the spacing of the textbook’s figures. \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{m}\) enter the dynamics only through their product, so the event figures have a slider for \(\bar{m}\) and keep \(\bar{b} = 2\).

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing m=M_BAR gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma.


PI_BAR, M_BAR, B_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.0   # the baseline: target 2%, m = 1/2, b = 2, nu = 1
PI_OLD = 4.0                                         # the inflation target before the disinflation
A_LAST = 9                                           # the demand shock lasts from period 1 to period 9
T_MAX = 20                                           # number of periods simulated after each event


def ad_output(pi, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, a=0.0, b=B_BAR):
    """Equation 13.3, the AD curve: Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar), in percent."""
    return a - b * m * (pi - pi_bar)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_e=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0):
    """Equation 13.4, the AS curve: pi = pi_e + nu Y~ + o, with expected inflation pi_e (= pi_{t-1})."""
    return pi_e + nu * Y + o


def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, o=0.0, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The point where the AD and AS curves cross: short-run output and inflation in one period."""
    Y = (a - B_BAR * m * (pi_e + o - pi_bar)) / (1 + B_BAR * m * nu)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu, o)

Let us try solve_asad on two cases: the steady state, and the first period of an inflation shock.

Python note. Y, pi = solve_asad(...) unpacks the two results into two variables. An f-string such as f"Y~ = {Y:.2f}" inserts a value into text; :.2f means “show two decimals”.


Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=2.0)
print(f"Steady state (expected inflation = target = 2%):  Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%")
Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=2.0, o=2.0)
print(f"Inflation shock o = 2 hits the steady state:      Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%")

Steady state (expected inflation = target = 2%):  Y~ = 0.00%,  pi = 2.00%
Inflation shock o = 2 hits the steady state:      Y~ = -1.00%,  pi = 3.00%


In the steady state output is at potential and inflation equals the target. The shock raises inflation by only 1 point, not 2, because the central bank answers with a recession of 1 percent.

One loop for every event
The events of this chapter play out over many periods. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. simulate repeats this step period by period. It takes one list of demand shocks \(\bar{a}\) and one list of inflation shocks \(\bar{o}\), one value per period, and returns a table with one row per period. shock_list builds those lists.

Python note. values.append(x) adds x at the end of the list values, and for t in range(1, 21) repeats the indented lines for t = 1, 2, …, 20. dict(period=0, Y=0.0) is a dictionary: a set of named values. rows[-1] is the last element of a list, and rows[-1]["pi"] its value named "pi". pd.DataFrame(rows) turns a list of dictionaries into a table, one row per dictionary.


def shock_list(size, last):
    """A shock of the given size in periods 1, ..., last and zero afterwards, for T_MAX periods."""
    values = []
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


NO_SHOCK = shock_list(0.0, 0)                   # T_MAX zeros


def simulate(a_list, o_list, pi_start=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Solve the AS/AD model period by period; period 0 is the old steady state with inflation pi_start."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, o=0.0, target=pi_start, pi_e=pi_start, Y=0.0, pi=pi_start)]
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]                   # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], o_list[t - 1], pi_bar, m, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], o=o_list[t - 1], target=pi_bar, pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

The table is the inflation shock of Figs. 6 to 9: inflation jumps to 3 percent in period 1, then falls to 2.5, 2.25, 2.125, …; the gap to the 2 percent target halves every period, and so does the recession. The column target is the inflation target behind each period’s AD curve, and pi_e is expected inflation, the height of that period’s AS curve at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\).


Drawing tools
Every diagram below uses the same axes and the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_ad and add_as draw one curve and write its name at its right end;
add_point marks a point with dashed guides to the axes, and add_arrow draws an arrow;
asad_figure starts a figure with one or two panels, and asad_axes fixes the axes and writes the title.


Python note. np.linspace(-15, 15, 241) creates 241 evenly spaced numbers from −15 to 15, one every 0.125. Because our model functions work on a whole array at once, one call gives a whole curve. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and add_trace(..., row=1, col=2) draws in the second panel. (x >= 0) & (y <= 8) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. Labels such as "AS<sub>2</sub>" use HTML to write AS₂. fig.data is the list of traces already drawn, min(a, b) and max(a, b) give the smaller and the larger of two numbers, and tickvals=None lets Plotly choose the tick marks itself. The axes stay fixed for every slider setting except a few extreme ones, where asad_axes widens them so that no dot falls off the chart. fig.update_annotations(yshift=16) moves every text already in the figure (here only the panel titles) 16 pixels up.


Y_GRID = np.linspace(-15, 15, 241)          # output levels at which we draw the AS curves
PI_GRID = np.linspace(12, -5, 137)          # inflation rates, high to low, at which we draw the AD curves
X_RANGE, PI_RANGE = [-4, 4], [-1, 8]        # fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move
FADED = "rgba(0,128,112,0.35)"              # light teal for the AS curves of earlier periods


def axis_names(col):
    """The names Plotly gives the axes of panel col: x and y in panel 1, x2 and y2 in panel 2."""
    if col == 1:
        return "x", "y"
    return f"x{col}", f"y{col}"


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw one curve in panel col and write its label at its last point inside the axes."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    inside = (x >= X_RANGE[0]) & (x <= X_RANGE[1]) & (y >= PI_RANGE[0]) & (y <= PI_RANGE[1])
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], xref=xref, yref=yref, text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_ad(fig, label, color, a=0.0, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, b=B_BAR, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw an AD curve (equation 13.3): output on the horizontal axis, inflation on the vertical axis."""
    add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_GRID, pi_bar, m, a, b), PI_GRID, label, color, dash, col)


def add_as(fig, label, color, pi_e=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw an AS curve (equation 13.4)."""
    add_curve(fig, Y_GRID, as_inflation(Y_GRID, pi_e, nu, o), label, color, dash, col)


def add_point(fig, Y, pi, label, col=1, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (Y, pi) with a dot and a label, and (if guides) dashed lines to both axes."""
    if guides:
        # the guides start far outside the chart: the axes cut them off at their edges, wherever these are
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[-100, Y, Y], y=[pi, pi, -100], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                                 hoverinfo="skip", line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[Y], y=[pi], mode="markers", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)
    if label != "":
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        # well above the dot and a little to the right: clear of the curves and the dashed guides through it
        fig.add_annotation(x=Y, y=pi, xref=xref, yref=yref, text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                           yanchor="bottom", xshift=4, yshift=8, font=dict(size=16))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, col=1):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref=xref, yref=yref, axref=xref, ayref=yref, text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")


def asad_figure(cols=1, titles=None):
    """An empty figure with cols panels side by side (titles: one short title per panel)."""
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=cols, subplot_titles=titles, horizontal_spacing=0.1)
    fig.update_annotations(yshift=16)           # lift the panel titles clear of curve labels at the top edge
    return fig


def asad_axes(fig, title, panels=1):
    """Fixed AS/AD axes in the first panels (no tick in the bottom-left corner) and the title readout."""
    x_range, pi_range = list(X_RANGE), list(PI_RANGE)
    for trace in fig.data:                       # the dots: widen an axis only if a dot would fall off the chart
        if trace.mode == "markers":
            x_range = [min(x_range[0], trace.x[0] - 0.5), max(x_range[1], trace.x[0] + 0.5)]
            pi_range = [min(pi_range[0], trace.y[0] - 0.4), max(pi_range[1], trace.y[0] + 0.8)]
    x_ticks, pi_ticks = list(range(-3, 4)), list(range(0, 8))
    if x_range != X_RANGE or pi_range != PI_RANGE:
        x_ticks, pi_ticks = None, None           # wider axes: let Plotly choose the ticks
    for col in range(1, panels + 1):
        fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Output, Ỹ (percent)", range=x_range, tickvals=x_ticks, zeroline=False,
                         row=1, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Inflation, π (percent)", range=pi_range, tickvals=pi_ticks, zeroline=False,
                         row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_layout(title=title, legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top",
                                               bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))



Countries and colors
The data figures at the end of this chapter (Figs. 16–21) can go beyond the textbook’s economies: the same series exist for many other countries. The file countries.csv lists every economy in the chapter’s multi-country files, with its region and whether it belongs to the OECD. We give each country a fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others, and two countries that are shown together never share a color. The function missing_or_off writes a short note for a chart title when a chosen country has no data or leaves the chart.

Python note. PALETTE.index(c) finds the position of color c, .pop(i) removes the item at that position and returns it, and .append puts it at the end. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. colors.get(other) is the color of other, or None if it has none yet. new + free + PALETTE joins three lists and [0] takes the first item: a color that no country uses yet if there is one, else one that no country of the same groups uses.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]      # too pale on a white page
PALETTE = list(px.colors.qualitative.Dark24)                                     # 24 dark colors ...
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:                                     # ... and 20 more
    if color not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append(PALETTE.pop(PALETTE.index("#2E91E5")))   # this blue is close to the U.S. navy: move it to the end


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country of its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.
    groups: lists of countries shown together (the website menus); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                    # colors of the countries already shown with this one
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    used.append(colors.get(other))
        free, new = [], []                           # free: not used in its groups; new: not used by any country
        for color in PALETTE:
            if color not in used:
                free.append(color)
                if color not in colors.values():
                    new.append(color)
        colors[name] = (new + free + PALETTE)[0]
    return colors

The website shows the OECD members and eight large emerging economies, so those countries get their colors first.

Python note. countries.groupby("region") hands over each region’s name with its rows, so regions becomes a list of country lists, one per region.


countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")

Python note. values.empty is true when a selection has no rows. ", ".join(names) glues a list of names into one text, with a comma between them.


def missing_or_off(part, column, countries, low, high):
    """Title text naming the chosen countries with no data in `part`, and those whose values leave [low, high]."""
    missing, off = [], []
    for name in countries:
        values = part[column][part.country == name]
        if values.empty:
            missing.append(name)
        elif values.min() < low or values.max() > high:
            off.append(name)
    note = ""
    if missing:
        note += "; no data: " + ", ".join(missing)
    if off:
        note += "; off the chart: " + ", ".join(off)
    return note

def compact(fig):
    """Shrink a website figure (short dates, 4 significant digits, a short hover), so the saved notebook stays small."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        x = pd.Series(trace.x if trace.x is not None else [], dtype=object).infer_objects()
        if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(x):
            trace.x = x.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist()
        if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
            trace.y = [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in trace.y]
        if "lines" in (trace.mode or "") and trace.hovertext is None:
            trace.hovertemplate = "%{fullData.name}<br>%{x}: %{y}<extra></extra>"
    return fig


def menu_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one dropdown menu."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner, shown = [], []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            shown.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            trace.visible = shown[-1] if i == first else False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "legend.title.text": f.layout.legend.title.text,
                  "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range, "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        visible = [shown[j] if o == i else False for j, o in enumerate(owner)]
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=110), updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=first, x=0, y=1.02,
                                                            xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])   # above the plot
    return compact(fig)

# @title Helper for the website group buttons (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def group_menu(fig, book, small=8):
    """Buttons that list one group of countries in the legend (a small group is drawn at once); `book` is always drawn."""
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    short = {"Europe and Central Asia": "Europe", "Asia and Pacific": "Asia-Pacific", "Middle East and Africa": "Africa, Mideast"}
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Americas": [], "Europe": [], "Asia-Pacific": [], "Africa, Mideast": []}
    for c, r in zip(countries.country, countries.region):
        if c in names:
            groups[short.get(r, r)].append(c)
    first = ["legendonly" if len(names) <= 40 else False] * len(names)   # a short legend lists every country
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        if not set(members) & set(names):
            continue                                   # no country of this group in the figure
        visible = []
        for j, n in enumerate(names):
            if n in book:
                visible.append(True)
            elif n in members:
                visible.append(True if len(members) <= small else "legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(first[j] if label == "Textbook" else False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(
        type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons)])
    return compact(fig)

title: Chapter 13: Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
section: Monetary policy rules and the AD curve
text:
Monetary policy rules and the AD curve
We combine the IS curve with the central bank’s rule to get the AD curve, then see how the strength of the policy response changes its slope.

Fig. 1: The aggregate demand curve
Goal. Build the AD curve from the IS curve and the policy rule, and see what each parameter does to it.
\[\left.\begin{array}{ll} \text{IS curve:} & \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r}) \\ \text{Policy rule:} & R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \end{array}\right\} \Rightarrow \text{AD curve: } \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\]
The AD curve slopes down, but not for the reason a demand curve for hamburgers does. It describes the central bank: when inflation is above target, the rule raises the real interest rate, investment falls, and output falls below potential. As with the IS curve, output goes on the horizontal axis.
The dot marks the point where inflation equals the target. There the interest-rate term is zero and output is \(\tilde{Y} = \bar{a}\): with no demand shock, potential output. When you change a parameter, the baseline curve stays behind as a dashed gray line.

Python note. if ... : runs the indented lines only when the condition is true. != means “is not equal to”, and comparing two groups of numbers in parentheses checks them all at once. x > 2.4 and y < 4.3 is true only when both conditions hold. We use it to leave out the baseline label when the new curve, or its own label, would run into it.


def ad_curve(pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, b=B_BAR, a=0.0):
    """Fig. 13.1: the AD curve, with the point where inflation equals the target."""
    fig = asad_figure()
    if (pi_bar, m, b, a) != (PI_BAR, M_BAR, B_BAR, 0.0):
        label = "AD (baseline)"
        if ad_output(-1.0, pi_bar, m, a, b) > 2.4 and ad_output(-0.3, pi_bar, m, a, b) < 4.3:   # new AD too close
            label = ""
        add_ad(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, a, pi_bar, m, b)
    add_point(fig, a, pi_bar, "π = π̄")
    asad_axes(fig, f"AD: Ỹ = {a:.1f} − {b * m:.2f} × (π − {pi_bar:.1f});   at π = π̄ = {pi_bar:.1f}%, Ỹ = {a:.1f}%")
    return fig

What to notice.

The slope depends on the product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\): each point of inflation above target costs \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 1\) point of output in the baseline. Raise \(\bar{m}\) or \(\bar{b}\) and the curve becomes flatter.
A demand shock \(\bar{a}\) and a new target \(\bar{\pi}\) shift the curve: \(\bar{a}\) moves it right or left, \(\bar{\pi}\) up or down. The dot always sits at \((\bar{a}, \bar{\pi})\).
A change in inflation itself does not shift the curve; it is a movement along it (Fig. 2).

Fig. 2: The AD curve after an inflation shock
Goal. See why higher inflation moves the economy along the AD curve instead of shifting it.
The economy starts in steady state at point \(A\): inflation at the 2 percent target, output at potential. Now inflation jumps to \(\pi' = 3\) percent. The policy rule raises the real interest rate by \(\bar{m}(\pi' - \bar{\pi}) = 0.5\) points, investment falls, and output falls to point \(B\). The readout in the title follows the chain: inflation, then the interest rate, then output. Figs. 2 and 3 share one function.

def inflation_rises(pi_new=3.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Figs. 13.2-13.3: inflation rises from the target to pi_new; the economy moves along AD from A to B."""
    Y_B = ad_output(pi_new, m=m)
    fig = asad_figure()
    if m != M_BAR:
        label = "AD (m̄ = 0.5)"
        if ad_output(-1.0, m=m) > 2.4 and ad_output(-0.3, m=m) < 4.3:   # the new AD would run into this label
            label = ""
        add_ad(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, m=m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_BAR, "A")
    if pi_new != PI_BAR:                                 # no second letter on top of A
        add_point(fig, Y_B, pi_new, "B")
    add_arrow(fig, -3.7, PI_BAR, -3.7, pi_new)      # inflation rises ...
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, -0.6, Y_B, -0.6)            # ... so output falls
    rate = m * (pi_new - PI_BAR)
    asad_axes(fig, f"π: {PI_BAR:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%   ⇒   R − r̄ = {rate:.2f}   ⇒   Ỹ: 0.00 → {Y_B:.2f}%")
    return fig

section: Aggregate supply and the AS/AD diagram
text:
Aggregate supply and the AS/AD diagram
Next comes the AS curve, the Phillips curve in levels. Putting it next to the AD curve gives the diagram that solves the model and shows its steady state.

Fig. 4: The aggregate supply curve
Goal. Read the Phillips curve as an upward-sloping aggregate supply curve.
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\]
At the start of period \(t\), last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) is already known. So the Phillips curve is a relation between this year’s inflation and output. When output is above potential, firms work overtime to meet demand, and they raise their prices by more than usual to cover the extra costs: inflation rises. The curve crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at \(\pi_{t-1}\) (plus any inflation shock \(\bar{o}\)), so it shifts whenever inflation changes.

def as_curve(pi_prev=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0):
    """Fig. 13.4: the AS curve, which crosses Y~ = 0 at last year's inflation plus the shock."""
    fig = asad_figure()
    if (pi_prev, nu, o) != (PI_BAR, NU_BAR, 0.0):
        label = "AS (baseline)"
        if abs(as_inflation(4.0, pi_prev, nu, o) - 6.0) < 0.6:   # the two labels at the right edge would overlap
            label = ""
        add_as(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    add_as(fig, "AS", TEAL, pi_prev, nu, o)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_prev + o, "")
    asad_axes(fig, f"AS: π = {pi_prev:.1f} + {nu:.2f} × Ỹ + {o:.1f};   at Ỹ = 0, π = {pi_prev + o:.1f}%")
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(r=120))               # room for the label "AS (baseline)" at the right edge
    return fig

         pi_prev=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="last year's inflation π_{t−1} (%)",

         nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE),
         o=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="inflation shock ō", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

Last year’s inflation and the shock \(\bar{o}\) move the curve up and down, one for one.
\(\bar{\nu}\) turns the curve around the dot: a steeper curve means prices react more to a boom or a slump.
Because \(\pi_{t-1}\) is expected inflation, the AS curve carries expectations into the diagram. That is the key to every event below.

Your turn. With \(\pi_{t-1} = 2\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), how far above potential must output be for inflation to reach 3.5 percent? Check it with as_inflation.

Fig. 5: The AS/AD framework
Goal. Put the two curves in one diagram and find the short-run equilibrium, and the steady state.
This diagram is the whole short-run model: the inputs are the parameters (\(\bar{\pi}\), \(\bar{m}\), \(\bar{\nu}\)) and expected inflation, the outcomes are this period’s output and inflation. In a steady state inflation does not change, so \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1}\). The AS curve then requires \(\tilde{Y}^* = 0\), and the AD curve then requires \(\pi^* = \bar{\pi}\): inflation on target and output at potential. The readout tells you whether the crossing point is a steady state.

def asad_diagram(pi_e=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Fig. 13.5: the AS and AD curves and the short-run equilibrium where they cross."""
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_as(fig, "AS", TEAL, pi_e, nu)
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m)
    add_point(fig, Y, pi, "")
    state = "the steady state"
    if pi_e != pi_bar:
        state = "not a steady state"
    asad_axes(fig, f"AS and AD cross at Ỹ = {Y:.2f}%, π = {pi:.2f}%: {state}")
    return fig

title: Chapter 13: Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
text:
Event 1: an inflation shock
A one-time jump in inflation, such as an oil price spike, hits an economy in its steady state. We follow the AS/AD diagram period by period as the economy finds its way back.

Fig. 6: The initial response to an inflation shock
Goal. See the first period of Event #1: an inflation shock, such as a lasting rise in the price of oil.
The shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) hits for one period only. It shifts the AS curve up by 2 points, from AS to AS₁. If output stayed at potential, inflation would rise one for one, to 4 percent. But the policy rule fights the higher inflation with a higher interest rate, so the economy slides down the AD curve, from \(A\) to \(B\): inflation rises and output falls at the same time. This is stagflation, the U.S. experience after the oil shocks of the 1970s.
Figs. 6 to 9 show the same event at different periods, so we write one function. It simulates the event with simulate and draws period t: the AS curves of the earlier periods in light teal, the current one in full color, and the path so far, with the textbook’s letters (\(B\), \(C\), \(D\) for periods 1, 2, 3).

Python note. path.loc[t] is the row of period t, and now.pi is its value in the column pi. path.pi_e[s] is the value of column pi_e in the row of period s. x in some_list is true when x is one of the elements, and "AD" if s == 0 else "AD₁" picks the first value when the condition holds, the second otherwise. round(x, 2) + 0.0 rounds to two decimals; adding 0.0 turns a rounded −0.0 into 0.0, so a title never shows “−0.00”.


def add_event_curves(fig, path, t, as_periods, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, col=1):
    """Curves of a simulated event at period t: the old AS, the AS of as_periods (the last one solid), every AD."""
    first, last = path.pi_e[0], as_periods[-1]
    today = path.pi_e[last] + path.o[last]                   # where today's AS crosses Y~ = 0
    near = 0.6 * max(1, nu)          # two AS labels closer than this would overlap (a steep AS exits at the top)
    same = today == first
    old_label = "AS" if same or abs(today - first) > near else ""     # no label on top of today's label
    add_as(fig, old_label, TEAL if same else GRAY, first, nu, dash="solid" if same else "dash", col=col)
    for s in as_periods:
        start = path.pi_e[s] + path.o[s]
        if start != first:                                   # skip curves that equal the original AS
            label = f"AS<sub>{s}</sub>" if s == last or (s == as_periods[0] and abs(start - today) > near) else ""
            add_as(fig, label, TEAL if s == last else FADED, path.pi_e[s], nu, path.o[s], col=col)
    drawn = []                                               # the AD curves already drawn: (a, target)
    for s in range(t + 1):
        pair = (path.a[s], path.target[s])
        if pair not in drawn:
            drawn.append(pair)
            name = "AD" if s == 0 else f"AD<sub>{s}</sub>"
            shift = abs(pair[0] - path.a[t] + B_BAR * m * (pair[1] - path.target[t]))   # 0 for today's AD
            if 0 < shift * min(1, 1 / (B_BAR * m)) < 0.6:          # an old label would sit on today's label
                name = ""
            add_ad(fig, name, BLUE if shift == 0 else GRAY, pair[0], pair[1], m,      # today's AD in blue
                   dash="solid" if shift == 0 else "dash", col=col)


def add_event_path(fig, path, t, letters, col=1):
    """The economy's path from A (period 0) to period t: dots, arrows, and the textbook's letters."""
    add_point(fig, path.Y[0], path.pi[0], "A", col)
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s], col)
        moved = (path.Y[s], path.pi[s]) != (path.Y[0], path.pi[0])   # with no shock, no letter on top of A
        if s in letters and moved:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], letters[s], col)
        else:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], "", col, guides=False)


SHOCK_LETTERS = {1: "B", 2: "C", 3: "D"}                     # the textbook's letters for periods 1-3


def inflation_shock(o=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figs. 13.6 and 13.8: the economy t periods after a one-period inflation shock o."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, SHOCK_LETTERS)
    now = path.loc[t]
    asad_axes(fig, f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:.2f}%   (shock ō = {o:.1f} in period 1 only)")
    return fig

Goal. See the whole event at once, in the AS/AD diagram and over time.
Panel (a) is the textbook’s summary: the jump from \(A\) to \(B\), then the slow return along the AD curve back to \(A\). Panel (b) adds the same path as two time series, so you can read how long the stagflation lasts. One function draws the summaries of all three events (Figs. 9, 11 and 15).

def add_time_paths(fig, path, col=2):
    """Inflation and output over time, with the inflation target, in panel col."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=path.period, y=path.pi, name="Inflation π", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=path.period, y=path.Y, name="Output Ỹ", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, T_MAX], y=[path.target[1], path.target[1]], name="Target π̄", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dot")), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Period", range=[-0.5, T_MAX + 0.5], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20], row=1, col=col)
    low = min(-3, path.Y.min() - 0.5, path.pi.min() - 0.5)     # wider than -3 to 7 only if a path would leave it
    high = max(7, path.pi.max() + 0.5)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Percent", range=[low, high], tickvals=list(range(-12, 14, 2)), row=1, col=col)


def event_summary(path, letters, as_periods, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figs. 13.9, 13.11, 13.15: (a) the whole path in the AS/AD diagram, (b) the same path over time."""

    add_event_curves(fig, path, T_MAX, as_periods, m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, T_MAX, letters)
    add_time_paths(fig, path)
    return fig

text:
Event 2: disinflation
Now the central bank lowers its inflation target. Because expectations adjust slowly, getting inflation down costs a recession along the way.

Fig. 10: The initial response to disinflation
Goal. See Event #2: the central bank lowers its inflation target, as Paul Volcker’s Fed did in the 1980s.
The economy starts in a steady state with a target, and inflation, of 4 percent. The central bank now adopts a new rule with the target \(\bar{\pi}' = 2\) percent. The target appears only in the AD curve, so AD shifts down to AD₁: at any inflation rate the new rule wants lower output. Inflation of 4 percent is now “too high”, the real interest rate rises, and the economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\). The function reuses add_event_curves and add_event_path: only the event changes.

def disinflation(pi_new=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figs. 13.10-13.11: t periods after the inflation target is cut from PI_OLD to pi_new."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, pi_new, m, nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, {1: "B"})
    if t > 1:
        add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_new, "C")                     # the new steady state
    now = path.loc[t]
    asad_axes(fig, f"Target {PI_OLD:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%.  Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:.2f}%")
    return fig

Fig. 11: The dynamics of disinflation
Goal. Follow the disinflation to the new steady state \(C\).
After period 1, firms expect lower inflation, so the AS curve shifts down period by period, just as after the inflation shock. The economy slides down AD₁ from \(B\) to the new steady state \(C\), where inflation equals the new target and output is back at potential. The summary function of Fig. 9 draws it; we add the point \(C\).

def disinflation_summary(pi_new=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Fig. 13.11: from A through B to the new steady state C, in the diagram and over time."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, pi_new, m, nu)
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B"}, [T_MAX], m, nu)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_new, "C")
    asad_axes(fig, f"Target {PI_OLD:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%: output lost over {T_MAX} periods = {round(-path.Y.sum(), 2) + 0.0:.2f}%")
    return fig

A more aggressive central bank (higher \(\bar{m}\)) makes the recession deeper and shorter, but the total loss stays near 2. Only the AS slope \(\bar{\nu}\) changes it: the total loss is \((\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu}\).
Why must there be a recession at all? Because firms keep expecting the old inflation. If everyone believed the new target at once, the economy could jump straight from \(A\) to \(C\). Fig. 20 returns to this idea.

Event 3: a positive aggregate demand shock
A temporary spending boom raises output and inflation. When the boom ends, the higher inflation it left behind has to be squeezed out with a recession.

Fig. 12: A positive aggregate demand shock
Goal. See the first period of Event #3: a boom in demand, for example from a boom in Europe that raises the demand for U.S. exports.
A positive \(\bar{a}\) shifts the AD curve out to AD₁: at every inflation rate, output is higher. Firms see the extra demand and raise their prices, so the economy moves up the AS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). Part of the shock shows up as more output, part as more inflation. In our baseline the shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) lasts nine periods. One function draws Figs. 12 to 14, with the textbook’s letters \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) at periods 1, 8 and 10.

Inflation approaches \(\pi^c = 4\) percent; after eight periods it is 3.992 percent and output is 0.008 percent. The textbook’s label “eight periods” is arbitrary: the economy gets close to \(C\) and never quite reaches it.

Fig. 14: The unraveling after the aggregate demand shock ends
Goal. See what happens when the boom ends: a recession.
Demand shocks are temporary: in the long run \(\bar{a} = 0\), because the shares of output must add up to 1. When the European boom ends after period 9, the AD curve shifts back to its original position. Output was already at potential, so this works like a negative shock: the economy jumps from \(C\) to \(D\), below potential. The recession then pulls inflation down, the AS curve shifts down period by period, and the economy slides down the original AD curve back to \(A\). Again the same function, now at \(t = 10\).

Goal. See the whole boom-and-bust cycle, and what happens if the shock ends sooner.
The economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), drifts to \(C\), jumps to \(D\) when the shock ends, and returns to \(A\): a counterclockwise loop. def demand_shock_summary(a=2.0, last=A_LAST, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Fig. 13.15: a demand shock a in periods 1 to last, in the AS/AD diagram and over time."""
    path = simulate(shock_list(a, last), NO_SHOCK, m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B", last: "C", last + 1: "D"}, [last], m, nu)
    asad_axes(fig, f"ā = {a:.1f} in periods 1–{last}: π peaks at {path.pi.max():.2f}%; sum of Ỹ = {round(path.Y.sum(), 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
    return fig
