title: Chapter 13: Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
text:
Empirical evidence
How well does the model describe real economies? We compare the fed funds rate with a simple policy rule, look for counterclockwise inflation-output loops, and see how forecasters missed the Great Recession.

Fig. 16: The fed funds rate, actual and predicted
Goal. Test the policy rule on U.S. data: does it predict the Federal Reserve’s interest rate?
The rule sets the real interest rate, but the Fed sets a nominal rate, the fed funds rate. The Fisher equation links the two, \(i_t = R_t + \pi_t\), so the rule implies
\[i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \qquad (13.5)\]
John Taylor picked numbers that are all built on the number 2: \(\bar{r} = 2\%\), \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and \(\bar{\pi} = 2\%\). Then \(i_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t\): when inflation rises by 1 point, the nominal rate rises by 1.5 points, so the real rate rises too. For inflation we use core PCE inflation (prices of consumer spending without food and energy), the measure that reproduces the textbook’s line.

For the United States it repeats the table above.

Python note. px.line with a list y=[...] draws one line per column. selector=dict(name=...) changes only the trace with that name. round(gap, 2) + 0.0 turns a rounded −0.00 into 0.00, and np.isnan(gap) is true when there were no quarters to average.


def policy_rule(pi, r_bar=2.0, m=M_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR):
    """Equation 13.5: the nominal interest rate i = r_bar + pi + m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return r_bar + pi + m * (pi - pi_bar)


def fed_funds_chart(r_bar=2.0, m=M_BAR, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 13.16: the actual policy rate of one country and the rate predicted by the policy rule."""
    part = rules[rules.country == country]
    actual = "Actual fed funds rate" if country == "United States" else "Actual policy rate"
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"date": part.date, actual: part.policy_rate,
                          "Policy rule": policy_rule(part.core_inflation, r_bar, m)})
    gap = round((chart[actual] - chart["Policy rule"])[chart.date >= "2009-01-01"].mean(), 2) + 0.0
    lines = chart[[actual, "Policy rule"]]
    low, high, ticks = -1, 22, [0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20]
    for wider_low, wider_high, wider_ticks in [(-5, 45, None), (-10, 110, None)]:   # only when a country needs it
        if lines.min().min() < low or lines.max().max() > high:
            low, high, ticks = wider_low, wider_high, wider_ticks
    title = f"Rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}, m̄ = {m:.2f}: actual minus rule since 2009 = {gap:.2f} points"
    if np.isnan(gap):
        title = f"Rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}, m̄ = {m:.2f} (no data since 2009)"
    legend = country + (" (off the chart)" if lines.min().min() < low or lines.max().max() > high else "")
    fig = px.line(chart, x="date", y=[actual, "Policy rule"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN], title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=2.5)
    fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", selector=dict(name="Policy rule"))
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1958-01-01", "2027-12-31"], yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=ticks),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text=legend)
    return fig

Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED; U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, PCE price index excluding food and energy (JCXFE), via FRED; for the other economies, Bank for International Settlements, central bank policy rates (WS_CBPOL) and OECD, Consumer price indices, CPI excluding food and energy (DSD_PRICES@DF_PRICES_ALL), via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared files: data/ch13/taylor_rule.csv and data/ch13/taylor_rule_countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 13.16 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
On the website, the second chart offers the 33 economies, with Taylor’s numbers r̄ = 2 and m̄ = 1/2.
What to notice.

The simple rule follows the big swings of the actual rate surprisingly well: the rise in the 1970s, the peak around 1980, and the long decline afterward.
From the late 1960s to 1980 the actual rate was well below the rule: monetary policy was too loose, and inflation rose through the 1970s.
In recessions (early 1990s, early 2000s and above all after 2008) the Fed set rates far below the rule. The full Taylor rule also responds to output, which explains part of this.
Lower \(\bar{r}\) to 1 or 0.5 percent, as many economists now do: the rule comes closer after 2008, but in 2021–2022 it still calls for rates far above the actual ones. The Fed raised rates late after the Covid-19 pandemic.
Choose the euro area, the United Kingdom or Canada: the same pattern. Their central banks also kept rates below the rule after 2009 (by 2.2, 3.3 and 2.6 points on average from 2009 to 2020) and even more in 2021–2022 (by 4.7, 5.9 and 5.5 points). The rule uses core consumer prices for them, not the core PCE index of the U.S. line.


Key numbers: how closely does the Fed follow the rule?

Python note. taylor[(taylor.date >= start) & (taylor.date <= end)] keeps the quarters between two dates. .corr() gives the correlation between two columns: 1 means they move perfectly together. idxmax() gives the row number of the largest value, and :%Y-%m in an f-string writes a date as year-month.


taylor["rule"] = policy_rule(taylor.core_inflation)
taylor["gap"] = taylor.fed_funds - taylor.rule
for start, end in [("1967", "1980-12-31"), ("1990", "1993-12-31"), ("2001", "2004-12-31"),
                   ("2009", "2020-12-31"), ("2021", "2022-12-31")]:
    part = taylor[(taylor.date >= start) & (taylor.date <= end)]
    print(f"{start}-{end[:4]}: actual minus rule = {part.gap.mean():+.2f} points on average")
book_span = taylor[taylor.date <= "2023-01-01"]
print(f"Correlation of the actual rate with the rule, 1960Q1-2023Q1: {book_span.fed_funds.corr(book_span.rule):.2f}")
print(f"Highest rule rate: {taylor.rule.max():.2f}% in {taylor.date[taylor.rule.idxmax()]:%Y-%m}")

1990-1993: actual minus rule = -0.94 points on average
2001-2004: actual minus rule = -1.67 points on average
2009-2020: actual minus rule = -2.71 points on average
2021-2022: actual minus rule = -6.74 points on average
Correlation of the actual rate with the rule, 1960Q1-2023Q1: 0.75

The actual rate was below the rule by 2.3 points on average from 1967 to 1980, by 2.7 points from 2009 to 2020, and by 6.7 points in 2021–2022. The correlation of 0.75 says the two lines move together most of the time.

Goal. Look for the model’s counterclockwise loops in U.S. data.
The model predicts that the economy moves in counterclockwise loops in a diagram with output on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis (Fig. 15): a boom raises inflation, high inflation leads the central bank to cause a recession, and the recession brings inflation down. Each point below is one year: the output gap \(\tilde{Y}\) (actual GDP relative to the Congressional Budget Office’s estimate of potential GDP) and CPI inflation.

There are two output-gap columns. output_gap uses today’s data; output_gap_2023 uses the data as they were published in March 2023, when the textbook was written. GDP and, above all, the CBO’s potential GDP get revised: today’s estimate of potential output for 2021 is lower, so the same year now looks like a small boom (+0.8 percent) instead of a slump (−1.3 percent). The textbook’s data stop in 2022, so output_gap_2023 is empty (NaN) after that. Always check which vintage of the data a claim is based on.

Python note. .isin([...]) is true for the rows whose value is in the list. A dictionary such as WINDOWS maps a name to its settings, and WINDOWS[years] looks them up. .where(condition, "") keeps a value where the condition is true and puts an empty text elsewhere: we label only a few key years and let hover show the rest. .astype(str) turns the years into text. part.assign(label=...) returns a copy of the table with the new column label. MOVED.get(year, "top center") looks up year in the dictionary MOVED and gives "top center" when the year is not in it.


WINDOWS = {"1960–1985": (1960, 1985, [-8, 7], [0, 15], [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]),
           "1985–2025": (1985, 2025, [-6, 3], [-1.5, 9], [0, 2, 4, 6, 8])}
VINTAGES = {"Current data": "output_gap", "Textbook data": "output_gap_2023"}   # the textbook used the March 2023 vintage
KEY_YEARS = [1960, 1966, 1969, 1974, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1982, 1985, 1989, 1991, 2000, 2009, 2011, 2015,
             2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2025]
MOVED = {2020: "bottom center", 2021: "middle right", 2025: "bottom center"}   # labels moved off nearby points


def loops_chart(years="1960–1985", vintage="Current data"):
    """Fig. 13.17: annual (output gap, inflation) points connected in time order."""
    first, last, x_range, y_range, y_ticks = WINDOWS[years]
    column = VINTAGES[vintage]
    part = loops[(loops.year >= first) & (loops.year <= last)].dropna(subset=[column])
    part = part.assign(label=part.year.astype(str).where(part.year.isin(KEY_YEARS), ""))
    fig = px.line(part, x=column, y="inflation", text="label", markers=True, hover_name="year",
                  labels={column: "Output gap, Ỹ (percent)", "inflation": "CPI inflation (percent)"},
                  title=f"Counterclockwise loops, {first}–{part.year.max()} ({vintage.lower()})")
    positions = []
    for year in part.year:
        positions.append(MOVED.get(year, "top center"))
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2), marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=7), textposition=positions)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis=dict(range=x_range, zeroline=True), yaxis=dict(range=y_range, tickvals=y_ticks))
    return fig

What to notice.

Follow the years in 1960–1985: the boom of the late 1960s raises inflation, the high inflation of 1974–75 and 1979–80 is followed by deep recessions (1975, 1982), and inflation falls. The loops run counterclockwise, as the model predicts.
After 1985 the loops are smaller: the Great Moderation. The big exceptions are the deep slump of 2009–2011, during which inflation rose instead of falling, and the jump to 8 percent inflation in 2022.
Switch to the textbook data: the whole 1985–2022 cloud moves left by about 1 point. The shape of the loops is the same, but statements about the level of the gap depend on the vintage.


Key numbers: two vintages of the same year
The textbook says that in 2009 “output was more than 5 percent below potential”, and that inflation rose from 2009 to 2011 despite the slump.

Python note. .set_index("year") labels the rows by year, so by_year.loc[2009, "inflation"] picks one value.

      f"{by_year.loc[2009, 'output_gap']:.2f}% (current data)")

print(f"Current minus textbook output gap, 1985-2022: {revision.mean():.2f} points on average, {revision.max():.2f} at most")

With the textbook’s data the 2009 gap is −5.20 percent; with today’s data it is −4.66 percent, so “more than 5 percent” is no longer true. Inflation did rise, from −0.32 to 3.14 percent, partly because of energy and commodity prices.


Loops in other countries
The OECD estimates the output gap of 40 economies, most of them since 1985, with one method for all. The file output_gaps_oecd.csv has these estimates, and inflation_annual.csv has CPI inflation for 194 economies (the World Bank’s numbers, and for the four economies of Fig. 19 the numbers of that figure). We join them by country and year. For the United States the OECD’s gap differs from the CBO’s: it is 0.2 points higher on average since 1985, and −3.98 percent in 2009 instead of −4.66. Potential output cannot be observed, so every estimate of the gap is a model.

def oecd_loops_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 13.17, extended: annual (output gap, inflation) points of one country, OECD estimates of the gap."""
    part = eo_loops[eo_loops.country == country]
    label = part.year.astype(str).where((part.year % 5 == 0) | (part.year == part.year.max()), "")
    x_range = [np.floor(part.output_gap.min()) - 1, np.ceil(part.output_gap.max()) + 1]
    y_range = [np.floor(min(part.inflation.min(), 0)) - 1, np.ceil(part.inflation.max()) + 1]
    fig = px.line(part.assign(label=label), x="output_gap", y="inflation", text="label", markers=True,

BOOK_FOUR = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Euro area", "Japan")


def oecd_chart(countries=BOOK_FOUR):
    """Fig. 13.19: annual CPI inflation in the chosen economies since 1960."""
    part = prices[prices.country.isin(countries)]
    low, high, ticks = -3, 26, [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25]
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(-10, 60), (-20, 120)]:     # a wider axis only when a chosen country needs it

    title = "Inflation was high everywhere in the 1970s and low after the 1980s"
    if set(countries) != set(BOOK_FOUR):
        title = "CPI inflation, percent a year" + missing_or_off(part, "inflation", countries, low, high)
    fig = px.line(part, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(countries)}, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=2.5)

                      yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=ticks),

Fig. 20: Costless disinflation by coordinating expectations
Goal. See how a credible central bank could lower inflation without a recession.
So far firms expected last year’s inflation (adaptive expectations). Under rational expectations, an idea developed by Robert Lucas, people use all the information they have, including the central bank’s announced target. The AS curve then uses expected inflation \(\pi^e_t\) instead of \(\pi_{t-1}\):
\[\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \qquad (13.6)\]
The Fed announces a cut in its target from 4 to 2 percent. If firms believe it and expect 2 percent, the AS curve moves down together with the AD curve, and the economy goes straight from \(A\) to \(B\) with output at potential. To see the middle ground, the slider sets the credibility of the announcement: the share of the cut that firms build into their expectations, \(\pi^e = \text{credibility} \times \bar{\pi}' + (1 - \text{credibility}) \times 4\). Credibility 0 is the adaptive case of Fig. 10.

def credible_disinflation(credibility=1.0, pi_new=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Fig. 13.20: the target falls from PI_OLD to pi_new; expectations follow it in proportion to credibility."""
    pi_e = credibility * pi_new + (1 - credibility) * PI_OLD
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=pi_new, m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    old_as, old_ad = "AS", "AD"
    if abs(pi_e - PI_OLD) < 0.6 * max(1, nu):          # no label when it would sit on the label of AS′
        old_as = ""
    if abs(pi_new - PI_OLD) * min(1, B_BAR * m) < 0.6:  # ... or on the label of AD′
        old_ad = ""
    if pi_e != PI_OLD:
        add_as(fig, old_as, GRAY, PI_OLD, nu, dash="dash")
    add_ad(fig, old_ad, GRAY, pi_bar=PI_OLD, m=m, dash="dash")
    add_as(fig, "AS′", TEAL, pi_e, nu)
    add_ad(fig, "AD′", BLUE, pi_bar=pi_new, m=m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_OLD, "A")
    add_point(fig, Y, pi, "B")
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, PI_OLD, Y, pi)
    asad_axes(fig, f"Credibility {credibility:.2f}: expected π = {pi_e:.2f}% → π = {pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {Y:.2f}%")
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.20 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed. The credibility slider, which spans the cases between adaptive and fully credible expectations, is our addition.
What to notice.

With full credibility, inflation falls to 2 percent at once and output stays at potential: a costless disinflation.
With credibility 0, we are back in Fig. 10: inflation falls only to 3 percent and output to −1 percent.
In between, every bit of credibility saves output. This is why central banks explain their policy, announce inflation targets, and build a reputation: managing expectations is one of the main tools of modern monetary policy. It also explains the time consistency problem: a central bank that might later be tempted to inflate cannot be fully believed, so a commitment to a rule (like Ulysses tied to the mast) can be worth more than discretion.


Key numbers: the cost of a disinflation
We compare the total output lost while inflation falls from 4 to 2 percent, under adaptive expectations (the whole path of Fig. 11) and with a fully credible announcement.

Y_credible, pi_credible = solve_asad(2.0, pi_bar=2.0)
print(f"Adaptive expectations: output lost over {T_MAX} periods = {-adaptive.Y.sum():.2f}% of potential output")
print(f"Fully credible target: period-1 output = {Y_credible:.2f}%, inflation = {pi_credible:.2f}%")

Adaptive expectations: output lost over 20 periods = 2.00% of potential output
Fully credible target: period-1 output = 0.00%, inflation = 2.00%


Under adaptive expectations the disinflation costs about 2 percent of a year’s output; with full credibility it costs nothing. The Lucas critique makes the general point: a model with fixed expectations can give wrong answers about a new policy, because people change their expectations when the policy changes.

title: Chapter 13: Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
text:
Concluding remarks

A monetary policy rule \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\) turns the IS curve into the downward-sloping AD curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\); the Phillips curve is the upward-sloping AS curve. Their crossing gives this period’s output and inflation; the steady state has inflation on target and output at potential.
Because expected inflation is sticky, every shock is followed by slow transition dynamics: an inflation shock brings stagflation, a lower target costs a recession, and a temporary demand boom must be paid for with a later recession. The economy moves in counterclockwise loops, and the U.S. data show them too.
A simple rule with Taylor’s numbers tracks the fed funds rate surprisingly well, with large gaps in the 1970s, after 2008 and in 2021–2022. Data revisions can change what the numbers say.
Expectations are central: a credible target can lower inflation at little cost, which is why modern central banks adopt inflation targets and value their reputation.
The next chapter turns to financial crises and how they fit into the short-run model.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 14: Financial Crises and the Short-Run Model
text:
Model overview
Why did the 2008 financial crisis cause such a deep recession, even though the Federal Reserve cut its interest rate to zero? This chapter adds one idea to the short-run model of Chapters 11 to 13: firms and households do not borrow at the central bank’s rate but at a higher one, and the gap between the two, a risk premium or financial friction, jumps when lenders get scared. A bigger friction raises borrowing costs even when the central bank is cutting, so it works just like a fall in aggregate demand. Add the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates, and falling inflation can push the real interest rate up and deepen the slump.
The model’s inputs are the usual IS, policy-rule and Phillips-curve parameters plus the friction and the demand shocks; its outcomes are output, inflation and the interest rates. Below we write the new equations, fix one illustrative set of numbers shared by every diagram, and build the drawing tools. We also set up two tools for the data figures, recession shading and a peak-to-trough calculator, which the sections on the crisis, the policy response, bubbles, the aftermath and the Great Depression all reuse.
The short-run model of Chapters 11 to 13 has three pieces: the IS curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r})\), the central bank’s choice of the real interest rate (the MP curve, or the policy rule \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\)), and the Phillips curve \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\). This chapter adds one equation. The central bank sets the fed funds rate \(R^{ff}_t\), but firms and households borrow at a higher rate. The difference is a risk premium, the financial friction \(\bar{f}\):
\[R_t = R^{ff}_t + \bar{f}. \qquad (14.1)\]
In normal times \(\bar{f} = 0\). In a financial crisis lenders fear they will not be repaid, \(\bar{f}\) jumps, and the rate that matters for investment rises even when the central bank cuts its own rate. Put equation (14.1) and the policy rule into the IS curve and you get the new AD curve:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \underbrace{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}_{\text{AD shock}} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \qquad (14.2)\]
The friction enters exactly like a fall in \(\bar{a}\). The last ingredient is the Fisher equation, which links the nominal interest rate \(i_t\) to the real one: \(R_t = i_t - \pi_t\). (The textbook prints equation 14.3 as \(R_t = i_t + \pi_t\); that is a typo, and the text around it uses \(R_t = i_t - \pi_t\).) When the nominal rate is stuck, falling inflation means a rising real interest rate.
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers, apart from a few examples. All the diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of values:

the IS curve: a marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 2\) percent and \(\bar{b} = 1\), so each point of interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) costs 1 percent of output;
the policy rule and the Phillips curve: an inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, \(\bar{m} = 1\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\);
2008: the housing bust lowers demand by \(\bar{a}' = -2\) and the crisis adds a risk premium \(\bar{f} = 4\) points;
1929: the Fed raises the interest rate by 3 points and the stock market crash lowers demand by \(\bar{a}' = -3\).

With these values the model reproduces the textbook’s example numbers: \(-2\) and \(-4\) percent in Fig. 2, and \(-3\), \(-6\) and \(-9\) percent in Figs. 12 and 13.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a=0.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. Names in capital letters, such as R_BAR, are constants we set once and never change.


R_BAR, B_BAR = 2.0, 1.0            # marginal product of capital 2%, interest sensitivity b = 1
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU = 2.0, 1.0, 0.5  # inflation target 2%, policy response m = 1, Phillips slope nu = 0.5
A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS = -2.0, 4.0    # 2008: the housing bust a' = -2 and a risk premium f = 4 points
HIKE, A_CRASH = 3.0, -3.0          # 1929: the Fed's hike of 3 points and the crash a' = -3


def is_output(R, a=0.0):
    """IS curve: short-run output Y~ = a - b (R - r_bar), in percent."""
    return a - B_BAR * (R - R_BAR)


def is_rate(Y, a=0.0):
    """The IS curve solved for the real interest rate, R = r_bar + (a - Y) / b (used to draw it)."""
    return R_BAR + (a - Y) / B_BAR


def borrowing_rate(R_ff, f=0.0):
    """Equation 14.1: firms and households borrow at R = R_ff + f."""
    return R_ff + f


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """The Fisher equation: the real interest rate R = i - pi."""
    return i - pi

The AS/AD part of the model needs three more functions: the new AD curve, the AS curve and the point where they cross. To find that point, put the AS curve into the AD curve and solve for output: \(\tilde{Y}_t = \left[\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})\right] / (1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\).

def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Equation 14.2, the new AD curve: Y~ = (a - b f) - b m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return a - B_BAR * f - B_BAR * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_prev=PI_BAR):
    """The AS curve (the Phillips curve): pi = pi_prev + nu Y~, with pi_prev last period's inflation."""
    return pi_prev + NU * Y


def solve_asad(pi_prev, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Where the AD and AS curves cross: this period's output and inflation."""
    Y = (a - B_BAR * f - B_BAR * m * (pi_prev - PI_BAR)) / (1 + B_BAR * m * NU)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_prev)

A quick check of the 2008 story with these functions:

Python note. An f-string such as f"Y~ = {Y:.1f}%" inserts a value into text; :.1f means “show one decimal”. Y, pi = solve_asad(...) unpacks the two results of a function into two variables.


R_ff = R_BAR + A_HOUSING / B_BAR                  # the cut that offsets the housing bust
R = borrowing_rate(R_ff, F_CRISIS)                # what firms pay once the crisis hits
print(f"Housing bust, Fed does nothing (B):  Y~ = {is_output(R_BAR, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")
print(f"Fed cuts R_ff to {R_ff:.1f}% (C):          Y~ = {is_output(R_ff, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")
print(f"Risk premium f = 4, so R = {R:.1f}% (D):  Y~ = {is_output(R, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")
Y, pi = solve_asad(PI_BAR, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS)
print(f"AS/AD, first year of the crisis:     Y~ = {Y:.1f}%, inflation = {pi:.1f}%")

Housing bust, Fed does nothing (B):  Y~ = -2.0%
Fed cuts R_ff to 0.0% (C):          Y~ = 0.0%
Risk premium f = 4, so R = 4.0% (D):  Y~ = -4.0%
AS/AD, first year of the crisis:     Y~ = -4.0%, inflation = 0.0%


The Fed’s cut would fully offset the housing bust, but the risk premium undoes it and more: output ends 4 percent below potential. In the AS/AD version the policy rule also reacts to inflation, so the first-year recession is 4 percent and inflation falls from 2 to 0 percent.

Drawing tools
All model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_curve draws one curve and writes its name at its right end; add_label skips a name that would sit on top of another one;
add_point marks a point with dashed guides to the axes, and add_arrow draws an arrow;
model_figure starts a figure with one or two panels, and model_axes fixes the axes and writes the title.


Python note. np.linspace(-7.5, 4.5, 121) creates 121 evenly spaced numbers from −7.5 to 4.5. Because our model functions work on a whole array at once, one call gives a whole curve. (x >= x0) & (y <= y1) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. A for loop over fig.layout.annotations looks at every label already written, and return inside the loop stops the function early.


FADED_TEAL, FADED_BLUE = "rgba(0,128,112,0.35)", "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"   # curves before a shock


def axis_names(col):
    """The names Plotly gives the axes of panel col: x and y in panel 1, x2 and y2 in panel 2."""
    if col == 1:
        return "x", "y"
    return f"x{col}", f"y{col}"


def add_label(fig, x, y, text, color, col=1):
    """Write a curve name at (x, y), unless another name already sits within 0.6 axis units."""
    xref, yref = axis_names(col)
    for old in fig.layout.annotations:
        if old.xref == xref and old.showarrow is False and abs(old.x - x) < 1.5 and abs(old.y - y) < 0.6:
            return
    fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, xref=xref, yref=yref, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                       yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, box, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw a curve in panel col and write its name at its last point inside box = (x range, y range)."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = box
    inside = (x >= x0) & (x <= x1 - 1.2) & (y >= y0) & (y <= y1)    # leave room for the text
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        add_label(fig, x[inside][-1], y[inside][-1], label, color, col)


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, box, guides="v", col=1, where="top right"):
    """Mark (x, y) with a dot and a letter placed `where`; dashed guides to the x-axis ("v"), both axes ("both") or none."""
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = box
    xs, ys = [x, x], [y, y0]
    if guides == "both":
        xs, ys = [x0, x, x], [y, y, y0]
    if guides != "none":
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xs, y=ys, mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition=where,
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, col=1):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref=xref, yref=yref, axref=xref, ayref=yref, text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")


Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and add_trace(..., row=1, col=2) draws in the second panel. fig.update_xaxes(..., row=1, col=col) changes the horizontal axis of one panel only.


def model_figure(cols=1, titles=None):
    """An empty figure with cols panels side by side (titles: one short title per panel)."""
    return make_subplots(rows=1, cols=cols, subplot_titles=titles, horizontal_spacing=0.1)


def model_axes(fig, title, box, y_title, x_ticks, y_ticks, panels=1):
    """Fixed axes in every panel, so that you can see the curves move, and the title readout."""
    for col in range(1, panels + 1):
        fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Output, Ỹ (%)", range=box[0], tickvals=x_ticks, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(title_text=y_title, range=box[1], tickvals=y_ticks, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_layout(title=title)



Tools for the data figures
Two data tools are used by several figures. shade_recessions shades the U.S. recessions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file recessions.csv lists, for each recession since 1953, the peak (the last month before the recession) and the trough (its last month). peak_to_trough finds the highest value of a series between two dates, the lowest value after it, and the fall in percent between the two.

Python note. pd.read_csv reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns, and parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2007-12-01" into real dates. zip(a, b) hands over one pair of values at a time. data[(data.date >= start) & (data.date <= end)] keeps the rows between two dates, .idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and .loc[label] picks that row.


recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after the date start (Figs. 4 and 6)."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    return fig


def peak_to_trough(data, column, start, end):
    """The peak of column between two dates, the lowest value after it, and the fall in percent (Figs. 7, 8)."""
    window = data[(data.date >= start) & (data.date <= end)]
    peak = window.loc[window[column].idxmax()]
    after = window[window.date >= peak.date]
    trough = after.loc[after[column].idxmin()]
    return peak, trough, 100 * (1 - trough[column] / peak[column])

Beyond the United States. The textbook’s data figures are about the United States, but most of their series exist for other countries too. Where they do, a subsection called Beyond the United States draws the same series for many countries, with the textbook’s countries picked to start with. Two more tools serve those charts: group_colors gives every country a color that stays the same whichever countries you pick, and that no other country shown with it uses, and fit_axis chooses the narrowest of a few fixed axis ranges that still holds every point, so the axis only widens when a country needs it.

Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 and Alphabet are lists of colors that Plotly ships with, and PALETTE.append(color) adds a color at the end of a list. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. colors.get(other) is the color of other, or None if it has none yet. new + free + PALETTE joins three lists and [0] takes the first item: a color that no country uses yet if there is one, else one that no country of the same groups uses.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]      # too pale on a white page
PALETTE = list(px.colors.qualitative.Dark24)                                     # 24 dark colors ...
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:                                     # ... and 20 more
    if color not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.remove("#2E91E5")
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                          # this blue is close to the U.S. navy: use it last


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country of its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.
    groups: lists of countries shown together (the website menus); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                    # colors of the countries already shown with this one
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    used.append(colors.get(other))
        free, new = [], []                           # free: not used in its groups; new: not used by any country
        for color in PALETTE:
            if color not in used:
                free.append(color)
                if color not in colors.values():
                    new.append(color)
        colors[name] = (new + free + PALETTE)[0]
    return colors


Python note. for bottom, top in ranges: unpacks each pair of the list ranges.


def fit_axis(low, high, ranges):
    """The first range (bottom, top) in the list that holds every value from low to high; else a range that just fits."""
    for bottom, top in ranges:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    pad = 0.05 * (high - low)
    return [low - pad, high + pad]

The website cannot run Python, so its versions of these charts draw every country at once and let you switch them on in the legend. The next helper does that. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the multi-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def legend_menu(fig, shown, groups=None):
    """Website version of a country picker: the countries in `shown` are drawn, the others wait in the legend.

    Without groups, every other country is in the legend ('legendonly'), one click away, and a menu offers
    "Show all". With groups ({menu label: [countries]}), the menu puts one group at a time in the legend.
    Traces that are not countries (showlegend=False) always stay visible. The y-axis rescales to what is shown.
    """
    def visibility(members):
        out = []
        for t in fig.data:
            if t.showlegend is False or t.name in shown:
                out.append(True)
            elif members is None or t.name in members:
                out.append("legendonly")
            else:
                out.append(False)
        return out
    if groups is None:
        buttons = [dict(method="restyle", label="Textbook view", args=[{"visible": visibility(None)}]),
                   dict(method="restyle", label="Show all", args=[{"visible": [True] * len(fig.data)}])]
    else:
        buttons = [dict(method="restyle", label="Textbook view", args=[{"visible": visibility([])}])]
        for label, members in groups.items():
            buttons.append(dict(method="restyle", label=label, args=[{"visible": visibility(members)}]))
    for trace, visible in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = visible
        compact(trace)
    fig.layout.yaxis.range = None
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True)
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=0, direction="down", x=1, y=1.02, xanchor="right",
                                        yanchor="bottom")], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig


def compact(trace):
    """Shorter website files: dates without the time of day, values rounded to 2 decimals."""
    if trace.x is not None and len(trace.x) > 0 and hasattr(trace.x[0], "strftime"):
        trace.x = pd.to_datetime(trace.x).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
        trace.y = np.round(np.asarray(trace.y), 2)


def region_groups(data):
    """{region: [countries]} for the website menus of long country lists."""
    groups = {}
    for region, rows in data.groupby("region"):
        groups["Add: " + region] = sorted(rows.country.unique())
    return groups

Financial frictions in the short-run model
We first measure the financial friction in the data, then add it to the IS/MP and AS/AD diagrams to see why a crisis acts like a large negative demand shock.

Fig. 1: The spread between corporate bonds and 10-year Treasuries
Goal. See the financial friction \(\bar{f}\) in the data: the gap between what companies and the government pay to borrow.
The U.S. government almost surely repays its debt, so its 10-year bonds (Treasuries) are the safe benchmark. Companies with a “BAA” rating are solid but not risk-free, so investors ask for a higher yield on their bonds. The difference between the two yields, the spread, is a measure of the risk premium \(\bar{f}\) in equation (14.1). In normal times it is about 2 percentage points.

What to notice.

The spread averaged about 2 points from 1996 to 2007, then jumped to 6 points in December 2008, three times its usual size.
In 2007–2008 the Treasury yield fell, as the Fed cut rates and investors fled to safety, but the BAA yield rose. Lower policy rates did not reach the companies that borrow.
Smaller spikes come with other moments of stress: 2002, after the 2001 recession and the dot-com crash; the oil-price collapse of early 2016; and the Covid-19 shock of spring 2020.


Beyond the United States: government bond spreads in the euro area
Moody’s BAA index covers U.S. companies, and long, free series of corporate bond yields exist only for the United States: indexes for other countries are sold by private data firms. But the euro area offers a clean risk premium of another kind. Its governments all borrow in euros, so when Italy pays more than Germany on a 10-year bond, the difference cannot come from the currency: it is the premium investors ask for the risk of default. The textbook notes that during the European debt crisis the rates on the debt of Greece, Ireland, Italy and Spain rose “as high as 7 percent” (Chapter 20 returns to that crisis). The file holds the OECD’s 10-year government bond yields of 13 euro-area countries and their spread over Germany, from the month each joined the euro.

Fig. 2: A housing bubble and a financial crisis
Goal. See why a rise in the financial friction can defeat the central bank’s interest-rate cut.
Panel (a) repeats an example from Chapter 12. The housing bubble bursts, households feel poorer and spend less, so \(\bar{a}\) falls and the IS curve shifts back to IS′. If the Fed did nothing, the economy would move from \(A\) to \(B\), a recession. The Fed answers by cutting the fed funds rate from \(\bar{r}\) to \(R^{ff}\) (MP′), just enough to bring output back to potential at \(C\).
Panel (b) adds the financial crisis. Firms now borrow at \(R = R^{ff} + \bar{f}\) (equation 14.1). With a large enough friction, the rate they pay ends above \(\bar{r}\) despite the Fed’s cut (MP″), and the economy lands at \(D\), a deeper recession than \(B\). Two shocks conspire: the fall in consumption, and the rise in borrowing costs.

Python note. np.full_like(IS_Y, R) makes an array as long as IS_Y in which every value is R: a flat line, our MP curve. "..." if col == 1 else "..." picks the first value when the condition holds, the second otherwise.


IS_BOX = ([-7.5, 4.5], [-4.5, 9.5])            # the fixed axes: output from -7.5 to 4.5, R from -4.5 to 9.5
IS_Y = np.linspace(-7.5, 4.5, 121)             # output levels at which we draw the curves


def draw_housing_panel(fig, col, a_new, R_ff, R):
    """One panel of Fig. 14.2: IS and IS', and the MP lines at r_bar, R_ff and (panel b) R = R_ff + f."""
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, is_rate(IS_Y, a_new), "IS′", TEAL, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, is_rate(IS_Y), "IS", FADED_TEAL, IS_BOX, col=col)
    if col == 2:
        add_curve(fig, IS_Y, np.full_like(IS_Y, R), "MP″", BLUE, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, np.full_like(IS_Y, R_ff), "MP′", BLUE if col == 1 else FADED_BLUE, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, np.full_like(IS_Y, R_BAR), "MP", FADED_BLUE, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_point(fig, is_output(R_BAR, a_new), R_BAR, "B", IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_ff, "C", IS_BOX, col=col)


def housing_crisis(a_new=A_HOUSING, f=F_CRISIS):
    """Fig. 14.2: (a) a housing bust and the Fed's cut, (b) the same with a financial crisis on top."""
    R_ff = R_BAR + a_new / B_BAR                   # the cut that brings output back to potential on IS'
    R = borrowing_rate(R_ff, f)                    # equation 14.1: the rate firms pay
    Y_B, Y_D = is_output(R_BAR, a_new), is_output(R, a_new)
    fig = model_figure(2, ("(a) The housing bust and the Fed's cut", "(b) Add a financial crisis"))
    for col in [1, 2]:
        draw_housing_panel(fig, col, a_new, R_ff, R)
    add_arrow(fig, -7.0, R_BAR, -7.0, R_ff, col=1)          # the Fed cuts its rate ...
    add_arrow(fig, Y_B, -3.8, 0.0, -3.8, col=1)              # ... and output returns to potential
    add_arrow(fig, -7.0, R_ff, -7.0, R, col=2)               # the risk premium pushes R back up
    add_point(fig, Y_D, R, "D", IS_BOX, col=2, where="bottom left")   # readable when D meets B or C
    title = (f"B: Ỹ = {Y_B:.1f}%;  the Fed cuts R<sup>ff</sup> to {R_ff:.1f}%;  "
             f"R = R<sup>ff</sup> + f̄ = {R:.1f}%, so D: Ỹ = {Y_D:.1f}%")
    model_axes(fig, title, IS_BOX, "Real interest rate, R (%)", [-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4], [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8], panels=2)
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 14.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With \(\bar{f} = 0\), points \(C\) and \(D\) coincide: the Fed’s cut fully offsets the housing bust.
With \(\bar{f} = 2\), \(D\) sits exactly at \(B\): the friction cancels the cut, and the economy is back where it would be if the Fed had done nothing. Any friction above 2 points leaves the economy worse off than \(B\).
In this baseline, output at \(D\) equals \(-\bar{b}\bar{f}\) whatever the housing shock: the Fed removed the housing shock, so only the friction is left.


Key numbers: the zero lower bound
Why not cut the fed funds rate further, to \(R^{ff} = \bar{r} + \bar{a}'/\bar{b} - \bar{f}\), so that firms again pay what brings output back to potential? Because \(R^{ff}\) here is a real rate. The nominal fed funds rate is \(i = R^{ff} + \pi\), and it cannot go below zero. With inflation at 2 percent, the lowest possible real fed funds rate is \(-2\) percent.

needed = R_BAR + A_HOUSING / B_BAR - F_CRISIS     # the real fed funds rate that would restore Y~ = 0

lowest = real_rate(0.0, pi)                       # the nominal rate at zero
R = borrowing_rate(lowest, F_CRISIS)
print(f"Best the Fed can do: R_ff = {lowest:.1f}%, so R = {R:.1f}% and Y~ = {is_output(R, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")

Real fed funds rate needed: -4.0%, a nominal rate of -2.0%
Best the Fed can do: R_ff = -2.0%, so R = 2.0% and Y~ = -2.0%


The cut needed would require a nominal rate of \(-2\) percent. At the zero lower bound the best the Fed can do is \(R = 2\) percent, which only brings output back to \(B\), \(-2\) percent. This is why the Fed turned to other tools (Figs. 9 and 10).

Fig. 3: The financial crisis in the AS/AD framework
Goal. Follow the crisis over time in the AS/AD diagram, and see how it can lead to deflation.
By the new AD curve (14.2), the housing bust (a lower \(\bar{a}\)) and the risk premium \(\bar{f}\) both shift the AD curve down to AD′. In period 1 the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\): a deep recession, and inflation below the 2 percent target. Firms expect last period’s inflation, so the AS curve then shifts down period by period, and the economy slides along AD′ toward \(C\), where output is back at potential but inflation is far below target. Because inflation started at only 2 percent, it can turn negative: deflation. Point \(D\) is where the economy would jump if the shocks suddenly ended: today’s AS curve meets the old AD curve.
As in Chapter 13, one function crisis_path solves the model period by period, and the figure shows period t.

Python note. rows.append(dict(...)) adds one dictionary of named values to the list rows, and rows[-1]["pi"] is the value named "pi" in the last one. pd.DataFrame(rows) turns the list into a table, one row per period, and path.loc[t] is the row of period t.


AD_BOX = ([-7.5, 7.5], [-7.5, 5.5])            # the fixed axes: output and inflation
AD_Y = np.linspace(-7.5, 7.5, 151)             # output levels at which we draw the curves
PERIODS = 15                                   # periods simulated after the shock


def ad_inflation(Y, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """The new AD curve (14.2) solved for inflation, pi = pi_bar + (a - b f - Y) / (b m) (used to draw it)."""
    return PI_BAR + (a - B_BAR * f - Y) / (B_BAR * m)


def crisis_path(a=A_HOUSING, f=F_CRISIS, m=M_BAR):
    """Fig. 14.3: the AS/AD model period by period after a lasting shock; period 0 is the old steady state."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, pi_prev=PI_BAR, Y=0.0, pi=PI_BAR)]
    for t in range(1, PERIODS + 1):
        pi_prev = rows[-1]["pi"]                  # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_prev, a, f, m)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, pi_prev=pi_prev, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def add_crisis_path(fig, path, t, a, f, m):
    """The AD shift, the jump from A to B in period 1, then the slide along AD' up to period t."""
    x = ad_output(5.0, m=m)                       # where the old AD curve reaches 5% inflation
    add_arrow(fig, x, 5.0, x, max(ad_inflation(x, a, f, m), AD_BOX[1][0]))
    add_point(fig, path.Y[1], path.pi[1], "B", AD_BOX, guides="both")
    for s in range(2, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s])
        add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], "", AD_BOX, guides="none")


def crisis_asad(t=8, a=A_HOUSING, f=F_CRISIS, m=M_BAR):
    """Fig. 14.3: the economy t periods into a lasting crisis, with the old and new AS and AD curves."""
    path = crisis_path(a, f, m)
    now = path.loc[t]
    pi_C = PI_BAR + (a - B_BAR * f) / (B_BAR * m)        # long run: Y~ = 0 on the new AD curve
    fig = model_figure()
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, ad_inflation(AD_Y, a, f, m), "AD′", BLUE, AD_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, ad_inflation(AD_Y, m=m), "AD", FADED_BLUE, AD_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, as_inflation(AD_Y, now.pi_prev), "AS′", TEAL, AD_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, as_inflation(AD_Y), "AS", FADED_TEAL, AD_BOX)
    add_crisis_path(fig, path, t, a, f, m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_BAR, "A", AD_BOX, guides="both")
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_C, "C", AD_BOX, guides="both")
    if t > 1:
        Y_D, pi_D = solve_asad(now.pi_prev, m=m)         # D: today's AS curve meets the old AD curve
        add_point(fig, Y_D, pi_D, "D", AD_BOX, guides="none")
    Y, pi = round(now.Y, 1) + 0.0, round(now.pi, 1) + 0.0   # + 0.0 turns a rounded -0.0 into 0.0
    title = f"Period {t}: Ỹ = {Y:.1f}%, π = {pi:.1f}%   |   long run at C: π = {pi_C:.1f}%"
    model_axes(fig, title, AD_BOX, "Inflation, π (%)", [-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], [-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4])
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 14.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

In period 1 the AD shock of \(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} = -6\) costs 4 percent of output, and inflation falls from 2 to 0 percent at \(B\).
From then on inflation keeps falling, period after period, and the economy approaches \(C\), with inflation at \(-4\) percent: deflation. Each period the economy closes one third of the remaining gap to \(C\).
A larger \(\bar{m}\) makes AD′ flatter: the policy rule cuts the real rate more as inflation falls. The first recession is milder, and \(C\) has less deflation.
The model assumes that the policy rule can always lower the interest rate. Deflation and the zero lower bound break that assumption, which is why the textbook prefers the IS/MP diagram for such times (Figs. 12 and 13).

Your turn. Find the policy response \(\bar{m}\) at which inflation in the long run, at \(C\), is exactly \(-2\) percent, as in the textbook’s figure. Then check: is the period-1 recession deeper or milder than with \(\bar{m} = 1\)?


Hint

At \(C\), output is zero, so \(\pi_C = \bar{\pi} + (\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f})/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\). Solve \(-2 = 2 - 6/\bar{m}\), then compare crisis_path(m=...).Y[1] for both values.

text:
Monetary policy, the output gap and money
How did the Fed respond, and how big was the hole it had to fill? These figures compare the fed funds rate with the Taylor rule, look at estimates of potential GDP, and track the growth of the money supply.

Fig. 4: The fed funds rate and the Taylor rule
Goal. Compare the Fed’s actual interest rate with the rate a Taylor rule recommends.
The Taylor rule is the policy rule of Chapter 13 with one more term: the real rate also responds to short-run output. With equal weights of one half and the Fisher equation, the nominal rate it recommends is
\[i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + 0.5\,(\pi_t - 2) + 0.5\,\tilde{Y}_t,\]
which is \(i_t = 1\% + 1.5\,\pi_t + 0.5\,\tilde{Y}_t\) for the traditional \(\bar{r} = 2\) percent. Many economists now think the long-run real rate has fallen to about 1 percent, so the textbook also shows the rule with \(\bar{r} = 1\). Inflation is core PCE inflation over the last four quarters, and short-run output uses the CBO’s estimate of potential GDP.

Each row is a quarter. fed_funds is the average fed funds rate, short_run_output and core_pce_inflation are the two inputs of the rule, and taylor_rbar2 and taylor_rbar1 are the rule computed with \(\bar{r} = 2\) and \(\bar{r} = 1\). short_run_output_vintage2023 is short-run output as it was measured in May 2023, when the textbook was written; it stops in 2023.

def taylor_rule(pi, Y, r_bar=2.0, weight=0.5):
    """Fig. 14.4: the Taylor rule, i = r_bar + pi + 0.5 (pi - 2) + weight Y~, in percent."""
    return r_bar + pi + 0.5 * (pi - PI_BAR) + weight * Y

Our function reproduces the rule in the data file. Now we draw it, and let you change \(\bar{r}\) and the weight on output.

def taylor_chart(r_bar=2.0, weight=0.5):
    """Fig. 14.4, first panel: the actual fed funds rate and the rate the Taylor rule recommends."""
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"date": taylor.date, "Actual fed funds rate": taylor.fed_funds,
                          "Taylor rule": taylor_rule(taylor.core_pce_inflation, taylor.short_run_output, r_bar, weight)})
    boom = chart[(chart.date >= "2002-01-01") & (chart.date < "2007-01-01")]
    gap = round((boom["Taylor rule"] - boom["Actual fed funds rate"]).mean(), 1) + 0.0   # + 0.0 avoids -0.0
    fig = px.line(chart, x="date", y=["Actual fed funds rate", "Taylor rule"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"Taylor rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}: rule minus actual rate in 2002–2006 = {gap:+.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    shade_recessions(fig, "2000-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1999-07-01", "2026-12-31"], legend_title_text="",
                      yaxis=dict(range=[-5, 11.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

From 2009 to 2015 the fed funds rate sat at zero. In 2009 the rule itself was near or below zero, so the Fed looked generous; but the risk premium of Fig. 1 meant firms did not borrow at those low rates.
From 2002 to 2006 the fed funds rate was well below the rule: policy may have been too loose for too long, helping the housing boom.
Inflation was low after 2008 but did not keep falling, although output was far below potential. A credible 2 percent target may have held expectations up.
Move \(\bar{r}\) down to 1: the rule is lower by 1 point in every quarter. From late 2021 to 2022, with core inflation near or above 5 percent, even that rule called for rates far above the actual ones.


Beyond the United States: the Taylor rule for 14 central banks
The same rule can be computed for any central bank, given its policy rate, inflation and an estimate of short-run output. The file taylor_world.csv holds them for 14 central banks with their own currency and an inflation target of 2 to 2.5 percent, as annual averages from 1999: the policy rate from the BIS, and core inflation, headline inflation and the output gap from the OECD’s Economic Outlook. Two differences from the U.S. chart above: the data are annual, and the output gap is the OECD’s estimate, not the CBO’s. The rule keeps the 2 percent target.

A data-hygiene moment. The OECD has no core inflation for some countries and years: those cells are empty. A rule needs an inflation rate in every year, so we take core inflation where it exists and headline inflation otherwise, and count how many years use the fallback.

Python note. a.fillna(b) keeps the values of a and fills its empty cells with the values of b in the same rows. .isna() is true for the empty cells, and .agg(["min", "max", "count"]) computes three summaries of each group at once. In the chart function, .dropna() drops rows with an empty cell, so a year with no rule counts as “no data”.

# @title Helper for the website country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with a dropdown menu.

    Like slider_figure, but each choice also sets its own axis ranges.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            compact(trace)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range,
                  "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        buttons.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down", x=1, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom")], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig



def taylor_world_chart(country="United States", r_bar=2.0):
    """Fig. 4 for other central banks: the policy rate and the Taylor rule, annual averages."""
    data = taylor_world[taylor_world.country == country]
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"year": data.year, "Policy rate": data.policy_rate,
                          "Taylor rule": taylor_rule(data.inflation, data.output_gap, r_bar)})
    late = chart[chart.year == 2022].dropna()
    gap = "no data for 2022"
    if not late.empty:
        diff = round(late["Taylor rule"].iloc[0] - late["Policy rate"].iloc[0], 1) + 0.0      # + 0.0 avoids -0.0
        gap = f"rule minus actual in 2022 = {diff:+.1f} points"
    fig = px.line(chart, x="year", y=["Policy rate", "Taylor rule"], markers=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}, r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}: {gap}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    low = min(chart["Policy rate"].min(), chart["Taylor rule"].min())
    high = max(chart["Policy rate"].max(), chart["Taylor rule"].max())
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1998.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=fit_axis(low, high, [(-5, 11.5), (-10, 20), (-15, 30)]),
                      legend_title_text="", legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

In 2022 every one of these central banks was far below its rule: by 6.8 points in the United States, 6.5 in the euro area and 13.8 in the United Kingdom. Inflation surprised them all at the same time. Japan, with inflation still near zero, was only 1.3 points below.
From 2002 to 2006 the rule was above the actual rate in the euro area too (by 1.4 points a year on average, 1.6 in the United States with annual data): “too low for too long” was not only an American story.
Look at your data. The OECD has no core inflation for the United Kingdom, so its rule uses headline inflation (the cell above counts those years). Pick Japan: the line has holes. From 1999 to 2006 and from 2013 to 2016 the Bank of Japan targeted the quantity of money instead of an interest rate, so the BIS records no policy rate for most of those years.

Fig. 5: What happened to potential GDP?
Goal. See how much of the “recovery” after 2008 came from a lower estimate of potential GDP.
Short-run output is the gap between actual and potential GDP. Potential GDP cannot be observed: the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates it with an extended Solow model, and it revises the estimate as new data arrive. Here we compare actual GDP with two CBO estimates of potential: the latest one, and the one the CBO made in 2007, just before the crisis.

What to notice.

Until 2002 the two estimates of potential are within half a percent of each other. Then they drift apart: the latest estimate is already 2.3 percent lower in 2007. After 2008 the 2007 estimate keeps rising along its old trend, while the latest estimate bends down.
Measured against the latest estimate, actual GDP was back at potential by about 2018. Measured against the 2007 estimate, it never came close.
Since 2018 actual GDP has been slightly above the latest estimate of potential, apart from the Covid-19 dip of 2020.


Beyond the United States: GDP, potential GDP and the old trend in OECD countries
The CBO’s estimates exist only for the United States, and old vintages of other countries’ potential GDP are hard to find. The OECD’s Economic Outlook publishes real GDP and potential GDP for its members, so we can draw the latest estimates; and we can build the “2007 view” ourselves, by extending each country’s average growth of 1997–2007 into the future. That old trend is what a forecaster who expected the pre-crisis growth to continue would have drawn. Both GDP and potential are set to 100 for actual GDP in 2007.

Python note. np.exp undoes np.log: if GDP grows at the log rate g per year, after t years it is np.exp(g * t) times larger. rows.year - end counts the years since 2007 (negative before it), and .where(rows.year >= end) keeps the values from 2007 on and leaves the earlier cells empty. In the title, 'below' if gap < 0 else 'above' picks one of two words.


TREND = "Trend of 1997–2007, extended"


def old_trend(rows, start=1997, end=2007):
    """GDP if it had kept growing at its average 1997-2007 rate after 2007 (a log-linear trend)."""
    x = rows.set_index("year").gdp
    g = np.log(x[end] / x[start]) / (end - start)
    return (x[end] * np.exp(g * (rows.year - end))).where(rows.year >= end)


def potential_world_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 5 for OECD countries: actual GDP, the OECD's potential GDP and the 1997-2007 trend (2007 GDP = 100)."""
    rows = potential_world[(potential_world.country == country) & (potential_world.year >= 1995)]
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"year": rows.year, "Actual GDP": rows.gdp, "Potential GDP (OECD, latest)": rows.potential_gdp})
    title = f"{country}: no GDP data for 1997, so no trend"
    if 1997 in rows.year.values:
        chart[TREND] = old_trend(rows)
        y2019 = chart[chart.year == 2019].iloc[0]
        gap = 100 * (y2019["Actual GDP"] / y2019[TREND] - 1)
        title = f"{country}: in 2019 GDP was {abs(gap):.1f}% {'below' if gap < 0 else 'above'} its 1997–2007 trend"
    lines = list(chart.columns[1:])
    fig = px.line(chart, x="year", y=lines, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN], title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Index, actual GDP in 2007 = 100", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", selector=dict(name=TREND))
    y_range = fit_axis(chart[lines].min().min(), chart[lines].max().max(), [(60, 140), (40, 200), (20, 300), (20, 450)])
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1994.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=y_range, legend_title_text="",
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

The United States did not lose more than others. Its GDP in 2019 was 14.2 percent below the 1997–2007 trend; the euro area’s was 16.9 percent below, Spain’s 30.9 and Greece’s 52.4 percent. Greece’s GDP in 2025 was still 14 percent below its 2007 level.
Pick Germany, Japan or Israel: 5.1, 5.8 and 1.3 percent below trend. Their pre-crisis growth was slow or steady, so the old trend was easier to keep up with.
The OECD, like the CBO, has revised potential down to where GDP went: for the United States its potential grew 1.9 percent a year from 2007 to 2019 (the CBO: 1.8), and both estimates sit almost on top of actual GDP since 2018.
Look at your data. The old trend is a counterfactual, not a fact. For fast-growing economies such as Latvia, Estonia or Ireland, ten boom years extrapolated give absurd paths, and the axis widens. Ireland’s GDP also jumped 25 percent in 2015, when multinational firms moved assets there: an accounting change, not a boom in production.



Key numbers: two estimates of the output gap

def output_gap(actual, potential):
    """Short-run output: the percent gap between actual and potential GDP."""
    return 100 * (actual / potential - 1)

Fig. 6: The growth rate of various money supply measures
Goal. Check whether the Fed repeated the mistake of the Great Depression, when the money supply collapsed.
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Great Depression on a Fed that let the money supply fall from 1929 to 1933. Bubbles in stock and home prices
Asset prices that rise far above their long-run averages can fall sharply, and when they do, wealth and spending fall with them. We look at the stock market and at real home prices.

Fig. 7: The price-earnings ratio in the stock market
Goal. Measure stock prices against company profits and look for bubbles.
In standard finance models, a stock is worth the present value of the profits it will earn. Robert Shiller’s price-earnings ratio divides the stock price index by the average real earnings of the previous ten years (it is often called the CAPE). When the ratio climbs far above its long-run average, prices have usually come back down. The textbook marks the average with a dashed line; the slider lets you choose the years behind that average.
Why only the United States? Shiller’s monthly prices and earnings, back to 1871, are free only for the U.S. stock market. Price-earnings ratios of this kind for other markets are compiled by private index firms and are not open data, so this figure stays American.

Python note. px.area draws a line and fills the area below it. cape.date.dt.year >= since is true for the months from the year since on. cape.cape.iloc[-1] is the last value of the column.


def cape_chart(since=1881):
    """Fig. 14.7: the price-earnings ratio and its average from the year since to today."""
    recent = cape[cape.date.dt.year >= since]
    average = recent.cape.mean()
    fig = px.area(cape, x="date", y="cape", color_discrete_sequence=["#5aa0d8"],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "cape": "Price-earnings ratio"},
                  title=f"Price-earnings ratio: {cape.cape.iloc[-1]:.1f} in {cape.date.iloc[-1]:%b %Y}; "
                        f"average since {since}: {average:.1f}")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[recent.date.iloc[0], cape.date.iloc[-1]], y=[average, average], mode="lines",
                             name=f"Average since {since}", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash")))
    for year in [1929, 1999]:
        top = cape.loc[cape[cape.date.dt.year == year].cape.idxmax()]
        fig.add_annotation(x=top.date, y=top.cape, text=f"{top.date:%b %Y}: {top.cape:.1f}", ax=-60, ay=-25)
    fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[0, 51], tickvals=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50]), showlegend=False)
    return fig

The ratio peaked in September 1929, just before the crash, and peaked even higher in December 1999, at the top of the dot-com boom. Both times prices then fell a long way.
The average over the whole sample is now 17.8 (the textbook’s 17.4 stopped in 2023). The average since 1990 is much higher: whether today’s high ratio is a bubble depends on which “normal” you believe in.
In 2026 the ratio is above 40, close to the 1999 record.

Fig. 8: Real home prices in the United States
Goal. See how unusual the housing boom of the 2000s was, and how far prices fell.
Shiller’s index of U.S. home prices is divided by the consumer price index, so it measures real home prices: the price of a house in terms of other goods. It is set to 100 in 1953. We use a ratio (log) scale, on which equal percentage changes look equally tall. The menu picks a boom-and-bust episode, and peak_to_trough measures it.

Python note. log_y=True gives a ratio scale. On such an axis, Plotly expects the range in powers of ten: np.log10(80) is the power of ten that gives 80. A dictionary such as EPISODES stores named values, and EPISODES[episode] gets the two dates of one episode. Dropdown shows a menu of choices.


homes = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-8.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).rename(columns={"real_home_price_1953_100": "price"})
EPISODES = {"1970s boom": ("1975-01-01", "1984-12-31"), "1980s boom": ("1985-01-01", "1997-12-31"),
            "2000s bubble": ("2000-01-01", "2015-12-31"), "2020s boom": ("2020-01-01", "2026-12-31")}


def home_prices(episode="2000s bubble"):
    """Fig. 14.8: real home prices on a ratio scale, with the peak and trough of one episode."""
    peak, trough, fall = peak_to_trough(homes, "price", *EPISODES[episode])
    fig = px.line(homes, x="date", y="price", log_y=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "price": "Index, 1953 = 100 (ratio scale)"},
                  title=f"{episode}: real home prices fell {fall:.1f}% from {peak.date:%b %Y} to {trough.date:%b %Y}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak.date, trough.date], y=[peak.price, trough.price], mode="markers+text",
                             text=["Peak", "Trough"], textposition=["top center", "bottom center"], showlegend=False,
                             marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(220)], tickvals=[80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200])
    return fig


Python note. *EPISODES[episode] unpacks the pair of dates into two separate arguments, start and end.

What to notice.

From 1953 to 2000 real home prices moved within a narrow band, between about 88 and 115. The boom of the 2000s pushed them far above anything seen before.
Real prices fell 35.7 percent from the end of 2005 to early 2012, exactly the textbook’s number. Household wealth fell with them, which is the drop in \(\bar{a}\) of Fig. 2.
Earlier booms, around 1979 and 1989, were also followed by real declines. After 2020 prices rose again and have eased only a little.

Its index is set to 100 in 2010 and is quarterly. For the United States it tells the same story: real prices fell 38.9 percent from the first quarter of 2006 to the third quarter of 2011 (Shiller: 35.7 percent). The Fed’s balance sheet and forward guidance
With its rate at zero, the Fed used other tools: it bought assets on a large scale, and it told markets how long rates would stay low.

Fig. 9: Financial assets of the Federal Reserve
Goal. See the size and the composition of the Fed’s balance sheet change during the crisis and after.
With the fed funds rate at zero, the Fed bought other assets on a huge scale: mortgage-backed securities and long-term Treasury bonds. This is quantitative easing (QE), done in three rounds after 2008 and again in 2020. The chart stacks the Fed’s assets by type, from the weekly balance sheet (the H.4.1 release).
The textbook reprints a chart of the Cleveland Fed that split Treasuries by purchase program; that chart is no longer published. We split Treasuries by remaining maturity instead: over one year (“long-term”) and within one year (“short-term”). So our long-term layer is not zero before 2009, as it is in the textbook.

What to notice.

In late 2008 the Fed first lent directly to banks and to credit markets (the green and dark layers). These loans were repaid within about two years.
QE1, QE2 and QE3 then added mortgage-backed securities and long-term Treasuries, step by step, until the balance sheet reached about 4.5 trillion dollars in 2015.
The Covid-19 purchases added more than 4 trillion dollars in two years. Since 2022 the Fed has let its holdings run off, to about 6.8 trillion dollars in 2026.


Beyond the United States: central bank balance sheets in 35 economies
Other central banks bought assets too: the European Central Bank (ECB), the Bank of Japan and the Bank of England all ran large QE programs. Dollars, euros and yen cannot be compared directly, so we divide each central bank’s total assets by its country’s GDP. The BIS publishes this ratio, quarterly from 2000. Fig. 10: The fed funds rate: actual and expected
Goal. See how forward guidance changed what financial markets expected of the Fed.
Firms borrow for years, so they care about long-term interest rates, and a long rate is roughly the average of the short rates expected over its life. def realized_rate(day):
    """The actual fed funds rate in the month of day, as text ("not known yet" for future months)."""
    later = actual[actual.date.dt.to_period("M") == day.to_period("M")]
    if later.empty:
        return "not known yet"
    return f"{later.fed_funds.iloc[0]:.2f}%"


def add_expected_path(fig, year, chosen):
    """One market forecast, made in June of year: thick if chosen, faint otherwise."""
    path = paths[["date", f"expected_{year}_06"]].dropna()
    width, color = 1.5, "rgba(127,178,58,0.45)"
    if chosen:
        width, color = 4, GREEN
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=path.date, y=path[f"expected_{year}_06"], mode="lines", name=f"Expected in June {year}",
                             line=dict(color=color, width=width, dash="dash")))
    return path


def expectations_chart(year=2009):
    """Fig. 14.10: the actual fed funds rate and the paths markets expected each June."""
    fig = px.line(actual, x="date", y="fed_funds", color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "fed_funds": "Percent"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3, name="Actual fed funds rate")
    for y in range(2008, 2027):
        path = add_expected_path(fig, y, y == year)
        if y == year:
            end, expected = path.date.iloc[-1], path.iloc[-1, 1]
    fig.add_vline(x="2012-01-25", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_annotation(x="2012-01-25", y=5.7, text="Jan 2012: the Fed says rates<br>stay low until late 2014", xanchor="left", ax=30, ay=0)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"June {year}: markets expected {expected:.2f}% for {end:%b %Y}; actual: {realized_rate(end)}",
                      showlegend=False, xaxis_range=["2007-07-01", "2029-06-30"], yaxis=dict(range=[-0.3, 6.2],
                      tickvals=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]))
    return fig

The aftermath: a productivity slowdown?
The recovery after 2009 was slow. One possible reason is that total factor productivity has grown more slowly since the mid-2000s.

Fig. 11: U.S. total factor productivity
Goal. Measure the productivity slowdown that may explain the slow recovery after 2008.
Total factor productivity (TFP) is output divided by a weighted combination of capital and labor: the \(\bar{A}\) of the production model. The Bureau of Labor Statistics measures it for the private business sector and for manufacturing. Both indexes are set to 100 in 2009 and drawn on a ratio scale. The average annual growth rate between two years is
\[g = 100 \times \frac{\ln(x_{\text{end}} / x_{\text{start}})}{\text{end} - \text{start}}.\]

Python note. np.log is the natural logarithm. data.set_index("year")[column] makes the years the row labels of a column, so x[2004] is the value of 2004.


tfp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-11.csv")


def growth_rate(data, column, start, end):
    """Average annual growth in percent from year start to year end, 100 ln(x_end / x_start) / (end - start)."""
    x = data.set_index("year")[column]
    return 100 * np.log(x[end] / x[start]) / (end - start)


LAST_PB = tfp.year[tfp.tfp_private_business.notna()].max()      # last year with data, private business
LAST_MFG = tfp.year[tfp.tfp_manufacturing.notna()].max()         # last year with data, manufacturing

print(f"Manufacturing 2004-{LAST_MFG}: {growth_rate(tfp, 'tfp_manufacturing', 2004, LAST_MFG):.2f}% a year")

Private business 2004-2025: 0.72% a year
Manufacturing 2004-2024: 0.06% a year

def tfp_title(data, countries, start):
    """The title of Fig. 11 for other countries: the fastest and slowest TFP growth from start to 2023."""
    growth, missing = {}, []
    for name in countries:
        rows = data[data.country == name]
        if start in rows.year.values:
            growth[name] = round(growth_rate(rows, "tfp_2009", start, 2023), 2) + 0.0   # + 0.0 avoids -0.00
        else:
            missing.append(name)
    title = f"TFP growth {start}–2023:"
    if growth:
        fast, slow = max(growth, key=growth.get), min(growth, key=growth.get)
        title = title + f" {fast} {growth[fast]:.2f}% a year"
        if slow != fast:
            title = title + f", {slow} {growth[slow]:.2f}%"
    if missing:
        title = title + f" (no {start} data: " + ", ".join(missing) + ")"
    return title

text:
The Great Depression in the short-run model
Finally, we use the same tools on the 1930s: a rate hike by the Fed and a stock market crash, followed by deflation that raised real interest rates.

Fig. 12: The Great Depression in the IS/MP framework
Goal. Rebuild the textbook’s worked exercise on the Great Depression, one shock at a time.
Three things went wrong after 1928, and each moved the economy further below potential:

A to B. Worried about a stock market bubble, the Fed raised interest rates (MP → MP′).
B to C. The bubble burst in October 1929. Lost wealth and uncertainty cut consumption and investment: \(\bar{a}\) fell and the IS curve shifted back to IS′.
C to D. The slump made inflation fall, through the Phillips curve, from about zero to deflation. The Fed kept the nominal rate \(i\) unchanged, so by the Fisher equation \(R = i - \pi\) the real rate rose (MP″).

The function depression_steps follows the three steps with our model functions, and great_depression draws them. Figs. 12 and 13 show the same event in two diagrams, so one function draws both; the diagram buttons switch between them, and the step slider walks from \(A\) to \(D\).

def depression_steps(hike=HIKE, a_crash=A_CRASH, nu=NU):
    """Exercise 2 (Figs. 14.12-14.13): output, real rate and inflation at the points A, B, C and D."""
    pi_0 = 0.0                                    # inflation was about zero in the late 1920s
    i = R_BAR + pi_0 + hike                       # the Fed raises its nominal rate
    R_B = real_rate(i, pi_0)
    Y_C = is_output(R_B, a_crash)                 # the crash shifts the IS curve back
    pi_D = pi_0 + nu * Y_C                        # Phillips curve: the slump at C lowers inflation
    R_D = real_rate(i, pi_D)                      # i stays fixed, so deflation raises the real rate
    rows = [("A", is_output(R_BAR), R_BAR, pi_0), ("B", is_output(R_B), R_B, pi_0),
            ("C", Y_C, R_B, pi_0), ("D", is_output(R_D, a_crash), R_D, pi_D)]
    steps = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["point", "Y", "R", "pi"])
    steps["d_pi"] = nu * steps.Y + 0.0            # the change in inflation (Fig. 14.13); + 0.0 avoids -0.0
    return steps

def draw_depression_ismp(fig, steps, step, a_crash):
    """Fig. 14.12: IS (and IS' from step C on), one MP line per step, and the points up to step."""
    if step >= 2:
        add_curve(fig, DEP_Y, is_rate(DEP_Y, a_crash), "IS′", TEAL, DEP_BOX)

    lines = [("MP", steps.R[0], 0), ("MP′", steps.R[1], 1), ("MP″", steps.R[3], 3)]
    for name, R, first in reversed(lines):

def draw_depression_phillips(fig, steps, step, nu):

                       xanchor="right", font=dict(size=13))      # bottom right, away from the curve


def great_depression(step=3, hike=HIKE, a_crash=A_CRASH, nu=NU, diagram="IS/MP"):
    """Figs. 14.12 and 14.13: the Great Depression step by step, in the IS/MP or the Phillips curve diagram."""
    steps = depression_steps(hike, a_crash, nu)
    now = steps.loc[step]
    fig = model_figure()
    if diagram == "IS/MP":

        title = f"{STEP_NAMES[step]}: Ỹ = {now.Y:.1f}%, R = {now.R:.1f}%, π = {now.pi:.1f}%"
