# @title Helper for the multi-country website figures (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
G7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]


def legend_menu(fig, data, shown):
    """Website version of a multi-country chart: the countries in `shown` are drawn, every other country is
    one click away in the legend, and buttons show a group (the textbook's countries, the G7, a region, all).
    Traces that are not countries, such as averages, always stay visible."""
    countries = set(data.country)
    groups = {"Textbook": list(shown), "G7": G7}
    for region in sorted(data.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = list(data[data.region == region].country.unique())
    groups["All"] = list(countries)
    for trace in fig.data:
        if trace.name in countries and trace.name not in shown:
            trace.visible = "legendonly"
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            visible.append(True if trace.name not in countries or trace.name in members else "legendonly")
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", pad=dict(r=4, t=0))],
                      margin=dict(t=120))
    return fig

def when(date, frequency):
    """A date as '2020Q2' for quarterly data, or as 'Apr 2020' for monthly data."""
    if frequency == "quarterly":
        return f"{date.year}Q{date.quarter}"
    return f"{date:%b %Y}"


def saving_chart(frequency="quarterly"):
    """Fig. 16.4: the personal saving rate, as quarterly averages or as monthly values."""
    if frequency == "quarterly":
        data, rate = saving, rate_q
    else:
        data, rate = monthly, rate_m
    high, low = rate.idxmax(), rate.idxmin()
    fig = px.area(data, x="date", y="saving_rate", labels={"date": "Year", "saving_rate": "Percent of disposable income"},
                  title=f"{frequency.capitalize()} data: highest {rate[high]:.1f}% ({when(high, frequency)}), "
                        f"lowest {rate[low]:.1f}% ({when(low, frequency)})")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2.5), fillcolor="rgba(138, 150, 163, 0.3)")
    fig.update_xaxes(range=["1969-07-01", "2027-01-01"])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 35], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35])     # no 0 next to the first year
    return fig

title: Chapter 16: Consumption
text:
Concluding remarks

In the neoclassical consumption model, a consumer chooses consumption today and in the future to maximize lifetime utility, subject to the intertemporal budget constraint: the present value of consumption equals total wealth, financial plus human wealth.
Diminishing marginal utility makes people want to smooth consumption. With log utility and \(\beta=1\), Irving consumes half of his total wealth today, and the Euler equation links consumption growth to \(\beta(1+R)\), which is why interest rates and growth rates are similar numbers.
So consumption follows permanent income: the marginal propensity to consume out of a temporary windfall is small, and the timing of taxes does not matter (Ricardian equivalence). Borrowing constraints and precautionary saving raise the MPC toward 1 for many low-wealth households.
U.S. data show household debt doubling relative to GDP before 2008 and the saving rate falling to about 2.5 percent, while household wealth rose relative to income.
The next chapter turns to the other big private spending decision, investment by firms.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 17: Investment
text:
Model overview
Investment is the part of GDP that builds the future: new machines, buildings, houses and inventories. This chapter explains how a firm decides how much capital to own. The key idea is a comparison of two uses of money. A firm can put a dollar in the bank and earn the interest rate, or buy capital and earn its marginal product. A profit-maximizing firm keeps adding capital until the two returns are equal, and the cost of using capital for a year is called the user cost.
The inputs are the interest rate, the depreciation rate, expected changes in the price of capital and taxes; the outcomes are the desired capital stock and the investment rate. The same comparison of returns also prices a share of stock. Below we write these equations once as Python functions. The first section uses them to draw the firm’s investment decision, the second applies them to the stock market, and the last looks at the parts of U.S. investment in the data.
The arbitrage equation. Gino’s pizza restaurant has some spare cash and two uses for it: a bank deposit that pays the interest rate \(R\), or a new pizza oven, bought at the price \(p_k\), used for a year and then sold. If Gino’s maximizes profits, the last dollar must earn the same in both uses, otherwise moving money to the better use would raise profits:
\[\underbrace{R\cdot p_k}_{\text{bank account}} = \underbrace{MPK + \Delta p_k}_{\text{pizza oven}} \qquad (17.2)\]
The oven earns its marginal product \(MPK\), plus a capital gain \(\Delta p_k\) when its price rises (a capital loss when it falls). With the price normalized to 1 and depreciation \(\bar{d}\) written out explicitly, the firm invests until
\[MPK = \underbrace{R + \bar{d} - \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k}}_{\text{user cost of capital}} \qquad (17.4)\]
The user cost of capital is the full cost of using one more unit of capital for a year: the interest given up, the wear and tear, minus any rise in the price of the capital good. A corporate income tax at rate \(\tau\) takes part of the marginal product, so the marginal product must be higher:
\[MPK = \frac{R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k}{1-\tau} \qquad (17.6)\]
Diminishing returns. With the production function of Chapter 4, \(Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}\), the marginal product of capital falls as capital rises:
\[MPK = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{K} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\bar{A}\left(\frac{L}{K}\right)^{2/3} \qquad (17.7)\]
(The textbook’s text prints \(L^{1/2}\) here, a typo: equation 17.7 needs the exponent \(2/3\).) Setting \(MPK\) equal to the user cost \(uc\) gives the desired capital stock, \(K^{\text{desired}} = L\,(\bar{A}/(3\,uc))^{3/2}\), and the capital-output ratio \(Y/K = 3\cdot uc\) (17.9).
Our baseline. We start from the textbook’s example: the real interest rate is 2 percent, capital wears out at 8 percent a year and its price does not change, which gives a user cost of 10 percent. We add \(\bar{A} = 0.3\) and \(L = 1\), chosen so that the desired capital stock is exactly \(K = 1\) (and output \(Y = 0.3\)). Figs. 1 and 2 both start from this baseline.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing gpk=0.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”. Names in capital letters, such as A_BAR, are constants that we set once and reuse.


A_BAR, L_BAR = 0.3, 1.0          # illustrative productivity and labor: the baseline desired capital is K = 1


def user_cost(R, d, gpk=0.0, tau=0.0):
    """User cost of capital: (R + d - gpk) / (1 - tau)   (equations 17.4 and 17.6; gpk is the capital gain)."""
    return (R + d - gpk) / (1 - tau)


def mpk(K, A=A_BAR, L=L_BAR):
    """Marginal product of capital: MPK = (1/3) A (L/K)^(2/3)   (equation 17.7)."""
    return A / 3 * (L / K) ** (2 / 3)


def desired_capital(uc, A=A_BAR, L=L_BAR):
    """Desired capital stock, where MPK = uc: K = L (A / (3 uc))^(3/2)   (from equation 17.7)."""
    return L * (A / (3 * uc)) ** (3 / 2)


def investment_rate(uc, g_K=0.02, d=0.08):
    """Investment rate: I/Y = (g_K + d) / (3 uc)   (equation 17.13)."""
    return (g_K + d) / (3 * uc)

The same arbitrage idea prices a stock. An investor can earn \(R\) in the bank, or buy a stock at the price \(p_s\) and receive its dividend plus the capital gain. The two returns must be equal:
\[R = \frac{\text{dividend}}{p_s} + \frac{\Delta p_s}{p_s} \qquad (17.15)\]
When dividends grow at a constant rate \(g\), the stock price grows at \(g\) too, and solving for the price gives
\[p_s = \frac{\text{dividend}}{R - g} \qquad (17.16)\]
Dividing by the earnings of the firm gives the price-earnings ratio, which depends on the share of earnings paid out as dividends (the payout ratio) and on \(R-g\):
\[\frac{p_s}{\text{earnings}} = \frac{\text{dividend}/\text{earnings}}{R - g} \qquad (17.17)\]

def stock_price(dividend, R, g=0.0):
    """Price of a stock: dividend / (R - g)   (equation 17.16; dividends grow at rate g)."""
    return dividend / (R - g)


def pe_ratio(payout, R, g):
    """Price-earnings ratio: (dividend / earnings) / (R - g)   (equation 17.17)."""
    return payout / (R - g)

Let us check the functions against the numbers in the textbook.

Python note. An f-string such as f"{uc:.1%}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1% shows a share as a percentage with one decimal (0.1 becomes 10.0%), and :.2f shows two decimals.


uc = user_cost(R=0.02, d=0.08)
uc_tax = user_cost(R=0.02, d=0.08, tau=0.35)
K = desired_capital(uc)
print(f"User cost, no tax:            {uc:.1%}   (textbook: 10 percent)")
print(f"User cost with a 35% tax:     {uc_tax:.1%}   (textbook: 'more than 15 percent')")
print(f"Desired capital, baseline:    K = {K:.2f}, with MPK = {mpk(K):.1%}")
print(f"Capital-output ratio check:   Y/K = {A_BAR * K ** (1 / 3) / K:.2f} = 3 x uc = {3 * uc:.2f}   (17.9)")
print(f"Stock, 10 dollar dividend, R = 5%:          {stock_price(10, 0.05):.0f} dollars   (textbook: 200)")
print(f"Stock, 10 dollar dividend, R = 5%, g = 2%:  {stock_price(10, 0.05, 0.02):.0f} dollars   (textbook: about 333)")

User cost, no tax:            10.0%   (textbook: 10 percent)
User cost with a 35% tax:     15.4%   (textbook: 'more than 15 percent')
Desired capital, baseline:    K = 1.00, with MPK = 10.0%
Capital-output ratio check:   Y/K = 0.30 = 3 x uc = 0.30   (17.9)
Stock, 10 dollar dividend, R = 5%:          200 dollars   (textbook: 200)
Stock, 10 dollar dividend, R = 5%, g = 2%:  333 dollars   (textbook: about 333)


The exact user cost with the tax is \(0.10/0.65 = 0.1538\), which rounds to 15.4 percent; the textbook writes \(\approx 0.153\).

Drawing tools
Figs. 1 and 2 are the same kind of diagram, so we write its drawing steps once:

capital_figure starts a diagram with fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move;
add_mpk draws the marginal product curve, and add_level draws a flat user-cost line; both write a label on the plot next to the line (its equation or its value), and add_label skips a label that would sit on top of another one;
add_point marks a desired capital stock with a dashed guide to the axis, and add_arrow draws an arrow.


Python note. np.linspace(0.05, K_max, 300) creates 300 evenly spaced numbers from 0.05 to K_max, the right end of the x-axis, which fig.layout.xaxis.range[1] reads from the figure. Because mpk works on a whole array at once, one call gives the whole curve. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and each add_trace adds one line or set of points. MPK <= 0.4 is true where the curve is inside the axes, K[inside] keeps those values, and [0] takes the first of them. A for loop over fig.layout.annotations looks at every label already written, and return inside the loop stops the function early.


K_RANGE, RETURN_RANGE = [0, 3], [0, 0.4]          # fixed axes of Figs. 1 and 2


def capital_figure(title):
    """An empty diagram: capital on the x-axis, returns per unit of capital (percent) on the y-axis."""
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.update_layout(title=title, showlegend=False,
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital, K", range=K_RANGE, tickvals=[0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3], zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Return per unit of capital", range=RETURN_RANGE,
                                 tickvals=[0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], tickformat=".0%", zeroline=False))
    return fig


def add_label(fig, x, y, text, color, xanchor="left"):
    """Write a line name at (x, y), unless another name already sits within 2 points of it."""
    for old in fig.layout.annotations:
        if old.showarrow is False and abs(old.x - x) < 0.5 and abs(old.y - y) < 0.02:
            return
    fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor=xanchor, yanchor="bottom",
                       font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_mpk(fig, A=A_BAR):
    """Draw the MPK curve of equation (17.7) and write its name next to its top-left end."""
    K_max = fig.layout.xaxis.range[1]                     # the right end of the x-axis
    K = np.linspace(0.05, K_max, 300)
    MPK = mpk(K, A)
    inside = MPK <= RETURN_RANGE[1]                       # the part of the curve inside the axes
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=K[inside], y=MPK[inside], mode="lines", name="MPK", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    add_label(fig, K[inside][0] + 0.05, MPK[inside][0] - 0.03, "MPK = (A/3)·(L/K)<sup>2/3</sup>", BLUE)


def add_level(fig, uc, label, color, dash="solid"):
    """Draw a flat user-cost line at the height uc and write its name at its right end."""
    K_max = fig.layout.xaxis.range[1]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, K_max], y=[uc, uc], mode="lines", name=label, line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    add_label(fig, K_max, uc, label, color, xanchor="right")


def add_point(fig, K, uc, label, anchor="left"):
    """Mark (K, uc) with a dot and a dashed guide down to the x-axis, labelled next to the guide."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[K, K], y=[0, uc], mode="lines", hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[K], y=[uc], mode="markers", name=label, marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=K, y=0, text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor=anchor, yanchor="bottom", font=dict(size=14))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, text=""):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1), with an optional text at its tail; nothing if the points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) > 0.03 or abs(y1 - y0) > 0.005:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text=text,
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")

title: Chapter 17: Investment
section: How firms choose their capital stock
text:
How firms choose their capital stock
The firm’s decision fits in one diagram: the marginal product of capital falls as capital rises, and the firm stops where it meets the user cost. A corporate tax raises that cost and shrinks the desired capital stock.

Fig. 1: How much should a firm invest?
Goal. Find the desired capital stock of a firm, and see how the interest rate, depreciation, capital gains and productivity change it.
The marginal product of capital falls as the firm adds capital: the first pizza oven adds a lot of pizzas, the tenth adds few. The user cost does not depend on how much capital the firm has, so it is a flat line. The firm keeps investing as long as one more unit of capital earns more than it costs, so it stops where the two lines cross, at \(K^{\text{desired}}\).
Investment is what moves the firm toward that point. The capital accumulation equation says that next year’s capital is this year’s investment plus the capital that did not wear out:
\[K_{t+1} = I_t + (1-\bar{d})\,K_t \qquad (17.8)\]
So a young firm that starts with \(K_0\) and wants \(K^{\text{desired}}\) next year must invest \(I = K^{\text{desired}} - (1-\bar{d})K_0\). The title shows this number. The arrow points from \(K_0\) to the desired capital stock.

Python note. if K_star > 2.6: runs the indented lines below it only when the condition is true. Here it widens the x-axis (update_xaxes) in the rare case of a very low user cost, when the desired capital stock would otherwise fall off the chart; tickvals=None lets Plotly choose the tick marks. round(x, 2) rounds a number to two decimals, and adding 0.0 turns a rounded -0.0 into 0.0, so the title never shows “-0.00”.


def desired_capital_diagram(R=0.02, d=0.08, gpk=0.0, A=A_BAR, K0=0.5):
    """Fig. 17.1: invest until the marginal product of capital falls to the user cost."""
    uc = user_cost(R, d, gpk)
    K_star = desired_capital(uc, A)
    I = round(K_star - (1 - d) * K0, 2) + 0.0        # investment that reaches K_star next year, equation (17.8)
    fig = capital_figure(f"User cost {uc:.1%}  |  desired capital {K_star:.2f}  |  investment from K0 = {K0:.1f}: {I:+.2f}")
    if K_star > 2.6:                                 # a very low user cost: widen the x-axis so K desired stays on it
        fig.update_xaxes(range=[0, 1.15 * K_star], tickvals=None)
    add_mpk(fig, A)
    add_level(fig, uc, f"R + d − Δp/p = {uc:.1%}", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, K_star, uc, "K<sup>desired</sup>")
    add_arrow(fig, K0, 0.03, K_star, 0.03, text="K<sub>0</sub>")
    return fig

Now the interactive version. Move the sliders and watch where the two lines cross.

Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.


interact(desired_capital_diagram,

Source. Adapted from Fig. 17.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

In the baseline the user cost is 10 percent and the desired capital stock is 1. A firm that starts with \(K_0 = 0.5\) must invest 0.54: half a unit to grow, and 0.04 to replace the capital that wears out.
A higher interest rate or faster depreciation raises the user cost and moves \(K^{\text{desired}}\) to the left. Because the MPK curve flattens out, a rise of 1 point in the user cost lowers desired capital by more when the user cost is low.
A capital gain lowers the user cost. Structures, whose land gets scarcer, often gain in value; computers lose value quickly, so their user cost is high. Set \(\Delta p/p = -0.04\): desired capital falls to 0.60.
Higher productivity \(\bar{A}\) shifts the MPK curve up, so the firm wants more capital at the same user cost.

Your turn. A firm can buy either computers, whose price falls by 4 percent a year, or a building, whose price rises by 2 percent a year. With \(R = 0.02\) and \(\bar{d} = 0.08\) for both, how much more capital does the firm want in buildings than in computers? Use user_cost and desired_capital in the cell below.


Hint

The capital gain enters the user cost with a minus sign: user_cost(0.02, 0.08, gpk=-0.04) for the computers and gpk=0.02 for the building. Then divide the two desired capital stocks.

Fig. 2: An increase in the corporate income tax
Goal. See why a corporate income tax lowers the capital stock that firms want.
The tax takes a share \(\tau\) of what each unit of capital earns, so the firm keeps only \((1-\tau)MPK\). To make an investment worthwhile, the marginal product before tax must now cover the user cost divided by \(1-\tau\) (equation 17.6). The user-cost line shifts up, and the firm moves up its MPK curve to a smaller capital stock. With the textbook’s numbers, a 35 percent tax raises the user cost from 10 to about 15 percent.

def corporate_tax_diagram(tau=0.35, R=0.02, d=0.08):
    """Fig. 17.2: a corporate income tax raises the user cost and lowers the desired capital stock."""
    uc0, uc1 = user_cost(R, d), user_cost(R, d, tau=tau)
    K0, K1 = desired_capital(uc0), desired_capital(uc1)
    fig = capital_figure(f"User cost {uc0:.1%} → {uc1:.1%}  |  desired capital {K0:.2f} → {K1:.2f} ({K1 / K0 - 1:+.0%})")
    add_mpk(fig)
    add_level(fig, uc1, f"τ = {tau:.0%}: {uc1:.1%}", TEAL)
    add_level(fig, uc0, f"τ = 0: {uc0:.1%}", GRAY, dash="dash")      # the old line, dashed
    add_point(fig, K0, uc0, "K<sup>initial</sup>")
    add_point(fig, K1, uc1, "K<sup>desired</sup>", anchor="right")
    add_arrow(fig, 0.06, uc0, 0.06, uc1)                              # the user cost shifts up
    add_arrow(fig, K0, 0.06, K1, 0.06)                                # desired capital falls
    return fig

What to notice.

With \(\tau = 0.35\) the user cost rises from 10.0 to 15.4 percent, and the desired capital stock falls by about half, from 1.00 to 0.52.
The capital stock falls by much more than 35 percent. Desired capital is proportional to \(uc^{-3/2}\), so it falls by the factor \((1-\tau)^{3/2} = 0.65^{1.5} \approx 0.52\).
A higher interest rate moves both user-cost lines up, and the tax multiplies every change in \(R\) by \(1/(1-\tau)\).


Key numbers: from desired capital to investment
After the tax, the firm has more capital than it wants. Equation (17.8) says it can simply stop investing and let depreciation do the work. How many years does that take?

Python note. A while loop repeats its indented lines as long as its condition is true. Here each pass is one year in which the capital stock shrinks by the depreciation rate, and years += 1 adds one to the counter.


K_initial = desired_capital(user_cost(0.02, 0.08))
K_target = desired_capital(user_cost(0.02, 0.08, tau=0.35))
K, years = K_initial, 0
while K > K_target:
    K = (1 - 0.08) * K                  # no new investment: equation (17.8) with I = 0
    years += 1
print(f"Capital falls from {K_initial:.2f} to {K_target:.2f}: {years} years with no investment at all")

Capital falls from 1.00 to 0.52: 8 years with no investment at all


In the long run the tax also lowers the investment rate. Equation (17.13) says that, for a given growth rate of capital \(g_K\), the investment rate is inversely proportional to the user cost. We use \(g_K = 2\) percent, an illustrative long-run growth rate:

s_after = investment_rate(user_cost(0.02, 0.08, tau=0.35))

print(f"Investment rate I/Y with a 35% tax:  {s_after:.1%}  (a fall by the factor 1 - tau = {s_after / s_before:.2f})")

def tax_table(year=2022):
    """Table 17.1 for one year: tax rates and user costs, with the U.S. user cost fixed at 10 percent."""
    table = taxes[taxes.year == year].copy()
    tau_us = table[table.country == "United States"].cit_rate.iloc[0] / 100
    uc_no_tax = 0.10 * (1 - tau_us)                       # the user cost before taxes
    table["user_cost"] = 100 * uc_no_tax / (1 - table.cit_rate / 100)       # equation (17.6)
    table = book.merge(table[["country", "cit_rate", "user_cost"]], on="country")
    names = {"book_rate": "tax rate, book", "cit_rate": f"tax rate, {year}",
             "book_user_cost": "user cost, book", "user_cost": f"user cost, {year}"}
    return table.rename(columns=names).round(1)

The stock market
The same comparison of returns tells us what a share of stock is worth. Here we compare the model’s price-earnings ratio with more than a century of U.S. stock-market data.

Fig. 3: The price-earnings ratio in the stock market
Goal. Read the price-earnings ratio of the U.S. stock market with the arbitrage equation for stocks.
Robert Shiller’s price-earnings (P/E) ratio divides the S&P 500 stock price index by the average real earnings of its companies over the previous ten years. Equation (17.17) says what the ratio should be: the payout ratio divided by \(R-g\). The teal line in the figure is this model ratio. With the textbook’s numbers from the stock example, \(R = 5\) percent and \(g = 2\) percent, and a payout ratio of one half, the model ratio is \(0.5/0.03 \approx 16.7\), close to the long-run average.
This figure stays U.S.-only: Shiller’s monthly data are the only free, long series of a ten-year P/E ratio. Ratios for other stock markets are sold by commercial data providers and cannot be shared here.

Each row is a month. cape is the P/E ratio and cape_average its average over all months since 1881. parse_dates=["date"] turns the text in the date column into real dates.

Python note. px.area draws a line and fills the area below it. cape.iloc[-1] is the last row of the table. if R > g: runs the indented lines only when the condition holds; else: handles the other case. Here it protects us from dividing by zero, because equation (17.16) has no finite price when \(g \geq R\). "Model" if model < 48 else "Model ↑" is a one-line if: it gives the first text when the condition holds and the second one otherwise. min(model, 48) keeps the label inside the chart.


def pe_chart(R=0.05, g=0.02, payout=0.5):
    """Fig. 17.3: the P/E ratio, its average, and the model ratio payout / (R - g) of equation (17.17)."""
    last, average = cape.iloc[-1], cape.cape.mean()
    fig = px.area(cape, x="date", y="cape", color_discrete_sequence=["#5aa0d8"],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "cape": "P/E ratio"})
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[cape.date.iloc[0], last.date], y=[average, average], mode="lines",
                             name="Average", line=dict(color="black", width=1.5, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_annotation(x="1981-01-01", y=average + 7, text=f"Mean 1881–{last.date.year}: {average:.1f}", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14))
    model_text = "model: no finite price, because g ≥ R"
    if R > g:
        model = pe_ratio(payout, R, g)
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[cape.date.iloc[0], last.date], y=[model, model], mode="lines",
                                 name="Model, equation (17.17)", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
        model_text = f"model: {payout:.2f} / ({R:.1%} − {g:.2%}) = {model:.1f}"
        label = "Model" if model < 48 else "Model ↑"      # a model line above the chart is not visible: point up
        fig.add_annotation(x=last.date, y=min(model, 48), text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                           xshift=6, font=dict(color=TEAL, size=14))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"P/E ratio {last.cape:.1f} in {last.date:%b %Y}  |  {model_text}",
                      xaxis=dict(range=["1881-01-01", "2041-01-01"]),     # room for the label on the right
                      yaxis=dict(range=[0, 50], tickvals=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50]), showlegend=False)
    return fig

What to notice.

The ratio is very volatile. It peaked in September 1929, before the crash, and reached its record, 44.2, in December 1999 at the top of the dot-com boom (the textbook dates this peak “in 2001”; by 2001 the ratio had already fallen to between 28 and 37). It was below 7 in 1920 and in 1982.
In 2026 the ratio climbed back to about 40, close to the 1999 record.
With the slider, the model line rises slowly at first and then very fast: a P/E ratio of 40 needs \(R-g = 1.25\) percent, against 3 percent for 16.7. Small changes in expected growth or in the interest rate can justify big changes in stock prices. That is why it is hard to tell a bubble from a change in the fundamentals.

Key numbers: house prices and leverage
The arbitrage equation also prices a house. An investor can keep the down payment in the bank, or buy a condominium with a mortgage, rent it out for a year and sell it. Equating the two returns gives
\[p^{\text{house}} = \frac{\text{rent}}{\tau\bar{x}R + (1-\tau)R + \bar{d} - \Delta p^{\text{house}}/p^{\text{house}}} \qquad (17.20)\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the down payment as a share of the price and \(\tau\) the tax rate at which mortgage interest can be deducted. We use illustrative numbers: a rent of 6,000 dollars a year, \(R = 4\) percent, \(\bar{d} = 2\) percent, \(\tau = 0.3\) and expected price growth of 2 percent.

def house_price(rent, R, d, gp, tau, x):
    """Price of a house: rent / (tau x R + (1 - tau) R + d - gp)   (equation 17.20; gp is the expected price growth)."""
    return rent / (tau * x * R + (1 - tau) * R + d - gp)


base = house_price(6000, 0.04, 0.02, 0.02, 0.3, 0.2)
print(f"Baseline price (20% down payment, 2% price growth): {base:,.0f} dollars")
print(f"Down payment falls to 10%:          {house_price(6000, 0.04, 0.02, 0.02, 0.3, 0.1) / base - 1:+.1%}")
print(f"Expected price growth rises to 3%:  {house_price(6000, 0.04, 0.02, 0.03, 0.3, 0.2) / base - 1:+.1%}")

Down payment falls to 10%:          +4.1%

With these numbers, cheaper credit (a smaller down payment) raises the price by about 4 percent, but a belief that prices will grow 1 point faster raises it by about half. Expected capital gains can feed on themselves, which is how a housing bubble grows.

title: Chapter 17: Investment
text:
Concluding remarks

The arbitrage equation says that two equally safe investments must earn the same return. Applied to physical capital, it says that a firm keeps adding capital as long as its marginal product is above the user cost of capital, \(R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k\), and stops where the two are equal.
A corporate income tax divides the user cost by \(1-\tau\). With diminishing returns, a 35 percent tax cuts the desired capital stock by about half and the investment rate by 35 percent.
Applied to stocks, the same equation gives \(p_s = \text{dividend}/(R-g)\): a stock is worth the present value of its dividends. The P/E ratio then depends on \(R-g\), which makes it very sensitive to expected growth and hard to use for spotting bubbles.
In the data, total investment and especially housing and inventories fall sharply in recessions.
The next chapter turns to the government and the macroeconomy: how governments spend, tax and borrow, and what their budget constraint implies for debt and deficits.

title: Chapter 18: The Government and the Macroeconomy
text:
Model overview
Governments buy goods and services, pay transfers such as pensions, and pay interest on their debt. They finance all this with taxes and, when taxes fall short, by borrowing. This chapter has no new model to solve: it describes government budgets with data. Behind the data, though, there are a few accounting equations that hold in every year and every country. They link each year’s deficit to the change in the debt, and they tell us that what matters for a country’s ability to borrow is its debt relative to GDP, which depends on the interest rate and on how fast the economy grows.
Below we turn each of these equations into a small Python function, together with a few tools for the charts. The sections that follow use them to look at U.S. spending, revenue and debt, compare them with other countries, ask whether deficits crowd out private investment, and study the long-run projections that make health spending the fiscal problem of this century.

The flow budget constraint (equations 18.1 and 18.2)
In every period the government’s uses of funds must equal its sources of funds:
\[\underbrace{G_t + Tr_t + iB_t}_{\text{uses}} = \underbrace{T_t + \Delta B_{t+1} + \Delta M_{t+1}}_{\text{sources}}. \tag{18.1}\]
The government buys goods and services \(G_t\), pays transfers \(Tr_t\) (Social Security, unemployment insurance, welfare) and pays interest \(i\) on its debt \(B_t\). It gets the money from taxes \(T_t\), from new borrowing \(\Delta B_{t+1} = B_{t+1} - B_t\) and from printing money \(\Delta M_{t+1}\). As in the textbook, we set \(\Delta M_{t+1} = 0\) and count transfers inside \(G_t\). Then the constraint says how the debt moves:
\[B_{t+1} = (1+i)B_t + \underbrace{G_t - T_t}_{\text{primary deficit}}. \tag{18.2}\]
The primary deficit \(G_t - T_t\) leaves out the interest payments. The total deficit \(G_t + iB_t - T_t\) includes them, and it is the deficit that newspapers (and Table 18.1) report.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a one-line description. We write the interest rate as a decimal number, so 5 percent is 0.05.


def next_debt(B, G, T, i):
    """Equation (18.2): next period's debt, (1 + i) B + G - T."""
    return (1 + i) * B + G - T


def primary_deficit(G, T):
    """Primary deficit: spending minus taxes, leaving out the interest payments."""
    return G - T


def total_deficit(G, T, i, B):
    """Total deficit: spending plus the interest on the debt, minus taxes."""
    return G + i * B - T

A quick check: Exercise 5 of the textbook. A government owes 5 trillion dollars at an interest rate of 5 percent, and GDP (20 trillion dollars) grows by 4 percent a year. In case (a) it balances its primary budget (\(G = T\)). In case (b) it balances its total budget, so taxes also pay the interest.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each value in the list [1, 2, 3]. In each pass, B_a = next_debt(B_a, ...) replaces the old debt by the new one. An f-string such as f"{B_a:.3f}" puts a number into the text, here with 3 decimals.


i, g = 0.05, 0.04                      # interest rate and GDP growth rate
B_a, B_b, Y = 5.0, 5.0, 20.0           # debt in cases (a) and (b), and GDP, trillions of dollars
for year in [1, 2, 3]:
    T_b = 4.0 + i * B_b                # case (b): taxes cover spending of 4.0 and the interest
    print(f"Year {year}: (a) primary deficit {primary_deficit(4.0, 4.0):.2f}, total {total_deficit(4.0, 4.0, i, B_a):.3f}"
          f"   (b) primary deficit {primary_deficit(4.0, T_b):.2f}, total {total_deficit(4.0, T_b, i, B_b):.2f}")
    B_a = next_debt(B_a, G=4.0, T=4.0, i=i)
    B_b = next_debt(B_b, G=4.0, T=T_b, i=i)
    Y = (1 + g) * Y
    print(f"   debt (a) {B_a:.3f} = {100 * B_a / Y:.2f}% of GDP,  debt (b) {B_b:.3f} = {100 * B_b / Y:.2f}% of GDP")

Year 1: (a) primary deficit 0.00, total 0.250   (b) primary deficit -0.25, total 0.00
   debt (a) 5.250 = 25.24% of GDP,  debt (b) 5.000 = 24.04% of GDP
Year 2: (a) primary deficit 0.00, total 0.263   (b) primary deficit -0.25, total 0.00
   debt (a) 5.512 = 25.48% of GDP,  debt (b) 5.000 = 23.11% of GDP
Year 3: (a) primary deficit 0.00, total 0.276   (b) primary deficit -0.25, total 0.00
   debt (a) 5.788 = 25.73% of GDP,  debt (b) 5.000 = 22.22% of GDP


In case (a) the total deficit is the interest bill, so the debt grows at the interest rate, 5 percent a year. In case (b) the primary surplus of 0.25 trillion pays the interest, and the debt stays at 5 trillion. With a balanced primary budget the debt-GDP ratio rises from 25 percent by about 1 percent a year: 5 percent minus 4 percent. With a balanced total budget the ratio falls by about 4 percent a year, as GDP grows.


The intertemporal budget constraint (equations 18.5 and 18.6)
In a world that lasts two periods, all debt must be repaid by the end: \(B_3 = 0\). Combining the flow constraints of the two periods gives the intertemporal budget constraint:
\[\underbrace{G_1 + \frac{G_2}{1+i}}_{\text{pdv of spending}} + \underbrace{(1+i)B_1}_{\text{initial debt}} = \underbrace{T_1 + \frac{T_2}{1+i}}_{\text{pdv of taxes}}. \tag{18.5}\]
A future amount is worth less today, so we divide it by \(1+i\): that is its present discounted value (pdv). Moving the taxes to the left gives equation (18.6): the pdv of the budget balances \(T - G\) must pay off the initial debt \((1+i)B_1\). The budget must balance, not period by period, but in present value.
Here is a two-period example with the textbook’s initial debt of 25 trillion dollars. The government spends 7 trillion in each period, collects 5 trillion of taxes in period 1, and must find the taxes of period 2.

def pdv(first, second, i):
    """Present discounted value of an amount in period 1 and one in period 2 (equation 18.5)."""
    return first + second / (1 + i)


B1, i = 25.0, 0.05                     # initial debt (trillions of dollars) and interest rate
G1, G2, T1 = 7.0, 7.0, 5.0
B2 = next_debt(B1, G1, T1, i)          # equation (18.3): the debt at the start of period 2
T2 = (1 + i) * B2 + G2                 # equation (18.4) with B3 = 0: period-2 taxes repay everything
print(f"B2 = {B2:.2f}, so the period-2 taxes must be T2 = {T2:.2f} trillion dollars")
print(f"Uses:    pdv of spending {pdv(G1, G2, i):.3f} + initial debt {(1 + i) * B1:.3f} = "
      f"{pdv(G1, G2, i) + (1 + i) * B1:.3f}")
print(f"Sources: pdv of taxes {pdv(T1, T2, i):.3f}")
print(f"Equation (18.6): pdv of the budget balances {pdv(T1 - G1, T2 - G2, i):.3f} = (1 + i) B1")

B2 = 28.25, so the period-2 taxes must be T2 = 36.66 trillion dollars
Uses:    pdv of spending 13.667 + initial debt 26.250 = 39.917
Sources: pdv of taxes 39.917
Equation (18.6): pdv of the budget balances 26.250 = (1 + i) B1


The deficit of 2 trillion in period 1 and the inherited debt must both be paid with a large surplus in period 2: taxes of 36.66 trillion against spending of 7. Borrowing today means higher taxes in the future.


The debt-GDP ratio
What matters for a country’s ability to pay is not the debt in dollars but the debt relative to GDP, the tax base. Let nominal GDP grow at the rate \(g\), and write \(b = B/Y\) for the debt-GDP ratio and \(d\) for the primary deficit as a share of GDP. Dividing equation (18.2) by GDP gives
\[b_{\text{next}} = \frac{1+i}{1+g}\, b + d \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b_{\text{next}} - b \approx d + (i - g)\, b.\]
The ratio rises with the primary deficit \(d\). It also rises when the interest rate is above the growth rate, and it falls when GDP grows faster than the interest rate, even with a balanced primary budget.

Python note. path = [] starts an empty list, and path.append(b) adds one value at its end. For a pandas Series with years as row labels, deficit.loc[1951:1974] keeps the years 1951 to 1974 (both included), and .sum() adds them up.


def next_debt_ratio(b, i, g, d):
    """Equation (18.2) divided by GDP: next year's debt ratio, (1 + i) / (1 + g) b + d."""
    return (1 + i) / (1 + g) * b + d


def debt_ratio_path(b, i, g, deficits):
    """The debt ratio after each year of a list of primary deficits (all in percent of GDP)."""
    path = []
    for d in deficits:
        b = next_debt_ratio(b, i, g, d)
        path.append(b)
    return path


def debt_change_parts(debt, deficit, start, end):
    """Split the change in the debt ratio from start to end into primary deficits and the rest."""
    change = debt[end] - debt[start]
    from_deficits = deficit.loc[start + 1:end].sum()
    return change, from_deficits, change - from_deficits

The ratio tool repeats case (a) of Exercise 5 without computing the debt and GDP separately:

case_a = debt_ratio_path(25.0, 0.05, 0.04, [0, 0, 0])      # a balanced primary budget for three years
print("Debt ratio, case (a):", np.round(case_a, 2))
print(f"Growth of the ratio: {100 * (case_a[0] / 25.0 - 1):.2f}% a year = 1.05 / 1.04 - 1")

Debt ratio, case (a): [25.24 25.48 25.73]
Growth of the ratio: 0.96% a year = 1.05 / 1.04 - 1


The part of a change that is not explained by primary deficits, change - from_deficits, is the effect of interest minus growth, \((i-g)\,b\), summed over the years. We use it on the U.S. data in Fig. 2.


Saving and investment (equation 18.7)
Adding and subtracting taxes in the national income identity splits total saving into three parts:
\[\underbrace{(Y - T - C)}_{\text{private saving}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}} + \underbrace{(IM - EX)}_{\text{foreign saving}} = I. \tag{18.7}\]
Investment is financed by households and firms, by the government and by foreigners. A budget deficit is negative government saving, so private or foreign saving must fill the gap, or investment falls. That fall is called crowding out.

def private_and_foreign_saving(investment, government_saving):
    """Equation (18.7) solved for the saving of households, firms and foreigners: I - (T - G)."""
    return investment - government_saving



Tools for the data
Four small tools help with the figures. period_mean averages a series over some years, and add_period_means draws those averages on a chart. per_person turns a share of GDP into dollars per person. actual_and_projection and one_legend_entry prepare the long-run projections of Figs. 6 and 7, where actual data (solid lines) are followed by projections (dashed lines).

Python note. zip(columns, colors) hands over one (column, color) pair at a time to the loop. fig.add_vrect shades a band between two x values, and fig.add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a straight line between two points.


def period_mean(series, start, end):
    """Average of a Series with years as row labels, from start to end (both included)."""
    return series.loc[start:end].mean()


def add_period_means(fig, data, columns, colors, start, end):
    """Shade the years start-end and draw each column's average over them (Figs. 1 and 5)."""
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start - 0.5, x1=end + 0.5, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    for column, color in zip(columns, colors):
        mean = period_mean(data[column], start, end)
        fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=start - 0.5, x1=end + 0.5, y0=mean, y1=mean,
                      line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash="dot"))
    return fig


def per_person(percent_of_gdp, gdp_billions, population_millions):
    """Dollars per person of a budget line given in percent of GDP (Table 18.1)."""
    return percent_of_gdp / 100 * gdp_billions * 1e9 / (population_millions * 1e6)


Python note. melt turns a wide table (one column per series) into a long one (one row per year and series), which is the shape Plotly Express likes. .map({0: ..., 1: ...}) replaces each value by its label, .copy() makes an independent copy, and pd.concat([a, b]) stacks two tables. trace.name.rsplit(", ", 1) cuts a text such as "Revenues, actual" at its last comma, into its two parts.


def actual_and_projection(data, names):
    """Long table for Figs. 6 and 7: one row per year and series, actual data and CBO projection.

    FY2025 is repeated in the projection, so that the dashed line starts where the solid line ends."""
    long = data.rename(columns=names).melt(id_vars=["year", "projection"], value_vars=list(names.values()),
                                           var_name="series", value_name="percent")
    long["segment"] = long.projection.map({0: "actual", 1: "CBO projection"})
    joint = long[long.year == 2025].copy()
    joint["segment"] = "CBO projection"
    return pd.concat([long, joint]).sort_values(["series", "segment", "year"])


def one_legend_entry(fig):
    """Plotly Express names each trace 'series, segment': keep one legend entry per series."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        series, segment = trace.name.rsplit(", ", 1)
        trace.update(name=series, legendgroup=series, showlegend=(segment == "actual"))
    return fig

Goal. See how large the federal government is, relative to the economy, and how its spending and revenue have changed since the 1930s.
The data are the federal outlays (spending) and receipts (revenue) as a percentage of GDP, from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). They are measured in fiscal years: the U.S. federal fiscal year 2025, for example, ran from October 2024 to September 2025.

spending_gdp_pct and revenue_gdp_pct are percentages of GDP, from FY1934 to FY2025. The menu draws the averages over one period as dotted lines. The textbook’s dashed lines at 18 and 20 percent stay on the chart.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names, which then appear in the legend, and set_index("year") makes the years the row labels, as period_mean needs. PERIODS is a dictionary: each name (the key) gives a pair of years (the value), and start, end = PERIODS[period] unpacks the pair. fig.add_hline draws a horizontal line across the chart.


named = revenue_spending.rename(columns={"spending_gdp_pct": "Spending", "revenue_gdp_pct": "Revenue"})
by_year = named.set_index("year")
PERIODS = {"FY1934–1939": (1934, 1939), "FY1950–1969": (1950, 1969), "FY1970–1997": (1970, 1997),
           "FY1998–2001": (1998, 2001), "FY2002–2025": (2002, 2025), "FY1975–2024": (1975, 2024)}


def budget_chart(period="FY1950–1969"):
    """Fig. 18.1: federal spending and revenue (% of GDP), with their averages over one period."""
    start, end = PERIODS[period]
    spending, revenue = period_mean(by_year.Spending, start, end), period_mean(by_year.Revenue, start, end)
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Spending", "Revenue"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Fiscal year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{period}: spending averaged {spending:.1f}% and revenue {revenue:.1f}% of GDP")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    for level in [18, 20]:                       # the textbook's dashed reference lines
        fig.add_hline(y=level, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))
    add_period_means(fig, by_year, ["Spending", "Revenue"], [BLUE, GREEN], start, end)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1930, 2028])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 46], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig

What to notice.

In the 1930s the federal government was small: revenue averaged 5.9 percent of GDP. World War II changed that. Spending peaked at 42.7 percent of GDP in FY1944, almost all of it for national defense.
In the two decades after the war, spending and revenue were both close to 17–18 percent of GDP, and the budget was roughly balanced (choose FY1950–1969).
From 1970 spending stayed above revenue in almost every year. FY1998–2001 were the exceptions, the only surpluses since 1969. Spending jumped in the Great Recession (FY2009) and in the Covid-19 pandemic (FY2020).
The textbook’s figure note says both averaged “about 20 percent” in recent decades. Choose FY1975–2024: spending averaged 21.1 percent, but revenue only 17.3 percent. That gap is the deficit of Fig. 2.


Key numbers: the war, the 1930s and the 20 percent ceiling

print(f"Average revenue, FY1934-1939: {period_mean(by_year.Revenue, 1934, 1939):.1f}% of GDP")

print(f"FY2025: spending {by_year.Spending[2025]:.1f}%, revenue {by_year.Revenue[2025]:.1f}% of GDP")

Revenue in FY1944: 20.5% of GDP
Average revenue, FY1934-1939: 5.9% of GDP

FY2025: spending 23.1%, revenue 17.3% of GDP


The textbook says spending peaked “at just under 44 percent” and revenue reached “nearly 21 percent” in 1944. Today’s OMB tables give 42.7 and 20.5 percent: GDP of the 1940s has since been revised up, so the shares are a little smaller. Revenue reached 20 percent of GDP only twice, in FY1944 and FY2000. This is the textbook’s “taxes have remained at or below 20 percent of GDP during virtually the entire history of the United States”.


Beyond the United States: government budgets in 38 countries
The federal budget is not the whole government: U.S. states and cities spend and tax, too. To compare countries we need general government, all levels together, which the OECD measures in the same way for every country. FINANCE_COUNTRIES = sorted(finance.dropna(subset=["revenue"]).country.unique())


def budget_by_country(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 18.1 for any country: general government spending and revenue (% of GDP, OECD)."""
    rows = finance[finance.country == country].dropna(subset=["revenue", "spending"])
    rows = rows.rename(columns={"spending": "Spending", "revenue": "Revenue"})
    title = f"{country}: no OECD data on government revenue and spending"

                 f"revenue {rows.Revenue.mean():.1f}% of GDP")
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y=["Spending", "Revenue"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1958, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 70], tickvals=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.99, y=1.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"),

# @title Helper for the website versions with a country menu (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, options, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(option) for every option and join the results with a dropdown menu.

    The website cannot run Python, so a figure with a country menu gets this precomputed version."""
    figures = [make_figure(o) for o in options]
    first = options.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range,
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(options[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", active=first, buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")],
                      margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

What to notice.

The U.S. general government, federal plus state and local, spent 39.6 percent of GDP in 2024 and collected 31.5 percent: 16 and 15 points more than the federal budget alone (23.3 and 17.0 percent in FY2024). Fig. 3 compares countries with this general-government measure.

def budget_table(year, release="actual (FY2027 Budget)"):
    """Table 18.1 for one fiscal year: each line in percent of GDP and in dollars per person."""
    row = budget[(budget.year == year) & (budget.release == release)].iloc[0]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Percent of GDP": row[list(LINES)].astype(float)})
    table["Dollars per person"] = per_person(table["Percent of GDP"], row.gdp_billions,
                                             row.population_millions).round(-2)
    return table.rename(index=LINES)

What to notice.

To pay for World War II the government ran deficits of up to 29.6 percent of GDP (FY1943), and the debt rose to 106.1 percent of GDP in FY1946: more than one year of the economy’s whole output.
Over the next 30 years the ratio fell to 23.2 percent (FY1974). The budget was close to balance in most of those years, so the deficits do not explain this decline. Economic growth does, as the key numbers below show.
The deficits from the late 1970s raised the ratio to 47.9 percent by FY1993. The surpluses of FY1998–2001 lowered it to 31.5 percent. Then the Great Recession (a deficit of 9.8 percent of GDP in FY2009) and the pandemic (14.5 percent in FY2020) raised it to 98.5 percent, and it reached 99.5 percent in FY2025.


Key numbers: primary deficits and growth
How did the United States pay off its war debt? Fig. 6’s file has federal revenue and spending excluding interest from FY1950, so their difference is the primary balance. The total balance of Fig. 2 minus the primary balance is the interest paid. We first combine the two files.

Python note. merge(..., on="year") joins two tables row by row, matching the years. Rows whose year is missing in one of the tables are dropped, so the result starts in FY1950.

From FY1950 to FY1974 the debt ratio fell by 55.4 points. Primary surpluses paid for only 14.1 points of that. The other 41.3 points came from the term \((i-g)\,b\): nominal GDP grew faster than the interest rate on the debt, so the debt shrank relative to the economy. With many countries on one chart, each country needs its own color, and it should keep that color when we add or remove other countries. Two small tools do this for the multi-country charts of this notebook (Figs. 2, 4 and 8).

Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 is a list of 24 colors, and + joins two lists. enumerate numbers the items of a list as the loop runs (0, 1, 2, …), and i % len(PALETTE) is the remainder of the division, which starts again at 0 when the colors run out. colors.update(fixed) overwrites some entries of the dictionary. In latest_text, .groupby("country").tail(1) keeps the last row of each country, .iloc[[0, -1]] keeps the first and the last row of a table, and for i, (_, row) in enumerate(...) numbers the rows that .iterrows() hands over one at a time.


PALETTE = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Light24     # 48 distinct colors


def country_colors(names, fixed):
    """One fixed color per country, so that a country keeps its color when the selection changes."""
    colors = {}
    for i, name in enumerate(sorted(names)):
        colors[name] = PALETTE[i % len(PALETTE)]
    colors.update(fixed)                        # the textbook's countries keep the colors of the book
    return colors


def latest_text(data, column, time):
    """The latest value of each chosen country, highest first; only the maximum and minimum for 3 or more."""
    if len(data) == 0:
        return "choose at least one country"
    last = data.sort_values(time).groupby("country").tail(1).sort_values(column, ascending=False)
    words = ["", ""]
    if len(last) > 2:
        last, words = last.iloc[[0, -1]], ["max ", "min "]
    parts = []
    for i, (_, row) in enumerate(last.iterrows()):
        parts.append(f"{words[i]}{row.country} {row[column]:.1f}")
    return "latest: " + ", ".join(parts)

The axes have two fixed sizes each: up to 150 percent of GDP, or up to 300 percent when a country above 150 percent is chosen; from 1900, or from 1800 when a chosen country’s data start earlier. list(range(50, top + 1, 50)) is the list of tick values 50, 100, … up to top.

GROSS_COLORS = country_colors(gross.country.unique(), {"United States": BLUE})


def gross_debt_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 18.2 for any countries: general government gross debt, percent of GDP (IMF)."""
    chosen = gross[gross.country.isin(countries)]
    top, start = 150, 1900
    if chosen.gross_debt.max() > 150:
        top = 300                               # a second, fixed scale for the most indebted countries
    if chosen.year.min() < 1900:
        start = 1800                            # some series start in the 19th century
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gross_debt", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=GROSS_COLORS, range_x=[start, 2027], range_y=[0, top],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gross_debt": "Percentage of GDP", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Gross debt, % of GDP, " + latest_text(chosen, "gross_debt", "year"))
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=list(range(50, top + 1, 50)))      # no 0 next to the first year
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

# @title Helper for the multi-country website figures (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
G7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]


def legend_menu(fig, data, shown):
    """Website version of a multi-country chart: the countries in `shown` are drawn, every other country is
    one click away in the legend, and buttons show a group (the textbook's countries, the G7, a region, all).
    Traces that are not countries, such as averages, always stay visible."""
    countries = set(data.country)
    groups = {"Textbook": list(shown), "G7": G7}
    for region in sorted(data.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = list(data[data.region == region].country.unique())
    groups["All"] = list(countries)
    for trace in fig.data:
        if trace.name in countries and trace.name not in shown:
            trace.visible = "legendonly"
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            visible.append(True if trace.name not in countries or trace.name in members else "legendonly")
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", pad=dict(r=4, t=0))],
                      margin=dict(t=120))
    return fig

def crowding_out_chart(country="United States"):

What the projection means for the debt
The projected primary deficits are not zero, so the debt keeps growing. How fast the ratio grows depends on the interest rate \(i\) and on the growth rate of nominal GDP \(g\), through debt_ratio_path. The sliders also let you cut the primary deficit in every year from FY2026, by raising taxes or cutting spending: the two “possible solutions” of the textbook.

Python note. max(path) and min(path) are the largest and smallest values of a list, and max(250, ...) is the larger of two numbers: the vertical axis stays at 0 to 250 unless the debt ratio would leave it. [50, 100, 150, 200, 250] if top == 250 else None is a one-line if: it gives the list of ticks when the axis has its usual size, and None (let Plotly choose) when it has grown.


cbo = projections[projections.projection == 1]
cbo_deficits = (cbo.spending_ex_interest - cbo.revenue).tolist()     # projected primary deficits, FY2026-2056
b_2025 = debt_by_year[2025]
debt_history = debt_deficit[debt_deficit.year >= 1940]


def debt_projection(i=4.0, g=4.0, cut=0.0):
    """The debt ratio after FY2025 under CBO's primary deficits minus a cut (all in percent of GDP)."""
    deficits = []
    for d in cbo_deficits:
        deficits.append(d - cut)
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, g / 100, deficits)
    top = max(250, 1.05 * max(path))                 # fixed axis, widened only when the debt ratio would leave it
    bottom = min(0, 1.1 * min(path))                 # below zero, the government owns more than it owes
    fig = px.line(debt_history, x="year", y="debt_public_gdp_pct", range_y=[bottom, top],
                  labels={"year": "Fiscal year", "debt_public_gdp_pct": "Debt held by the public (% of GDP)"},
                  title=f"Debt in FY2056: {path[-1]:.1f}% of GDP (FY2025: {b_2025:.1f}%), "
                        f"average primary deficit {np.mean(deficits):.2f}%")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cbo.year, y=path, name="Projection", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3, dash="dash"),
                             showlegend=False))
    fig.add_hline(y=b_2025, line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=2025, x1=2056, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1938, 2058])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[50, 100, 150, 200, 250] if top == 250 else None)
    return fig

title: Chapter 18: The Government and the Macroeconomy
text:
Concluding remarks

The U.S. federal government spends about 23 percent of GDP and collects about 17 percent. The deficit, about 6 percent of GDP in recent years, is financed by selling bonds, and the debt held by the public is back near 100 percent of GDP, the level of 1946.
The flow budget constraint links each year’s deficit to the change in the debt. The intertemporal budget constraint says that the budget must balance in present value: borrowing today means surpluses, and higher taxes, later.
What matters is the debt relative to GDP. When GDP grows faster than the interest rate, the ratio falls even without surpluses: that is how the United States paid down its World War II debt.
U.S. government spending is low compared with other rich countries, and its debt ratio is typical. Large deficits have not lowered the U.S. investment rate, because private and foreign saving rose.
The fiscal problem of the twenty-first century is the rise of health spending, in the U.S. and in every rich country. Chapter 19 turns to the international economy, including the foreign saving that has financed much of the U.S. deficit.

Text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it, and it is there for human readers. The try ... except block runs one Colab-only line and simply skips it anywhere else.


# Libraries used in this chapter
import numpy as np                    # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


Every figure of this chapter can also show other countries. On the website, the many-country versions get a menu, built by two more helpers.

def country_groups(regions, book):
    """Menu groups: the textbook's countries, the G7, large emerging economies, then the World Bank regions."""
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Large emerging": EMERGING}
    for region in sorted(regions.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = list(regions[regions.region == region].country)
    return groups


def group_menu(fig, groups, start, title):
    """Show one group of countries at a time. A trace belongs to the country named before ', ' in its legendgroup.
    Each group gets a y range that covers its values; in groups of more than 15 countries it leaves out extreme
    outliers (double-click the chart to show them)."""
    owners = [t.legendgroup.split(", ")[0] for t in fig.data]
    buttons = []
    for name, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in members for o in owners]
        ys = np.concatenate([np.asarray(t.y, dtype=float) for t, v in zip(fig.data, visible) if v] or [np.zeros(1)])
        ys = ys[np.isfinite(ys)] if np.isfinite(ys).any() else np.zeros(1)
        lo, hi = ys.min(), ys.max()
        if len(set(o for o, v in zip(owners, visible) if v)) > 15:     # large groups: leave out extreme outliers
            q5, q95 = np.percentile(ys, [5, 95])
            lo, hi = max(lo, q5 - 0.3 * (q95 - q5)), min(hi, q95 + 0.3 * (q95 - q5))
        pad = 0.06 * (hi - lo) + 0.5
        buttons.append(dict(label=name, method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": visible}, {"yaxis.range": [lo - pad, hi + pad], "yaxis.autorange": False}]))
    first = list(groups).index(start)
    for t, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[first]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        t.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis_range=buttons[first]["args"][1]["yaxis.range"], yaxis_tickvals=None,
                      margin=dict(t=115), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down",
                                                             x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig

        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "yaxis.autorange": rng is None,
                  "yaxis.range": list(rng) if rng is not None else None}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=115), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start),

title: Chapter 19: International Trade
text:
Model overview
This chapter has no single model to solve. Instead, it rests on a few rules of national income accounting that always hold: what a country produces is either used at home or sold abroad on net, and a country that buys more from the world than it sells must borrow the difference. Written as equations, these rules link exports, imports, saving, investment and the foreign debt, and they turn every trade chart below into a statement about borrowing and lending.
We write these rules once, as small Python functions, and reuse them for every figure. We also use them to work through the textbook’s small trade examples: two islands that trade across time, a North and a South that trade apples for computers, and what happens when workers can move instead of goods. These examples explain why countries trade and who gains; the data sections that follow show how much they trade and what the deficits add up to.
We start with two definitions, then turn each accounting rule into a function. The examples follow as subsections (Tables 19.1 to 19.5).
The trade balance. Exports \(EX\) are goods and services that a country sells abroad, and imports \(IM\) are those it buys abroad. The trade balance, or net exports, is the difference, \(NX \equiv EX - IM\). A positive \(NX\) is a trade surplus, a negative one a trade deficit. The charts always show such flows as a share of GDP, \(100 \times X / Y\), so that years and countries of different size can be compared.
The national income identity. Everything an economy produces, \(Y\), is consumed (\(C\)), invested (\(I\)), bought by the government (\(G\)) or sold abroad on net (\(NX\)): \(Y = C + I + G + NX\). Solved for net exports,
\[NX = Y - (C + I + G), \qquad\text{so}\qquad NX < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; C + I + G > Y \quad (19.1)\]
and \(NX > 0 \Rightarrow C + I + G < Y\) (19.2). A country with a trade deficit uses more goods than it produces; the rest comes from abroad, on credit.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description. The same function works for single numbers and for whole columns of a data table, because pandas does arithmetic on every row at once.


def share_of_gdp(x, gdp):
    """Any variable as a percent of GDP: 100 x / Y."""
    return 100 * x / gdp


def net_exports(exports, imports):
    """The trade balance (net exports): NX = EX - IM."""
    return exports - imports


def net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G):
    """The national income identity Y = C + I + G + NX solved for NX (equations 19.1 and 19.2)."""
    return Y - (C + I + G)

A quick check with round numbers: an economy produces 100, consumes 70, invests 20 and its government buys 15.

Y, C, I, G = 100, 70, 20, 15
NX = net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G)
print(f"NX = {Y} - ({C} + {I} + {G}) = {NX}, or {share_of_gdp(NX, Y):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"Domestic uses C + I + G = {C + I + G} > Y = {Y}: the country runs a trade deficit")

NX = 100 - (70 + 20 + 15) = -5, or -5% of GDP
Domestic uses C + I + G = 105 > Y = 100: the country runs a trade deficit



Trade balances from GDP shares
The Penn World Table, the source of Figs. 3 and 4, does not report net exports directly. It reports the shares of GDP that go to consumption, investment and government purchases: \(c = C/Y\), \(i = I/Y\) and \(g = G/Y\). Dividing the identity by \(Y\) gives the trade balance as a share of GDP, \(NX/Y = 1 - c - i - g\). In code, this is the same identity with \(Y = 1\):

def trade_balance_share(c, i, g):
    """NX as a percent of GDP from the GDP shares of C, I and G: 100 (1 - c - i - g)."""
    return 100 * net_exports_from_uses(1, c, i, g)


def share_of_us_gdp(share, gdp, gdp_us):
    """Rescale a share of a country's own GDP to a share of U.S. GDP (Fig. 19.3, second bar)."""
    return share * gdp / gdp_us


print(f"c = 0.55, i = 0.25, g = 0.18: trade balance {trade_balance_share(0.55, 0.25, 0.18):.1f}% of GDP")

c = 0.55, i = 0.25, g = 0.18: trade balance 2.0% of GDP




Saving, investment and the trade balance (equation 19.6)
Total saving pays for investment. Saving comes from three sources: households, \(Y - T - C\); the government, \(T - G\); and foreigners, \(IM - EX\), the goods they send us on credit. Domestic saving is \(S \equiv (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = Y - C - G\). Put into the identity, \(Y - C - G = I + NX\), that is
\[\underbrace{NX}_{\text{trade balance}} = \underbrace{S - I}_{\text{net capital outflow}}. \quad (19.6)\]
A country that invests more than it saves (\(S < I\)) must borrow the difference abroad, and it does so by running a trade deficit. Two more functions measure the data over time: an average over a window of years and the sum of past flows, which turns yearly trade balances into a stock of foreign assets or debt.

Python note. For a table whose rows are years, data.loc[start:end] keeps the rows from start to end, both included, and .mean() averages them (one average per column). .cumsum() is the cumulative sum: row by row, the sum of all values so far.


def domestic_saving(I, NX):
    """Domestic saving S = Y - C - G, from equation (19.6): S = I + NX."""
    return I + NX


def net_capital_outflow(S, I):
    """Equation (19.6): the trade balance equals domestic saving minus investment, NX = S - I."""
    return S - I


def period_average(data, start, end):
    """Simple average over the years start to end (rows are years): one number per column."""
    return data.loc[start:end].mean()


def accumulate(start_value, flows):
    """Net foreign assets: start from start_value and add each year's trade balance."""
    return start_value + flows.cumsum()


S = Y - C - G                                   # the economy of the quick check above
print(f"S = {S}, I = {I}: S - I = {net_capital_outflow(S, I)}, the same as NX = {NX}")
print(f"... and back again: S = I + NX = {domestic_saving(I, NX)}")

S = 15, I = 20: S - I = -5, the same as NX = -5
... and back again: S = I + NX = 15




Trade across time (Table 19.1)
Two islands grow wheat, which cannot be stored. Oddtopia has a harvest of 100 bushels in odd years and nothing in even years; Eventopia has the opposite luck. Each island lends half of a good harvest to the other and is repaid the next year, so both eat 50 bushels every year. With no investment and no government, \(NX = Y - C\): the harvest minus what is eaten. The sum of past trade balances is what the other island owes.

Python note. pd.DataFrame({...}) builds a table from a dictionary of columns. The for loop repeats the indented lines for each island, and island + " harvest" glues two pieces of text into a column name. .T turns the table on its side, so that the years become columns, as in the textbook.

Eventopia: average trade balance 0, consumption always 50


Each island runs a deficit in its bad years and a surplus in its good years, and both smooth their consumption perfectly: this is risk sharing. The average trade balance is zero: in the long run, trade must be balanced, because nobody lends without being repaid. A deficit today is a promise of a surplus later.


Comparative advantage: the North and the South (Tables 19.2 to 19.5)
Two countries consume two goods, apples and computers, and spend half of their income on each. Labor is the only input (Table 19.2). Prices are quoted in apples, so an apple costs 1, a computer costs \(p\) apples, and the wage \(w\) is in apples too. With half of income spent on each good, a worker eats \(w/2\) apples (19.3) and buys \(w/(2p)\) computers (19.4).

x_n, z_n, L_n = 160, 16, 100        # North: apples or computers per worker, number of workers (Table 19.2)
x_s, z_s, L_s = 100, 2, 400         # South
print(f"North / South productivity: apples {x_n / x_s:.1f} times, computers {z_n / z_s:.0f} times")

North / South productivity: apples 1.6 times, computers 8 times


The North is better at both goods: it has an absolute advantage in both. But its lead is much larger in computers (8 times) than in apples (1.6 times), so it has a comparative advantage in computers, and the South in apples.
Autarky (no trade). A worker can make \(x\) apples or \(z\) computers, so the wage is \(w = x\) apples, and both sectors pay the same only if a computer costs \(p = x/z\) apples. Half of the workers make each good.

Python note. pd.Series({...}) builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary. pd.DataFrame then puts two such lists side by side as the columns “North” and “South”. pd.concat([...], axis=1, keys=[...]) places two tables next to each other under two headings.


def autarky(x, z, L):
    """Table 19.3: a closed economy whose L workers each make x apples or z computers."""
    w = x                        # the wage in apples: what a worker makes in the apple sector
    p = x / z                    # the price of a computer: both sectors must pay the same wage
    return pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w,
                      "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                      "Apples per person": w / 2,              # equation (19.3), an apple costs 1
                      "Computers per person": w / 2 / p,       # equation (19.4)
                      "Workers making apples (%)": 50,
                      "Workers making computers (%)": 50,
                      "Apples produced": L / 2 * x,
                      "Computers produced": L / 2 * z})


table_19_3 = pd.DataFrame({"North": autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n), "South": autarky(x_s, z_s, L_s)})
book_19_3 = pd.DataFrame({"North": [160, 10, 80, 8, 50, 50, 8000, 800],
                          "South": [100, 50, 50, 1, 50, 50, 20000, 400]}, index=table_19_3.index)

Free trade. Computers cost 10 apples in the North and 50 in the South, so it pays to buy computers in the North and sell them in the South (arbitrage). Each country then makes only the good it is relatively good at: the North makes only computers and the South only apples. World spending on computers equals world spending on apples (each is half of world income), so \(p \times \text{computers} = \text{apples}\), and the world price is \(p = \text{apples} / \text{computers}\).

def free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s):
    """Table 19.4: the North makes only computers, the South only apples, and they trade."""
    computers = L_n * z_n                      # world production of computers
    apples = L_s * x_s                         # world production of apples
    p = apples / computers                     # half of world spending goes to each good
    w_n, w_s = z_n * p, x_s                    # wages in apples
    north = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_n, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_n / 2, "Computers per person": w_n / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 0, "Workers making computers (%)": 100,
                       "Apples produced": 0, "Computers produced": computers})
    south = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_s, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_s / 2, "Computers per person": w_s / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 100, "Workers making computers (%)": 0,
                       "Apples produced": apples, "Computers produced": 0})
    return pd.DataFrame({"North": north, "South": south})

Some basic facts about trade
We begin with the U.S. numbers: how much the country sells abroad and buys from abroad, and how the gap between the two has grown since the 1970s. Then we put the United States next to the rest of the world.

Fig. 1: U.S. import and export shares of GDP
Goal. See how much more the United States trades today than 75 years ago.
The file us_trade.csv holds the U.S. national accounts we need, in billions of current dollars: GDP, exports, imports, net exports, private investment and the net international investment position (Fig. 6), plus the same position as it was published in July 2023.

Python note. set_index("year") makes the years the row labels, so that us.loc[2006] is the row of 2006 and us.exports is one column, a Series with years as labels. NaN (“not a number”) marks a missing value: the investment position starts only in 1976.
