Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: Exports of goods and services (EXPGSA), Imports of goods and services (IMPGSA) and Gross domestic product (GDPA). Prepared file: data/ch19/us_trade.csv, checked against data/ch19/fig19-1.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

In the 1950s exports and imports were each only about 4 to 5 percent of GDP. Since then exports have more than doubled and imports more than tripled.
The two lines move together until the early 1970s, and then they separate: imports have been above exports every year since 1976. The gap between them is the trade deficit of Fig. 2.
Trade falls sharply in world recessions (2009, 2020) and in the strong-dollar years of the mid-1980s, when U.S. exports dropped to 7 percent of GDP.


Key numbers: how much does the United States trade?
The textbook says that exports and imports rose “from under 5 percent of GDP in the 1950s to around 12 and 15 percent of GDP, respectively, in recent years” (Jones 2024).

Python note. ~ means “not”: ~above is True in the years when imports were not above exports. .idxmax() gives the label (here the year) of the largest value.


fifties = shares.loc[1950:1959]
print(f"1950s: highest export share {fifties.Exports.max():.2f}% ({fifties.Exports.idxmax()}), "
      f"highest import share {fifties.Imports.max():.2f}%")
print(f"2022, the textbook's last year: exports {shares.Exports[2022]:.2f}%, imports {shares.Imports[2022]:.2f}%")
above = shares.Imports > shares.Exports
print(f"Imports have been above exports every year since {above[~above].index.max() + 1}")
openness = shares.Exports + shares.Imports
print(f"Exports + imports: {openness[1950]:.1f}% of GDP in 1950, {openness.max():.1f}% at the peak "
      f"({openness.idxmax()}), {openness[last]:.1f}% in {last}")

1950s: highest export share 5.07% (1957), highest import share 4.28%
2022, the textbook's last year: exports 11.65%, imports 15.18%
Imports have been above exports every year since 1976
Exports + imports: 8.0% of GDP in 1950, 30.8% at the peak (2011), 24.6% in 2025


The textbook’s “respectively” lists the two numbers the wrong way round: exports are about 12 percent of GDP (11.65 in 2022) and imports about 15 percent (15.18). And “under 5 percent” holds only after rounding: exports reached 5.07 percent in 1957. Exports and imports together, a common measure of how open an economy is, went from 8 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 30.8 percent in 2011.


Beyond the United States: how open is each economy?
The textbook shows only the United States. The World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI) publish the same two shares, exports and imports of goods and services as a percent of GDP (series NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS and NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS), for almost every economy. The file wdi_trade.csv has one row per economy and year from 1960 to 2025 (most economies start later, and 2025 is still missing for many). Its column trade_balance is exports minus imports (NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS), which we use in Fig. 2. The small file countries.csv gives each economy’s World Bank region and income group.

Python note. .nunique() counts the different values in a column. Subtracting two Series lines them up by their labels (here the years), and a year that one of them lacks gives NaN, which .max() skips. For the United States the WDI copy the BEA’s numbers, so the two sources should agree.


world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")         # World Bank WDI, percent of GDP
regions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")       # World Bank region and income group of each economy
us_wdi = world[world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year")
gap = max((us_wdi.exports - shares.Exports).abs().max(), (us_wdi.imports - shares.Imports).abs().max())
print(f"{world.country.nunique()} economies, {world.year.min()}-{world.year.max()}; the U.S. rows start in "
      f"{us_wdi.index.min()} and differ from the BEA data by at most {gap:.2f} points")

Each economy gets one fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others. Plotly offers 44 dark enough colors, fewer than the 214 economies, so group_colors hands them out such that the economies of one menu group (the G7, a region, …) never share a color, as far as 44 colors allow.

LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]     # too pale on a white background
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:   # 24 + 26 colors, 44 of them kept
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy


Python note. For each country, score gives every color a cost: 1 for each country that already uses it, 10 for each one in a large group (Europe has more countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group small enough to avoid any clash. a if test else b gives a when the test is True. min(PALETTE, key=score.get) picks the color with the lowest cost (the first one on ties). When no color is free, PALETTE[::-1] (the list in reverse order) makes the search start from the end of the list, so that the leftovers take the last, rarely used colors.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (the menu views); fixed: the textbook countries' colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        score = {}                                  # the cost of each color: lower is better
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)            # 1 per country using it anywhere
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10      # a clash in a small group costs most
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)                              # the cheapest color
        if score[best] >= 10:                       # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


COLORS = group_colors(regions.country, country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]).values(), {"U.S.": BLUE})

The dictionary COLORS maps each economy to its color, and color_discrete_map=COLORS makes Plotly use it, in Colab and on the website. fit_range keeps the textbook’s axis range when the data fit in it; otherwise it returns None, which lets Plotly choose a range that shows every value.

def fit_range(values, book_range):
    """The textbook's axis range if every value fits in it, otherwise None (Plotly then chooses)."""
    if values.min() >= book_range[0] and values.max() <= book_range[1]:
        return book_range
    return None

The figure function draws Fig. 19.1 for any list of economies. The title reports exports plus imports, the openness of each economy, in its latest year.

Python note. .melt(...) stacks the export and import columns into one column share, with a new column flow that says which is which; line_dash="flow" then draws exports solid and imports dashed. .groupby("country").last() keeps each economy’s last row. ", ".join(names) glues a list of texts together, and a if test else b gives a when the test is True and b otherwise: the title names two economies and counts the rest.


FLOWS = {"Exports and imports": ["Exports", "Imports"], "Exports": ["Exports"], "Imports": ["Imports"]}


def trade_shares_world(countries=("U.S.",), flow="Exports and imports"):
    """Fig. 19.1 for any economies: exports and imports, percent of GDP (World Bank WDI)."""
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)].rename(columns={"exports": "Exports", "imports": "Imports"})
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))
    long = rows.melt(id_vars=["country", "year"], value_vars=FLOWS[flow], var_name="flow", value_name="share")
    last = rows.dropna(subset=["Exports", "Imports"]).groupby("country").last()
    names = []
    for name in last.index[:2]:
        names.append(f"{name} {last.Exports[name] + last.Imports[name]:.0f}%")
    more = f" + {len(last) - 2} more" if len(last) > 2 else ""
    fig = px.line(long, x="year", y="share", color="country", line_dash="flow", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "flow": "Flow"},
                  title="Latest exports + imports, % of GDP: " + ", ".join(names) + more)
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(long.share.dropna(), [2, 18.5]))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig


Python note. SelectMultiple is a list from which you can choose several items: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click. Its value is the list chosen at the start, here only the United States, as in the textbook.


interact(trade_shares_world,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value=["U.S."], rows=8,
                                  description="economies", style=WIDE),
         flow=ToggleButtons(options=list(FLOWS), value="Exports and imports", description="flows"));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: exports and imports of every economy, one group at a time
fig = trade_shares_world(tuple(world.country.unique()), "Exports and imports")
group_menu(fig, country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]), "Textbook",
           "Exports (solid) and imports (dashed), percent of GDP: choose a group in the menu")





                                
                                            




Sources. Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Exports of goods and services, % of GDP (NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS) and Imports of goods and services, % of GDP (NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS); World Bank, country and lending groups (regions and income groups of the menus). Prepared files: data/ch19/wdi_trade.csv and data/ch19/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
On the website, the menu above the chart shows one group of economies at a time; click a name in the legend to hide it, and double-click the chart to show extreme values that the chosen range leaves out.
How open is the United States compared with other economies?

in_2024 = world[world.year == 2024].set_index("country")
openness_2024 = (in_2024.exports + in_2024.imports).sort_values()
rank = list(openness_2024.index).index("U.S.") + 1
print(f"In 2024 the U.S. is number {rank} of {len(openness_2024)} economies, counting from the least open")
openness_2024.loc[["U.S.", "Brazil", "China", "Japan", "India", "Germany", "Ireland", "Singapore"]].round(1)

The United States is one of the least open economies in the world: in 2024 only four of 172 economies traded less relative to their GDP. Large economies trade less, because much of their trade happens inside their own borders. Small trading hubs such as Singapore (313 percent) and Luxembourg (351 percent) import goods and re-export them, so their exports and imports can each exceed GDP.
Your turn. In which year did U.S. imports first exceed 15 percent of GDP? And in which years since then were they below 14 percent? Then add China in the picker: in which year did China’s exports peak as a share of GDP?


Hint

Keep the rows that pass a test: shares[shares.Imports > 15]. Its first row label, .index[0], is the first year. For the second question, filter the years after that one with shares.loc[year:] and a second test. For China, world[world.country == "China"].set_index("year").exports.idxmax() gives the year.


# Your turn: try it here




Fig. 2: The U.S. trade balance as a share of GDP
Goal. Measure the U.S. trade deficit and test the rule that trade must balance in the long run.
The trade balance is exports minus imports. We compute it with net_exports, turn it into a share of GDP, and check it against the figure’s data file, which was computed from the BEA’s own net-exports series.

The Oddtopia example says that the trade balance must average zero over a long period. The figure function shades a window of years and reports the average trade balance in it, using our period_average.

Python note. min(a, b) and max(a, b) give the smaller and the larger of two numbers, so the window stays valid even if the two sliders cross. (series < 0).sum() counts the years with a deficit, because each True counts as 1. add_vrect shades a band between two x values, and add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a segment.


def trade_balance_chart(start=1976, end=2025):
    """Fig. 19.2: the U.S. trade balance (% of GDP), with its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)         # in case the sliders cross
    avg = period_average(us.trade_balance, start, end)
    deficits = (us.trade_balance.loc[start:end] < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(us.reset_index(), x="year", y="trade_balance", color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title=f"{start}–{end}: average trade balance {avg:+.2f}% of GDP, "
                        f"deficits in {deficits} of {end - start + 1} years")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=start, x1=end, y0=avg, y1=avg, line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1990, y=1.6, text="Above zero: exports > imports", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1965, y=-4.5, text="Below zero: imports > exports", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-6.5, 2.5], tickvals=[-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2])   # no label in the corner
    return fig

Beyond the United States: who runs deficits, who runs surpluses?
Does trade balance in the long run in other countries? The same figure, for any economy, uses the WDI trade balance of wdi_trade.csv. The dotted lines are each economy’s average over the chosen years.

Python note. go.Scatter(x=[start, end], y=[avg, avg], mode="lines") draws one straight segment. legendgroup=name ties it to the economy’s line, so that a click on the legend hides both, and showlegend=False keeps it out of the legend.


def add_average(fig, series, name, start, end):
    """Draw the average of a yearly series from start to end as a dotted segment, and return the average."""
    avg = period_average(series, start, end)
    if avg == avg:                                         # NaN (no data in the window) is not equal to itself
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[start, end], y=[avg, avg], mode="lines", name=name + ", average",
                                 legendgroup=name, showlegend=False,
                                 line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=3, dash="dot")))
    return avg


def trade_balance_world(countries=("U.S.",), start=1976, end=2024):
    """Fig. 19.2 for any economies: the trade balance (% of GDP, WDI) and its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)          # in case the sliders cross
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y="trade_balance", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    names = []
    for name in sorted(set(rows.country)):
        avg = add_average(fig, rows[rows.country == name].set_index("year").trade_balance, name, start, end)
        if avg == avg:
            names.append(f"{name} {round(avg, 1) + 0.0:+.1f}%")     # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
        else:
            names.append(f"{name}: no data")
    more = f" + {len(names) - 2} more" if len(names) > 2 else ""
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Average trade balance {start}–{end}: " + ", ".join(names[:2]) + more,
                      legend_title_text="")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.trade_balance.dropna(), [-6.5, 2.5]))
    return fig

The second bar of the textbook’s figure shows each country’s trade balance as a share of U.S. GDP, so the bars of different countries can be added up and compared with the U.S. deficit: we multiply the share of own GDP by the country’s GDP and divide by U.S. GDP.
You can add any country to the figure. Two small tools keep the textbook’s countries first and say which chosen countries have no data (PWT 10.01 has only the nine textbook countries).

Python note. .isin(list) is True for the rows whose value is in the list. .melt(id_vars="country") turns the two measure columns into rows, one row per country and measure, the long shape that px.bar needs. With color="Measure" and barmode="group", the bars of the two measures stand side by side. A function can return two results at once, order, missing, and the caller unpacks them into two names.


FIG3 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "China", "France", "Germany"]


def book_order(countries, book, available):
    """The chosen countries with data, the textbook's first and in its order, and the chosen ones without data."""
    order, missing = [], []
    for name in list(book) + sorted(countries):
        if name in countries and name not in order and name not in missing:
            if name in available:
                order.append(name)
            else:
                missing.append(name)
    return order, missing


def world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing):
    """The title of Fig. 3: the U.S. deficit and the largest surplus in percent of U.S. GDP."""
    if missing:
        return f"{year}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    if len(bars) == 0:
        return "Choose at least one country"
    text = f"{year} ({vintage}): "
    if "U.S." in bars.index:
        text += f"U.S. deficit {-bars.loc['U.S.', 'Share of own GDP']:.1f}% of GDP; "
    top = bars["Share of U.S. GDP"].idxmax()
    value = round(bars.loc[top, "Share of U.S. GDP"], 2) + 0.0     # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    if value > 0:
        return text + f"largest surplus {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
    return text + f"smallest deficit {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"


def world_balance_chart(year=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG3):
    """Fig. 19.3: the trade balance as a share of own GDP and of U.S. GDP, in one year."""
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    year = min(year, source[source.vintage == vintage].year.max())     # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    rows = source[(source.year == year) & (source.vintage == vintage)].set_index("country")
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG3, rows.index)
    one = rows.loc[order]
    bars = pd.DataFrame({"Share of own GDP": one.trade_balance,
                         "Share of U.S. GDP": share_of_us_gdp(one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, rows.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"])})
    long = bars.reset_index().melt(id_vars="country", var_name="Measure", value_name="Percent")
    fig = px.bar(long, x="country", y="Percent", color="Measure", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_map={"Share of own GDP": BLUE, "Share of U.S. GDP": GREEN},
                 labels={"country": "", "Percent": "Percent"}, title=world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    book = fit_range(long.Percent, [-9, 12.5])           # the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title=""))
    return fig

Trade and growth around the world
Should fast-growing countries borrow from abroad to invest? Here we check whether the fastest growers really run trade deficits.

Fig. 4: The trade balance in rapidly growing countries
Goal. Test whether fast-growing countries borrow from abroad, as consumption smoothing predicts.
A country that expects to be much richer tomorrow should borrow today, like a student who expects a high income later: it should run trade deficits. The textbook checks this for five fast-growing economies. Each bar is the simple average of the yearly trade balance over a window of years. We first make a table with one row per year and one column per country, so that period_average gives one average per country.

Python note. .pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance") turns a long table into a wide one: years as rows, countries as columns. [FIG4] then keeps the columns in the textbook’s order. With text_auto=".1f", px.bar writes each bar’s value, with one decimal, on the bar.


FIG4 = ["China", "India", "Singapore", "Ireland", "S. Korea"]
fast = pwt[pwt.country.isin(FIG4)]


def fast_growers_chart(start=2000, end=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG4):
    """Fig. 19.4: the average trade balance (% of own GDP) of fast-growing (or any chosen) economies."""
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    wide = source[source.vintage == vintage].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")
    end = min(end, wide.index.max())                         # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG4, wide.columns)
    avg = period_average(wide[order], start, end)
    bars = avg.rename("average").reset_index()
    title = f"{start}–{end} ({vintage}): {(avg > 0).sum()} of {len(avg)} economies ran trade surpluses on average"
    if missing:
        title = f"{start}–{end}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    fig = px.bar(bars, x="country", y="average", text_auto=".1f", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN], labels={"country": "", "average": "Percent of own GDP"},
                 title=title)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    book = fit_range(avg.dropna(), [-5, 30])                 # the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
    return fig

Two series behave strangely. Singapore’s balance jumps from −33 percent of GDP in 1993 to +15 percent in 1998. The identity \(NX = S - I\) links the trade balance to saving. This section compares the U.S. budget deficit, investment and the trade deficit over time.

text:
Net foreign assets and foreign debt
Years of trade deficits add up to a debt to the rest of the world. We measure that debt for the United States and for every other economy.

Fig. 6: Net international investment position of the United States
Goal. Follow how decades of trade deficits turned the United States from a lender into a debtor.
The net international investment position (NIIP) is what U.S. residents own abroad (foreign shares, bonds, factories) minus what foreigners own in the United States, at the end of each year. When it is negative, it is the net foreign debt. Each year’s trade deficit is new borrowing, so the position should fall by about the size of the deficit. With our function accumulate, we start from the 1976 position and add the trade balance of every later year, as in the Oddtopia table. We also compare the current data with the same series as published in July 2023, which the textbook used.

title: Chapter 19: International Trade
text:
Concluding remarks

Trade has become much more important: U.S. exports and imports have risen from about 4 percent of GDP each in 1950 to 11 and 14 percent. Since 1976 imports have exceeded exports every year, and the trade deficit reached 5.7 percent of GDP in 2006.
The national income identity shows what a deficit means: with \(NX < 0\), a country uses more than it produces (\(C + I + G > Y\)), and it invests more than it saves (\(NX = S - I\)). The deficit is borrowing from the rest of the world, and the sum of past deficits is the net foreign debt, about 70 percent of U.S. GDP today.
Trade can make everyone better off: across time it shares risks (Oddtopia and Eventopia), and across goods it lets countries specialize by comparative advantage (the North and the South). Free migration follows absolute advantage and can raise world output even more.
The data hold surprises: the textbook’s fast-growing economies run surpluses, not deficits, and the large U.S. budget deficits of the 1980s and 2000s came with large trade deficits (the twin deficits). Looking beyond the textbook’s countries changes both stories: across all economies, faster growth goes with slightly smaller trade balances, and the twin deficits are clear in some countries (Germany, Greece) but not in others.
The data also teach care: the textbook’s “2019” bars are 2017 data, revisions changed the recent U.S. foreign debt by up to 16 points of GDP, and two sources for the same country can differ by vintage and definition.
The next chapter, exchange rates and international finance, brings trade into the short-run model and asks how the exchange rate adjusts.

Python note. import loads a library, a toolbox written by other people. We give each library a short nickname, for example np for NumPy, so that the code stays short. Text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it, and it is there for human readers. The try ... except block runs one Colab-only line and simply skips it anywhere else.


# Libraries used in this chapter
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays

import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece (model figures)

from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider, IntSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


The data figures can show many countries. On the website they use the helpers below: a legend you can click, a slider that changes the data of every line at once, and a menu of country groups.


Show the helper code
# @title Helpers for the many-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def compact(y):
    """Round to 4 significant digits, so that the saved figure stays small."""
    return [None if v is None or v != v else float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in y]


def slim(trace):
    """Make a line smaller: rounded y, and the hover label from the trace name instead of one text per point."""
    trace.y = compact(trace.y)
    if trace.hovertext is not None and len(trace.hovertext) > 0 and trace.hovertext[0] == trace.name:
        trace.hovertext = None
        trace.hovertemplate = trace.hovertemplate.replace("%{hovertext}", "%{fullData.name}")
    return trace


def legend_only(fig, keep):
    """Show the traces named in keep; list the others in the legend only, so a click adds them."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        trace.visible = True if trace.name in keep else "legendonly"
        slim(trace)
    return fig


def data_slider(make_figure, name, values, start, title, label=None, **fixed):
    """A slider whose steps replace the y data of every line (matched by name), so legend clicks are kept.

    Lines missing at the start value are added empty. title is a text with {} where the slider value goes."""
    figures = {v: make_figure(**{name: v}, **fixed) for v in values}
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[start].layout)
    for v in [start] + list(values):
        for t in figures[v].data:
            if t.name not in [u.name for u in fig.data]:
                t.y = t.y if v == start else [None] * len(t.y)
                fig.add_trace(slim(t))
    steps = []
    for v in values:
        ys = {t.name: compact(t.y) for t in figures[v].data}
        new_y = [ys.get(t.name, [None] * len(t.y)) for t in fig.data]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(v), args=[{"y": new_y}, {"title.text": title.format(v)}]))
    fig.update_layout(title=title.format(start), sliders=[dict(
        active=values.index(start), steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60), currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
text:
Model overview
An exchange rate is a price: how much of another country’s money one dollar buys. This chapter looks at it over two horizons. In the long run, goods should cost about the same everywhere once prices are written in one currency, so the exchange rate follows the price levels of the two countries and a country with more inflation ends up with a weaker currency. In the short run, prices hardly move, and the exchange rate jumps with interest rates instead: when U.S. interest rates rise, investors want dollars, the dollar gets stronger and U.S. goods become harder to sell abroad.
That second link brings trade into the short-run model of earlier chapters. Net exports now fall when the interest rate rises, just like investment, and a change in foreign interest rates becomes a demand shock at home. Below we write these equations once, pick one set of illustrative parameters, and define the functions and tools that the rest of the notebook reuses: first for the long-run data on currencies and prices, then for the two model diagrams, and finally for the history of exchange-rate regimes, currency crises and the euro crisis.
Exchange rates in the long run. Call \(E\) the nominal exchange rate: how many units of foreign currency one dollar buys, for example 0.92 euros. The law of one price says that, in the long run, a good sells for the same price everywhere once prices are written in the same currency. With \(P\) the U.S. price and \(P^w\) the foreign (“world”) price,
\[EP = P^w. \qquad (20.1)\]
Apply it to the whole basket of goods of each economy. The quantity theory of money pins down the two price levels in the long run, so the law of one price pins down the exchange rate:
\[\bar{E} = \frac{\bar{P}^w}{\bar{P}}. \qquad (20.3)\]
The real exchange rate \(EP/P^w\) is the price of U.S. goods in units of foreign goods. If the law of one price holds, it equals 1 in the long run, \(\overline{RER} = \bar{E}P/\bar{P}^w = 1\) (20.4). In the short run, \(E\) jumps with financial news while prices are sticky, so the real exchange rate moves with \(E\).
Exchange rates in the short-run model. When the U.S. real interest rate \(R_t\) rises, investors want dollars, the dollar appreciates, U.S. goods become expensive and net exports fall. When the foreign real interest rate \(\bar{R}^w\) rises, the opposite happens:
\[\frac{NX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}\,(R_t - \bar{R}^w). \qquad (20.6)\]
Adding and subtracting the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\) shows that net exports react to \(R_t - \bar{r}\) just like investment does. The IS curve keeps its old form, with two new pieces:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}), \qquad \bar{b} \equiv \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}, \qquad
\bar{a} \equiv \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} - 1 + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}). \qquad (20.8)\]
So a foreign interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) works as a positive aggregate demand shock \(\bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\). Combined with the policy rule of Chapter 13, the IS curve gives the AD curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\), and the Phillips curve gives the AS curve \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\).
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers. Both model diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of parameters:

marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent, as in Chapter 11’s example, and no demand shock at home, \(\bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} = 1\);
interest sensitivities \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), so the total \(\bar{b} = 2\) is the value of Chapters 11 and 13, split half and half between investment and trade;
inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), as in Chapter 13;
the foreign shock of Fig. 5: the foreign real interest rate is 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), at 7 percent, in periods 1 to 9 and back at \(\bar{r}\) afterwards.


Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing b_nx=B_NX gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. Names in capital letters, such as R_BAR, are constants that we set once and never change.


R_BAR, B_I, B_NX = 5.0, 1.0, 1.0            # marginal product of capital (%), interest sensitivities
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 1.0       # inflation target (%), policy response, Phillips-curve slope
RW_GAP, A_LAST, T_MAX = 2.0, 9, 20          # foreign rate minus r_bar in periods 1-9; periods simulated


def long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P):
    """Equation 20.3: the long-run nominal exchange rate E = P_w / P (foreign currency per dollar)."""
    return P_w / P


def real_exchange_rate(E, P, P_w):
    """The real exchange rate E P / P_w: foreign goods needed to buy one U.S. good (equation 20.4)."""
    return E * P / P_w


def net_exports(R, R_w=R_BAR, a_nx=0.0, b_nx=B_NX):
    """Equation 20.6: net exports in percent of potential output, NX/Y = a_nx - b_nx (R - R_w)."""
    return a_nx - b_nx * (R - R_w)


def foreign_shock(R_w, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """The part of a_bar that comes from abroad in equation 20.8: b_nx (R_w - r_bar)."""
    return b_nx * (R_w - r_bar)


def is_curve(R, a=0.0, b_i=B_I, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """Equation 20.8, the open-economy IS curve: Y~ = a - (b_i + b_nx) (R - r_bar), in percent."""
    return a - (b_i + b_nx) * (R - r_bar)


def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX):
    """The AD curve of Chapter 13 with the open-economy b: Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return a - b * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS curve of Chapter 13: pi = pi_e + nu Y~, with expected inflation pi_e = last period's inflation."""
    return pi_e + nu * Y


def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The point where the AD and AS curves cross: short-run output and inflation in one period."""
    Y = (a - b * m * (pi_e - PI_BAR)) / (1 + b * m * nu)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu)

Let us try the functions on a few textbook cases.

Python note. An f-string such as f"E = {E:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals” and :+.1f also shows the sign. Y, pi = solve_asad(...) unpacks the two results of the function into two variables.


E = long_run_exchange_rate(P_w=92.0, P=100.0)       # a chip costs 92 euros in Germany and 100 dollars in the U.S.
print(f"Law of one price: E = {E:.2f} euros per dollar")
print(f"Real exchange rate at that E: {real_exchange_rate(E, 100.0, 92.0):.2f}; at E = 1.00: "
      f"{real_exchange_rate(1.0, 100.0, 92.0):.2f}")
print(f"Net exports when R rises from 5% to 6%: {net_exports(6.0):+.1f}% of potential output")
print(f"IS curve at R = 6%: Y~ = {is_curve(6.0):+.1f}% (without the trade channel: {is_curve(6.0, b_nx=0.0):+.1f}%)")
a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + RW_GAP)
Y, pi = solve_asad(PI_BAR, a)
print(f"Foreign rate 2 points above r_bar: a = {a:.1f}; first period Y~ = {Y:+.2f}%, inflation = {pi:.2f}%")

At 0.92 euros per dollar the chip costs the same in both countries, so the real exchange rate is 1. At 1 euro per dollar U.S. chips are about 9 percent too expensive. With the trade channel, a 1-point rise in the interest rate lowers output by 2 percent instead of 1. And a foreign interest rate 2 points above \(\bar{r}\) is a demand shock of \(\bar{a} = 2\): the same shock as Chapter 13’s aggregate demand shock, so the same dynamics follow.

One loop for the dynamics
Fig. 5 follows the economy period by period. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. simulate repeats this step; shock_list builds the list of demand shocks, one value per period.

Python note. values.append(x) adds x at the end of the list values, and for t in range(1, 21) repeats the indented lines for t = 1, 2, …, 20. dict(period=0, Y=0.0) is a dictionary, a set of named values, and rows[-1]["pi"] is the value named "pi" in the last element of the list. pd.DataFrame(rows) turns a list of dictionaries into a table, one row per dictionary.


def shock_list(size, last=A_LAST):
    """A demand shock of the given size in periods 1, ..., last and zero afterwards, for T_MAX periods."""
    values = []
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


def simulate(a_list, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Solve the AS/AD model period by period; period 0 is the steady state (Y~ = 0, pi = pi_bar)."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, pi_e=PI_BAR, Y=0.0, pi=PI_BAR)]
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]                   # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], m, b, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Inflation rises from 2 to 3 percent in period 1 and climbs toward 4 percent while the shock lasts. When the shock ends in period 10, output falls below potential and inflation starts back down to 2 percent.


Drawing tools
Both model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_curve draws a curve and writes its name at its last point inside the axes, as the textbook does;
add_point marks a point with a dot, a letter and dashed guides to the axes;
add_arrow draws an arrow between two points.


Python note. (x >= 0) & (y <= 8) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. add_annotation with axref="x" and ayref="y" draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y), both in axis units. Labels such as "AS<sub>8</sub>" use HTML to write AS₈.


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, x_range, y_range, dash="solid"):
    """Draw one curve and write its label at its last point inside the axes (no label if label is "")."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    inside = (x >= x_range[0]) & (x <= x_range[1]) & (y >= y_range[0]) & (y <= y_range[1])
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, x0, y0, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (x, y) with a dot and a label; with guides, dashed lines to the axes at x0 and y0."""
    if guides:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x, x], y=[y, y, y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition="top right",
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16), marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, color="black"):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=color)



Tools for comparing countries
The textbook’s data figures show a few countries. Every one of them can show many more: the data files of this chapter hold the same series for up to 200 economies, from the World Bank, the IMF, the OECD, the Federal Reserve and the Penn World Table. The file countries.csv lists the economies with their World Bank region and income group, and says which are OECD members and since when each euro member uses the euro.

Three small tools are shared by the data figures:

group_colors gives every country a fixed color, so a line keeps its color when you add or remove others. The textbook’s countries keep the textbook’s colors, and the countries of one menu group (the G7, a region, …) never share a color, as far as Plotly’s 44 dark enough colors allow;
ratio_ticks chooses round tick values for a ratio-scale axis that spans less than a factor of 10 (Plotly’s own ticks crowd there; over wider spans we let Plotly choose);
missing_note adds a note to a title when a chosen country has no data;
high_low names the countries with the highest and the lowest value, for the titles;
book_order puts the textbook’s countries first in a bar chart.


Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 and .Alphabet are lists of colors that Plotly provides; we drop the pale ones. In group_colors, for each country, score gives every color a cost: 1 for each country that already uses it, 10 for each one in a large group (Europe has more countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group small enough to avoid any clash. a if test else b gives a when the test is True. min(PALETTE, key=score.get) picks the color with the lowest cost (the first one on ties). When no color is free, PALETTE[::-1] (the list in reverse order) makes the search start from the end of the list, so that the leftovers take the last, rarely used colors.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]     # too pale on a white background
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:   # 24 + 26 colors, 44 of them kept
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (the menu views); fixed: the textbook countries' colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        score = {}                                  # the cost of each color: lower is better
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)            # 1 per country using it anywhere
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10      # a clash in a small group costs most
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)                              # the cheapest color
        if score[best] >= 10:                       # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Round tick values between low and high for a ratio-scale axis; None (Plotly's ticks) beyond a factor of 10."""
    if high / low >= 10:
        return None
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 6):
        for step in [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 6))
    return ticks


Python note. ", ".join(missing) glues a list of texts into one text, with ", " between them. In f"{value:{fmt}}" the format itself is a variable: fmt=".0f" shows no decimals, ".1f" one. In a Plotly title, <br> starts a new line and <sup>...</sup> writes smaller text.


def missing_note(wanted, found):
    """A second, smaller title line naming the chosen countries that have no data ('' if all have data)."""
    missing = []
    for name in wanted:
        if name not in set(found):
            missing.append(name)
    if len(missing) == 0:
        return ""
    if len(missing) > 3:
        return f"<br><sup>no data for {len(missing)} of the chosen countries</sup>"
    return "<br><sup>no data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"


def high_low(values, fmt=".0f"):
    """'A 12, B 3': the countries with the highest and the lowest value (one name only for one country)."""
    text = f"{values.idxmax()} {values.max():{fmt}}"
    if len(values) > 1:
        text = text + f", {values.idxmin()} {values.min():{fmt}}"
    return text


def book_order(countries, book):
    """The textbook's countries in the textbook's order, then the others alphabetically (for bar charts)."""
    order = []
    for name in book:
        if name in countries:
            order.append(name)
    for name in sorted(countries):
        if name not in order:
            order.append(name)
    return order


print(ratio_ticks(67, 142), ratio_ticks(1, 50), missing_note(("Japan", "Kosovo"), ["Japan"]))

Exchange rates in the long run
We start with the data: how the dollar has moved against the yen and the euro, and whether the gap in inflation between two countries explains the move, as the law of one price predicts.

Fig. 1: The U.S. exchange rate versus the yen and the euro
Goal. See how the price of a dollar has moved since the end of fixed exchange rates in 1971.
The exchange rate here is the price of a dollar in foreign currency: how many yen, or how many euros, one dollar buys. A fall is a depreciation of the dollar, a rise an appreciation. The two series have very different units (hundreds of yen, about one euro), so the textbook draws them on two vertical scales.

Python note. parse_dates=["date"] tells read_csv that the column date holds dates, so Plotly draws a proper time axis. .tail() shows the last five rows. The euro only exists since 1999, so the column eur_per_usd is empty (NaN, “not a number”) before that.

From 1971 to 1995 the dollar lost three quarters of its value against the yen: from 358 yen in January 1971 to 84 in April 1995.

def dollar_index(countries=("Japan", "Euro area"), base=1999, scale="linear"):
    """Fig. 20.1 for any currency: units of the currency per dollar, index = 100 in the base year."""
    picked = fx_all[fx_all.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    level = picked[picked.year == base].groupby("country").per_usd.mean()     # average of the base year
    picked["index"] = (100 * picked.per_usd / picked.country.map(level)).round(1)
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    latest = picked.groupby("country")["index"].last()                        # each currency's last month
    title = f"No data in {base} for these currencies"
    if len(latest) > 0:
        title = f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100), latest: " + high_low(latest)
    fig = px.line(picked, x="date", y="index", color="label", hover_name="label", color_discrete_map=FX_COLORS,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"), title=title + missing_note(countries, level.index),
                  labels={"date": "Year", "index": f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100)"})
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    if scale == "ratio" and len(picked) > 0:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ratio_ticks(picked["index"].min(), picked["index"].max()))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", xaxis_range=["1965-01-01", "2027-06-01"])   # no tick label in the corner
    return fig

The Balassa-Samuelson effect in the Big Mac data
The explanation is that only traded goods obey the law of one price. Haircuts and restaurant meals cannot be shipped, and their prices follow local wages. As an economy grows, wages rise, nontraded goods become dearer, and the real exchange rate appreciates. So richer countries should have dearer Big Macs (the burger includes the work of the staff and the rent of the restaurant). We check this with the latest Big Mac release and GDP per person.

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: The open economy in the short-run model
text:
The open economy in the short-run model
Now prices are sticky and the exchange rate reacts to interest rates. These two model figures show how this flattens the IS curve and turns a rise in foreign interest rates into a demand shock.

Fig. 4: Increasing interest rates and the IS curve
Goal. See why the IS curve is flatter in an open economy: a higher interest rate lowers net exports as well as investment.
The central bank raises the real interest rate from \(\bar{r}\) to \(R'\). The economy moves along the IS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). Two forces lower output:
\[\uparrow R \;\Rightarrow\; \downarrow \frac{I}{\bar{Y}} \quad\text{and}\quad
\uparrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow E \Rightarrow \uparrow \frac{EP}{P^w} \Rightarrow \downarrow \frac{NX}{\bar{Y}}.\]
From equation (20.8), \(\tilde{Y}' = -(\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})(R' - \bar{r})\). The dashed gray line is the IS curve without the trade channel (\(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\)), the closed economy of Chapter 11.

R_LINE = np.linspace(9, 2, 141)              # real interest rates, high to low, at which we draw the IS curves
R_UP = np.linspace(2, 9, 141)                # the same rates, low to high: the label then goes at the upper end
X_IS, R_AXIS = [-11, 5], [2, 9]              # fixed axes, so that you can see the curve turn


def tightening(R_new=6.0, b_nx=B_NX, b_i=B_I):
    """Fig. 20.4: the central bank raises R from r_bar to R_new; the economy moves along the IS curve."""
    Y_new = is_curve(R_new, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if b_nx > 0:
        add_curve(fig, is_curve(R_UP, b_i=b_i, b_nx=0.0), R_UP, "IS without trade", GRAY, X_IS, R_AXIS, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, is_curve(R_LINE, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx), R_LINE, "IS", BLUE, X_IS, R_AXIS)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    if R_new != R_BAR:                                                        # B is A when the rate does not change
        add_point(fig, Y_new, R_new, "B", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    add_arrow(fig, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_BAR, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_new)              # the interest rate rises ...
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3, Y_new, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3)            # ... and output falls
    invest = -b_i * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0                                    # + 0.0 avoids printing -0.0
    trade = -b_nx * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0
    fig.update_layout(title=f"R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ′ = {Y_new + 0.0:.1f}%   "
                            f"(investment {invest:.1f}, net exports {trade:.1f})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=X_IS, tickvals=list(range(-10, 5, 2)),
                                 zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Real interest rate, R (percent)", range=R_AXIS, tickvals=list(range(3, 9)),
                                 zeroline=False))
    return fig


Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

         b_i=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="investment sensitivity b̄ᵢ", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 20.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the baseline, raising \(R\) from 5 to 6 percent lowers output by 2 percent: 1 point through investment and 1 point through net exports. Without trade, output would fall by only 1 percent.
Raise \(\bar{b}_{nx}\): the IS curve turns flatter and point \(B\) moves left. The more net exports react to the exchange rate, the more powerful monetary policy is.
Nothing else changes: the curve still passes through \(A\), because at \(R = \bar{r}\) there is no gap to react to.

Your turn. With \(\bar{b}_i = 1\), what value of \(\bar{b}_{nx}\) makes a 1-point rise in \(R\) lower output by 3 percent? Find it with the sliders, then check it with is_curve.

Output falls by \((\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})\) percent per point. Try is_curve(6.0, b_nx=2.0).

Fig. 5: An increase in foreign interest rates
Goal. Follow the international transmission of monetary policy: the European Central Bank raises its interest rate, and the U.S. economy booms, then slumps.
When the foreign real interest rate rises to \(\bar{R}^w = 7\) percent, 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), investors move from dollars to euros, the dollar depreciates, U.S. goods become cheap and U.S. net exports rise. In equation (20.8) this is a positive demand shock, \(\bar{a} = \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 2\), so the AD curve shifts out to AD₁. Then the familiar dynamics of Chapter 13 take over:

period 1: the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), with output and inflation above normal;
periods 2–9: inflation rises, the Fed raises U.S. interest rates, and the economy climbs AD₁ toward \(C\) (period 8 in the textbook), with output back at potential but inflation above target;
period 10: the foreign rate falls back to \(\bar{r}\), the shock ends, AD shifts back, and the economy drops to a recession at \(D\); it then slides down AD back to \(A\).

The function draws period t: the original AS curve, the AS curve of period t, both AD curves (the one that holds in period t in full color), the path so far with the textbook’s letters, and the path still to come in gray.

Y_LINE = np.linspace(-6, 6, 121)                # output levels at which we draw the AS curves
PI_LINE = np.linspace(12, -4, 161)              # inflation rates, high to low, at which we draw the AD curves
X_AD, PI_AXIS = [-3.5, 3.5], [-0.5, 7.5]        # fixed axes
LETTERS = {0: "A", 1: "B", 8: "C", 10: "D"}     # the textbook's letters for periods 0, 1, 8 and 10
FADED = "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"                  # light blue for the AD curve that does not hold in period t


def add_asad_curves(fig, a, pi_e, t, m, b):
    """The AS curves (original and period t) and the AD curves (original and shifted) of Fig. 5."""
    add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, PI_BAR), "AS", TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.05:                                   # skip the AS of period t if it is the old one
        label = f"AS<sub>{t}</sub>" if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.6 else ""
        add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, pi_e), label, TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    shock_on = 1 <= t <= A_LAST
    ad_label = f"AD = AD<sub>{t}</sub>" if t > A_LAST else "AD"
    add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_LINE, 0.0, m, b), PI_LINE, ad_label, FADED if shock_on else BLUE, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if a != 0:
        label = "AD<sub>1</sub>" if abs(a) > 0.8 and abs(a / (b * m)) > 0.6 else ""  # no label on top of AD's
        add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_LINE, a, m, b), PI_LINE, label, BLUE if shock_on else FADED, X_AD, PI_AXIS)


Python note. for x, y in written: goes through a list of pairs and unpacks each pair into x and y. A letter is left out when its point lies within 0.3 points of output and 0.6 points of inflation of a point that already has one, as happens when a small shock or a strong policy response keeps \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) close to \(A\).


def add_path(fig, path, t):
    """The economy's path up to period t (dots, arrows, letters) and the rest of the path in gray."""
    future = path[path.period >= t]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=future.Y, y=future.pi, mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"), marker=dict(color=GRAY, size=5)))
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s])
    written = []                                        # the points that already carry a letter
    for s in range(t + 1):
        if s in LETTERS:
            letter = LETTERS[s]
            for x, y in written:
                if abs(path.Y[s] - x) < 0.3 and abs(path.pi[s] - y) < 0.6:
                    letter = ""                         # too close to a letter already written: leave it out
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], letter, X_AD[0], PI_AXIS[0], guides=False)
            if letter != "":
                written.append((path.Y[s], path.pi[s]))


def foreign_rate_shock(gap=RW_GAP, t=10, b_nx=B_NX, m=M_BAR):
    """Fig. 20.5: period t after the foreign real interest rate rises gap points above r_bar in periods 1-9."""
    a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + gap, b_nx)                 # equation 20.8: the demand shock from abroad
    b = B_I + b_nx
    path = simulate(shock_list(a), m, b)
    now = path.loc[t]
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_asad_curves(fig, a, now.pi_e, t, m, b)
    add_path(fig, path, t)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:+.2f}%   "
                            f"(Rʷ − r̄ = {gap:.1f}, so ā = {a:.2f} in periods 1–{A_LAST})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Output, Ỹ (percent)", range=X_AD, tickvals=list(range(-3, 4)), zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Inflation, π (percent)", range=PI_AXIS, tickvals=list(range(0, 8)), zeroline=False))
    return fig


Python note. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers, here the period t. path.loc[t] is the row of period t, and now.pi is its value in the column pi.


interact(foreign_rate_shock,
         gap=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="foreign rate gap Rʷ − r̄", style=WIDE),
         t=IntSlider(value=10, min=1, max=20, step=1, description="period t", style=WIDE),
         b_nx=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="net-export sensitivity b̄ₙₓ", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 5 with a precomputed slider for the period
slider_figure(foreign_rate_shock, "t", [1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, 20], start=10, label="period t")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 20.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

At \(B\) (period 1) output is 1 percent above potential and inflation 3 percent: half of the shock goes into output, half into inflation, because \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\) as in Chapter 13.
At \(C\) output is back at potential, but inflation is close to \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m}) = 4\) percent. The AS curves of periods 8, 9 and 10 are almost the same line, which is why the textbook draws \(C\) and \(D\) on one curve, AS₈.
When the shock ends, the economy pays for the boom with a recession at \(D\): output 1 percent below potential.
The U.S. did nothing, yet its economy boomed and slumped: a change in interest rates abroad is a demand shock at home.

Exchange-rate regimes and the policy trilemma
Countries have chosen very different ways to manage their currencies, from the gold standard to free floating. This section follows that history and the trade-off behind every choice, including what happens when a fixed rate breaks.

Fig. 6: The U.K.-U.S. exchange rate
Goal. Read two centuries of exchange-rate history in one line: the gold standard, Bretton Woods and floating rates.
Under the gold standard each country fixed the price of an ounce of gold in its currency. From 1834 the United States paid about 20.67 dollars an ounce and the United Kingdom 4.25 pounds, so a dollar was worth \(4.25/20.67 \approx 0.206\) pounds. Under Bretton Woods (1944 to the early 1970s) other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at 35 dollars an ounce. Since 1973 the major currencies float.

What to notice.

For most of the 19th century the line is flat at the gold parity. The exception is the Civil War: the U.S. left gold, and in 1864 the dollar fell to 0.100 pounds, half its value.
Bretton Woods shows up as long flat steps: 0.357 pounds (2.80 dollars per pound) in the 1950s and 1960s, 0.417 (2.40 dollars) after the pound’s devaluation in 1967.
Since 1973 the line moves a lot every year. And over the two centuries the dollar appreciated, from 0.22 pounds in 1791 to 0.76 in 2025, as the U.S. economy overtook the British one.


Key numbers: how stable is each regime?
We measure stability by the typical yearly change of the exchange rate: the standard deviation of its percent changes.

Python note. .pct_change() computes the percent change from one row to the next (here, from one year to the next), and .std() the standard deviation, the typical size of the changes. A dictionary maps each name to a pair of years, and first, last = REGIMES[name] unpacks the pair.

Fig. 7: The policy trilemma in open economies
Goal. See why an open economy can have at most two of three good things: a stable exchange rate, its own monetary policy, and free flows of international finance.
The textbook draws the policy trilemma as a triangle: the three goals are its corners, and each side is a regime that achieves the two goals at its ends and gives up the one opposite. Here the triangle is live. A small model from the chapter computes what happens when the foreign central bank (say, the Fed) raises its interest rate by \(\Delta i^w\), while your economy needs its own interest rate to change by \(\Delta i^{need}\):

with free financial flows, the exchange rate moves with the interest gap (Section 20.3: \(\uparrow i \Rightarrow \uparrow E\)), \(\%\Delta E = \eta\,(\Delta i - \Delta i^w)\), with an illustrative \(\eta = 5\) percent per point;
floating exchange rate: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\), and the exchange rate moves;
currency board (or monetary union): to keep \(E\) fixed, the interest rate must follow abroad, \(\Delta i = \Delta i^w\);
capital controls: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\) and keeps \(E\) fixed, because it rations the trade in its currency, so money cannot flow freely.


ETA = 5.0                                       # percent change of E per point of interest gap (illustrative)
LOST = {"floating exchange rate": "stable exchange rate", "currency board": "monetary autonomy",
        "capital controls": "free financial flows"}     # the goal each regime gives up: the opposite corner


def trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need):
    """Fig. 20.7 as a model: the change in the domestic interest rate and the percent change in E."""
    if regime == "currency board":
        di = di_world                           # the peg forces the domestic rate to follow the foreign rate
    else:
        di = di_need                            # floating or capital controls: the central bank chooses
    if regime == "floating exchange rate":
        dE = ETA * (di - di_world)              # free capital flows move the exchange rate
    else:
        dE = 0.0                                # fixed by the peg, or by rationing the currency
    return di, dE + 0.0, LOST[regime]


print(trilemma_outcome("floating exchange rate", 1.0, 0.0))

CORNERS = {"stable exchange rate": (1.0, 1.732), "monetary autonomy": (0.0, 0.0), "free financial flows": (2.0, 0.0)}
CORNER_TEXT = {"stable exchange rate": (1.0, 1.83, "center", "bottom", "Exchange-rate stability"),
               "monetary autonomy": (-0.08, 0.0, "right", "middle", "Independent<br>interest rate"),
               "free financial flows": (2.08, 0.0, "left", "middle", "Open capital<br>account")}
SIDES = {"floating exchange rate": ("monetary autonomy", "free financial flows", 1.0, -0.12, 0),
         "currency board": ("stable exchange rate", "free financial flows", 1.57, 0.94, 51),
         "capital controls": ("monetary autonomy", "stable exchange rate", 0.43, 0.94, -51)}
SIDE_TEXT = {"floating exchange rate": "Let the currency float", "currency board": "Hard peg: currency board, euro",
             "capital controls": "Peg behind capital controls"}

The four dictionaries above hold the geometry: the corners of the triangle, where each label goes, and which two corners each side joins (with its label position and angle). draw_triangle uses them.

def draw_triangle(fig, regime):
    """The trilemma triangle: the chosen side thick and green, the goal it gives up marked with a gray cross."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 2, 1, 0], y=[0, 0, 1.732, 0], fill="toself", fillcolor="#e6f5f1", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"))
    for side in SIDES:
        start, end, x, y, angle = SIDES[side]
        chosen = side == regime
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[CORNERS[start][0], CORNERS[end][0]], y=[CORNERS[start][1], CORNERS[end][1]],
                                 mode="lines", line=dict(color=GREEN if chosen else GRAY, width=9 if chosen else 2),
                                 name=SIDE_TEXT[side], showlegend=False))
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=SIDE_TEXT[side], textangle=angle, showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=13, color=TEAL if chosen else GRAY))
    for goal in CORNERS:
        kept = goal != LOST[regime]
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[CORNERS[goal][0]], y=[CORNERS[goal][1]], mode="markers", name=goal,
                                 showlegend=False, marker=dict(size=20, color=GREEN if kept else GRAY,
                                                               symbol="circle" if kept else "x")))
        x, y, xanchor, yanchor, text = CORNER_TEXT[goal]
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, xanchor=xanchor, yanchor=yanchor, showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=14, color="black" if kept else GRAY))


Python note. fill="toself" fills the shape that the points of the trace enclose, here the triangle. textangle=51 turns a text by 51 degrees, so that it runs along a side, and xanchor="right" makes a text end at its point instead of being centered on it. visible=False hides the axes, and the small margin lets the triangle fill the figure. The box at the top right, an annotation with a border, holds the readout.


def trilemma(regime="floating exchange rate", di_world=1.0, di_need=0.0):
    """Fig. 20.7: the policy trilemma; the foreign rate rises by di_world, the economy needs di_need."""
    di, dE, lost = trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need)
    flows = "blocked" if regime == "capital controls" else "free"
    fig = go.Figure()
    draw_triangle(fig, regime)
    fig.add_annotation(x=2.72, y=1.97, xanchor="right", yanchor="top", showarrow=False, align="left",
                       font=dict(size=13, color=BLUE), bordercolor=BLUE, borderpad=6, bgcolor="white",
                       text=f"Interest rate: {di:+.1f} pt<br>Exchange rate: {dE:+.1f}%<br>Capital flows: {flows}")
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.75, 2.75])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.38, 2.0])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{regime.capitalize()}: Δi = {di:+.1f}, %ΔE = {dE:+.1f}; lost: {lost}",
                      margin=dict(l=30, r=30, t=60, b=30))
    return fig

What to notice.

The Fed raises its rate by 1 point and your economy needs no change. With a floating rate you keep your interest rate, and your currency depreciates by 5 percent: the United States today.
With a currency board the exchange rate stays put, but your interest rate must rise by 1 point although your economy did not need it: Argentina in 1991–2001.
With capital controls you keep both, but only by blocking the free trade in your currency: China in 1996–2005.
Set the needed change equal to the foreign one: then the currency board costs nothing. The trilemma bites only when your economy needs a different policy from the anchor country.

def crisis_chart(countries=BOOK_CRISIS, base=1991, scale="linear"):
    """Fig. 20.8 for any countries: the dollar value of each currency, index = 100 at the end of the base year."""
    picked = fx_crisis[fx_crisis.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    start = picked[picked.year == base].set_index("country").per_usd_eop
    picked["index"] = 100 * picked.country.map(start) / picked.per_usd_eop
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    low = picked.sort_values("index").head(1)                    # the deepest fall among the chosen currencies
    title = f"No data at the end of {base} for these countries"
    if len(low) > 0:
        title = (f"Currencies vs the dollar ({base} = 100): lowest {low.country.iloc[0]}, "
                 f"{low['index'].iloc[0]:.3g} in {low.year.iloc[0]}")
    fig = px.line(picked, x="year", y="index", color="country", hover_name="country", markers=True,
                  color_discrete_map=CRISIS_COLORS, log_y=(scale == "ratio"), range_x=[1987.5, 2025.5],
                  title=title + missing_note(countries, start.index),
                  labels={"year": "Year", "index": f"Dollar value of the currency ({base} = 100)"})
    fig.add_vline(x=base, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    if scale == "linear":
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, max(120, 1.05 * picked["index"].max())] if len(picked) > 0 else [0, 120])
    elif len(picked) > 0:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ratio_ticks(picked["index"].min(), picked["index"].max()))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

    picked = yields_all[yields_all.country.isin(countries) & (yields_all.date >= "1995-01")]

        title = (f"10-year bond yields: highest since 2008 {peak.country.iloc[0]}, "
                 f"{peak['yield'].iloc[0]:.1f}% in {peak.date.iloc[0]}")
    top = max(14.5, picked["yield"].max() + 1.5) if len(picked) > 0 else 14.5
    bottom = min(-2.0, picked["yield"].min() - 0.5) if len(picked) > 0 else -2.0
    fig = px.line(picked, x="date", y="yield", color="country", hover_name="country", color_discrete_map=YIELD_COLORS,
                  title=title + missing_note(countries, picked.country.unique()), range_y=[bottom, top],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "yield": "10-year government bond yield (percent)"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    for date, text in [("1999-01", "euro"), ("2012-07", "Draghi")]:
        fig.add_vline(x=date, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
        fig.add_annotation(x=date, y=0.97, yref="paper", text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                           font=dict(color=GRAY))
    ticks = list(range(0, int(top), 2)) if top <= 20 else None
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", yaxis_tickvals=ticks, xaxis_range=["1992-07", "2027-01"])
    return fig

What to notice.

In 1995 Italy and Spain paid 4 to 6 points more than Germany. By the end of 1998 all three yields were close to 4 percent, and they moved together until 2008.
In 2011–2012 the Italian yield rose above 7 percent and the Spanish one to 6.8 percent, while Germany’s fell. After Mario Draghi promised in July 2012 that the ECB would do “whatever it takes”, the gaps closed again.
German yields were negative in mid-2016 and from April 2019 to January 2022: investors paid the German government to hold their money.
Add Greece, Portugal and Ireland, the three euro countries that needed rescue loans: Greece’s yield reached 29.2 percent in February 2012, Portugal’s 13.9 percent in January 2012 and Ireland’s 12.4 percent in July 2011.
Look at your data: the lines start and stop at different dates. Greece’s starts in mid-1997, Estonia’s only in 2020 (its government has almost no long-term debt), and Russia’s ends in 2018.


Key numbers: the spreads over Germany
The spread is the gap between a country’s yield and Germany’s. It measures how much more investors want to be paid to lend to that government.

BOOK_LENDING = ("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Italy", "Germany")
LENDING_YEARS = {1998: "1998", 2002: "2002", 2007: "2007", 2023: "2023 (latest)"}


def lending_chart(countries=BOOK_LENDING):
    """Fig. 20.10 for any countries: bank lending to the private sector, percent of GDP, in four years."""
    picked = credit_all[credit_all.country.isin(countries) & credit_all.year.isin(LENDING_YEARS)].copy()
    picked["credit"] = picked.bank_credit                                   # the textbook's series, to 2021
    latest = picked.year == 2023
    picked.loc[latest, "credit"] = picked.loc[latest, "private_credit"]     # all private credit in 2023
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["credit"])
    wide = picked.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="credit")
    title = "Bank lending in percent of GDP"
    if 1998 in wide.columns and 2007 in wide.columns and (wide[2007] - wide[1998]).notna().any():
        rise = (wide[2007] - wide[1998]).dropna()
        title = f"Bank lending, 1998–2007: largest rise {rise.idxmax()}, {round(rise.max()):+d} points of GDP"
    picked["year"] = picked.year.map(LENDING_YEARS)
    fig = px.bar(picked, x="country", y="credit", color="year", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8"],
                 title=title + missing_note(countries, wide.index),
                 category_orders={"country": book_order(countries, BOOK_LENDING), "year": list(LENDING_YEARS.values())},
                 labels={"country": "", "credit": "Domestic bank lending (percent of GDP)"})
    top = max(200, 1.05 * picked.credit.max()) if len(picked) > 0 else 200
    fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[0, top], legend_title_text="")

The IMF publishes the current account of almost every economy, year by year since 1980 (current_account_imf.csv). period_means turns the yearly numbers into the textbook’s period averages, for any countries.

Python note. groupby("country").ca_gdp.mean() averages the years of each country. rows.append({...}) collects one dictionary per country and period, and pd.DataFrame(rows) turns the list into a table.


ca_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "current_account_imf.csv")
CA_PERIODS = {"1993–1997": (1993, 1997), "2003–2007": (2003, 2007), "2008–2011": (2008, 2011),
              "2021–2025 (latest)": (2021, 2025)}


def period_means(countries):
    """The current account of each country averaged over each textbook period (one row per country and period)."""
    rows = []
    for label in CA_PERIODS:
        first, last = CA_PERIODS[label]
        span = ca_all[ca_all.country.isin(countries) & (ca_all.year >= first) & (ca_all.year <= last)]
        means = span.groupby("country").ca_gdp.mean()
        for country in means.index:
            rows.append({"country": country, "period": label, "balance": means[country]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["country", "period", "balance"])

Key numbers: the interest bill on a debt of 100 percent of GDP
A government with debt \(D\) must pay interest \(R \cdot D\) every year, so the interest bill in percent of GDP is the debt-GDP ratio times the interest rate. If investors fear a default and ask for a higher rate, the bill grows, which makes a default more likely: the crisis can be self-fulfilling.

def interest_bill(debt_ratio, R):
    """Yearly interest payments in percent of GDP: debt-GDP ratio (percent) times the interest rate (percent)."""
    return debt_ratio * R / 100

def ulc_chart(base=1995, countries=BOOK_ULC):
    """Fig. 20.13 for any countries: unit labor costs, each country's index = 100 in the base year."""

    title = f"No unit labor costs in {base} for these countries"
    if len(last) > 0:

    fig = px.line(picked, x="year", y="index", color="country", hover_name="country", color_discrete_map=ULC_COLORS,

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
text:
Concluding remarks

The nominal exchange rate is the price of a currency; the real exchange rate \(EP/P^w\) is the price of goods. In the long run the law of one price sets the real exchange rate to 1 and ties the nominal rate to relative price levels, so more inflation means a weaker currency.
The law of one price holds only loosely. Japan’s real exchange rate rose 2.5-fold until 1995, and Big Macs cost more in rich countries: nontraded goods get dearer as wages rise (the Balassa-Samuelson effect).
In the short run, prices are sticky and the exchange rate moves with interest rates. Net exports then react to the interest rate like investment, which makes the IS curve flatter, and a rise in foreign interest rates is a positive demand shock at home that ends in a recession when it is reversed.
The policy trilemma: an open economy can have at most two of a stable exchange rate, monetary autonomy and free capital flows. Gold, Bretton Woods, currency boards, capital controls and the euro are different choices of two, and the crises in Mexico, Asia, Argentina and the euro area show what happens when a choice breaks down.
The next chapter, Parting Thoughts, looks back at the whole book and at the open questions of macroeconomics.
